After nearly thirty:years of individual breeding, the Shropshire sheep husbandry assumed dimensions that entitled it to be broug.ht under a precise system for its own preservation and judicious development. With this object in view, the American Shropshire AsAociation was formed February sth, 1684. DAIRYING ON TIIE CoNTINENT.—The dairymen in Italy are improving their facilities and butter to such an ex- tent as to become formidable rivals to the Dutch in the export trade with India, China, and other Oriental cus- tomers. Italy has a much longer butter-producing sea- son than Denmark, and threatens to supply French markets with large quantities, thus forcing French and Danish butter upon the English buyers, reacting upon the American export trade in butter, which has already suffered considerably from European competition, the value having fallen for the ten months of this season to something like £530,836, against £681,559 for same time last year, and in quantity from 19,910,9571b5. in 1884-65 to 16,953,0471b5. in 1885-86. TROUBLESOME HORSES.—" V. A. L." writes :—When a horse or horses hug the carriage pole, a very simple re- medy is to take two brushes with short stumps of the rush-like material—the name of which I forget for the moment—which is used for making brooms and brushes. If these be cut down to half-inch lengths and strapped to the pole where the shoulders would touch it when the horses lean towards it, it will irritate them quite enough to prevent them repeating- this disagreeable habit many times. Short sharp tin tacks, with their points just issuing from a piece of thick leather, would be more suddenly effective, but unless care was taken that they were only just through the leather, they might tear the skin in the case of a horse stumbling or making a blun- der in turning a corner. I have many times seen a brush formed of short, stiff material, tied on the pole of a Lon- don omnibus, when a horse had a propensity to lean towards it in a disagreeable and dangerous way. KEEPING A HORSE.—A. W. G. says :—" I intend getting a pony about 13 hands high. 1. Please say how much it will cost per week to feed him. 2. Also the quantity of corn and hay he would consume per week. 3. About how much will I need to pay for a pony—a fairly good. looking one. 4. How often should he be comfied and brushed, and feet washed?" 1. The cost ought not to exceed 10s. to 12s. per week, depending of course on the kind of food and its market value at the time. 2. Two bushels of oats and about 2001bs. of hay, a few beans in place of the oats is a good addition; a bran mash to be given once or twice a week. 3. Depends entirely on kind, soundness, &c.—say £25 to £35. 4. To be thoroughly combed and brushed at least every morning, and also after having been out. It is a moot point whether wash- ing the feet is good practice or not; do it only when they are wet and muddy, and be sure they are thoroughly dried afterwards. It is the want of thoroughly drying which does harm. BRITISII DAIRY FARMERS' ASSOCIATION.—At the last meeting of the council of this association. Mr. E. C. Tis- dall in the chair, the report of the show committee was also presented. It recommended that the next dairy show be held on Oct. sth, 6th, 7th, and Bth; that the offer of the English Guernsey Cattle Society, to give a silver medal in each of the classes for bulls, cows, and heifers, for the best bred animal in England, and entered, or eligible for entry, in the herd book of the society, be accepted with thanks; that the classification suggested by the British Goat Society for goats be adopted, to- gether with their proposod prizes. biit that the associa- tion prizes be £2, £l, and 10s. in each class; and that the association adopt the code of prize colours suggested by Mr. Walter Gilbey, with a view to secure uniformity at different shows. The committee had revised the schedule of prizes for live stock, and partially for dairy produce, and it was proposed to present a full report at a subsequent meeting of the council. The committee had considered Professor Long's proposals with regard to a scholarship, and they recommended as follows "That a sum of £2O be offered by the British Dairy Farmers' Association to provide a scholarship to be com- peted for by dairy farmers, or persons intending to start upon the business of dairy farming or dairying. Candi- dates must not be less than 18 years of age. They will be subjected to a written and a viva race examination in butter-making at the society's rooms, 191, Fleet-street, E.C., on Thursday, May 13th, and a practical examina- tion at Mr. Tisdall's dairy, Kensington. The successful candidate will be required to devote at least two months to the acquisition of knowledge of butter-making in Normandy, and to keep a journal of his experience dur- ing the whole period of his scholarship, sending a copy of it weekly to the British Dairy Farmers' Association." Swonross UDDRR.—T. C. W. says:—" During this spring I have had two of my most valuable dairy cows taken with swollen udders a few days before calving. In the first case, which was a valuable Shorthorn cow, the milk went poor in all her quarters. She seemed heavy and stupid for a fortnight before due to calve, but ate her food as usual. After she had her calf this illness turned to her lungs, and though I promptly had my vet.'s ad- vice and treated accordingly, she died. The other has calved, and I think we shall get her through with the loss of one quarter of her udder, which is still very hard. Would some of your experienced readers or your vet. kindly tell me the probable cause of the attacks, and also whit treatment would be advisable in any future case?" It is not an uncommon occurrence for cows having a constitutional tendency to tuberculosis (con- sumption) to suffer with swelled udders from very slight exciting causes, such as an injury or chill to that organ; in fact, in well-bred animals an obstinate swelling of the udder is often one of the first indications of a scrofulous state of the system, and I think that " T.C.W.'s" cow (No. 1) was constitutionally diseased before the swelled udder was noticed, hence the reason why her lungs be- came affected, ending in death. Cow No. 2 may be a similar case. only in its earlier stages, or she may have suffered from an ordinary attack of garget, brought on by injury or cold, and I am inclined to think this was so, in whicli case the treatment for garget, as given in the Gazette a few weeks since, will be efficacious. When there are reasons to suspect a cow has a constitutional tendency to tuberculosis, she should be fed liberally, especially with oily foods, besides which she should be drenched with half *a pint of cod-liver oil and two drachms of bromide of potash, dissolved in water, two or three times a week; the local applications to the udder should be the same as in ordinary garget—viz., hot fomentations, followed by camphorated oil, well rubbed in, twice a day, and occasional smearings with extract of belladonna. He says that three founda- tion rules, which should form the basis of agricultural exhibitions are—(a) No unsound animal shall receive a premium prize under any circumstances; (b) no animal without a pedigree shall be eligible to competition; (C) all awards shall be made upon a schedule of points of merit by three competent judges, who shall make up their three several decisions without consultation with each other. The maximum number of points of excel- lence is fixed at a hundred, in accordance with the basis established at bench shows and poultry exhibitions, and by the American Jersey Cattle Club. So that no unfafr- ness may arise in the exhibition ring between the judges, it is proposed that each judge shall be furnished with a card, which shall correspond in number with evaesl7,:hhoowrsne in each class. Upon this is to be printed the highest number of points of excellence, which points, by the cards, will be distributed among the different parts of the carcass and extremities. The following are the rules suggested for governing the awards, each of which it is insisted upon should be followed implicitly: —,-(a) There shall be no consultation among the several judges; (5) they shall each mark upon their cards the ' highest number of points of excellence the several parts of each horse are entitled to, so as to ascertain the approximation of each horse to the standard of ex. cellence ; (c) these cards are to be given to the superin- tendent of the department, whose duty it shall be to ascertain which horse has received the highest average, and which the next highest average, which he shall thereupon publicly announce; upon said horses he shall confer the first and second premiums respectively; (d) these cards, each to be signed by the judge filling the same, shall be delivered to the secretary, who shall pre- serve the same and properly enter the awards in a book prepared for that purpose for future reference. A MODERN OBERON.

, -Charge! And with lily-lance well held in rest A child came speeding o'er the shaven grass. . The linnets whispering in their leafy nest, Sang him their sweetest as they heard him pass; Then watched with jewel-eyes th' unequal fray : 'Twixt boy and roses, as with shouts of glee He stormed the crimson banners spray on spray, And waved his lily-lance in victory. The August sunshine through the sheltering boughs ; Came pouring in a long continuous stream Of molten glory, and athwart his brows ; It cast an aureole, whose flickering gleam 1-- Awoke the beauty in the childish eyes, ; As, resting with his lilies in his hand, —A very Oberon in modern guise— He stood the conqueror of Fairyland! Then homeward in a stately, martial way, The rebel-roses at his careless feet, He marched triumphant, and an amorous ray Of golden sunshine, that had found him sweet And brave and king-like in his recent fight, Crept softly upward to the dimpled breast And lay there lovingly, as bathed in light, He passed contented to his noonday rest. lb.-London Society for April. SPRING.
'Hark! the sound of music rare

Fills the tranquil morning air! By the zephyrs borne along Comes the echo of the song: "Hasten, Spring, sweet season, hasten! Come and cheer the haunts of men, With thy soul-inspiring presence Making earth look bright again! Long have Winter's bonds enthralled us, Long held fast and firm the earth; Come, break through the chains which held us, Fill the land with joy and mirth. When upon the fleeting Old Year . (Which nor hand nor voice could stay) Followed close the blithesome NPvi' Year Young and merry, bright and gay, Janus, heaven's warder, open Wide the gates of heaven threw, And, with swift and fawn-like footsteps, Entered in the yearling new. Once again we praise thee, Janus, Ope those gates celestial wide, And admit the merry Spring-time, Meet to be a New Year's bride." 'IL. The singers cease, and all is still; The echoes die on vale and hill; .. But, lovely as the blushing morn, Born by Zephyru.s along, Sweet verdant Spring approaches earth • Responsive to the song. Where'er she steps the flowers spring up • As if by magic power; The land once more in beauty smiles, ; • In its awakening hour. ,The lark, Spring's certain harbinger, . Soars through the azure sky,

sation.i Never assume a patronising, air to those of inferior position. Every man thinks he can edit a paper and poke a fire better than anybody else in this world. There are one hundred wais of dooing a thing—one write and ninety-nine ron,.-0. E. PoTrs. Self-respect and respeot.for others are indicated by the manner and deportment of man and woman. It is folly for an eminent man to think of escaping censure, and a weakness to be affected with it. It is a common error, of which a wise man will be- ware, to measure the worth of our neighbour by his con- duct towards ourselves. SMOKING HIM.—" You look", said an Irishman to a pale, haggard smoker, "as if you had come out of your grave to light your cigar and couldn't find your way back

again:" - Be polite to your own and other people's servants. Haughtiness towards them will not increase their respect for you. Do not forget the usual courtesy on receiving anything you may have requested. This may be done without giving room for the slightest liberty. The testimony of a woman before a Salt Lake court the other day in a polygamy case was in substance that "she didn't know whether her husband had another wife or not; it wasn't of sufficient importance to talk about." It is a fact to be recognised by all !just persons, that the strong traits of our common human nature dominate the world, If this be true (and it is) it becomes equally clear that in the breeding of better human nature lies the sole hope of our future improvement." IfTrusxxo THE BABY.--A paper published in Dundee gives a novel glimpse into the ways of tramps. There Is one in the neighbourhood, it seems, who, with his wife and family, haVe been "living on the baby" for the last three weeks. They have not slain and eaten it. That would be killing the goose that lays the golden 'eggs. This is what they do, in the words of the father :—" We " gets 'im christened at all the towns we passes, and Just then, you see, parson makes us all comfortable with summat to eat and money for beds. On days awful bad we had to do .'im twice." This is the exception to the a rule that the "unemployed "re in sorest distress when they are parents. But it is not every tramp who fle- ,serves, so thoroughly as this one, to have a baby.

This scheme of reform seems extremely plausible, and is certainly worthy of trial in this country. At any rate the reasons for an award would be easily ascertained, and the prize animals would become more instructive in consequence.

div.head: MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.
div.p: THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.

THE ORIGIN OF THE DOMESTIC FOWL. 7tfl'hough considerable attention has been given to the study of the question as to the origin of the domestic fowl, we appear as far from a settlement thereof as ever. Naturalists are agreed so far, but beyond that there are differences which they are unable to agree upon. For a time, the opinion of the late Professor Darwin, that our domestic fowls are derived :from one stock, the Gallus Bankiva, or wild fowl of India, found almost general acceptance; but more recently, doubts have been thrown upon this view. The question is therefore still in a state of uncertainty, and in the absence of clearer information than we have yet been able to obtain, it is likely to re- main so. There is one thing, however, certain, namely, that the majority of our breeds of fowls are derived from the wild fowl named above, and also that all our breeds owe their origin to Eastern and Southern Asia. Naturalists recognise four members of the genus Gallus. These are as follow :—The Gallus Sonneratii, which is found in the more southern districts of India. At one time it was thought to be the parent of our do- mestic breeds, but students have noted in it such marked differences, and the fowl does not exhibit, so far as has yet been seen, any of its peculiarities, that there is now no one who gives it this position; second, the Gallus ,Stanleyii, which is only found in the island of Ceylon. With the exception of the colour of the comb, this genus resembles the domestic fowl so very closely that some naturalists were at one time inclined to regard it as the parent species. It has, however, a singularly different voice, and as this has never been known to be found in our fowls this cannot be accepted. Third, the Gallus Furcatus. This variety inhabits Java, and the islands eastward as far as Flores, but it is so different in many characteristics that no one regards it as the parent of any of our races of domestic poultry. It has green plumage an unserrated comb, and a single Median wat- tle. With respect to the latter point, Mr. Lewis Wright in his "Book of Poultry" tells of a light Brahma hen which showed this peculiar characteristic :—" There is not a vestige of the ordinary wattles at the side of the base of the lower mandible, but instead thereof an im- mense single wattle hanging in the true meridian line, giving the whole head a most peculiar expression, which is added to by the shapeless character of the comb." He also states that Mr. Wragg, of Stoke Park, Ipswich, one 1 of the most experienced breeders of Asiatic fowls in England, has had at various times birds with single wattles. Mr. Wright points out another resemblance between the Gallus Furcatis, namely, the forked tail, a most prominent feature of the Brahma; and fourth, the Gallus Bankiva. Of this variety Darwin says it "has a much wider geographical range than the three previous species; it inhabits Northern India as far west as Scinde, and ascends the Himalaya to a height of 4,000 ft. ; it inhabits Burmah, tlse Malay Peninsula, the Indo-Chinese countries, the Philippine Islands, and the Malayan Archipelago as far eastward as Timor. This species varies considerably in the wild state. Mr. Blyth informs me that the speci- mens, both male and female, brought from near the Himalaya, are rather paler coloured than those brought from other parts of India; whilst those from the Malay peninsula and Java are brighter coloured than the Indian birds. . . . The wild Gallus Bankiva agrees most closely with the black-breasted red game breed, in colour- ing and in all other respects, except in being smaller and in the tail being carried more horizontally; but the man- ner in which 'the tail is carried is highly variable in many of our breeds. . . . It is a significant fact that the voice of both male and female Gallus Bankiva closely resembles, as Mr. Blyth and others have noted, the voice of both sexes of the common domestic fowl, but the last note of the crow of the wild bird is rather less pro- longed. Captain Hutton, well known for his researches into the natural history of India, informs me that he has seen several crossed fowls from the wild species and the Chinese Bantam; these crossed fowls breed freely with Bantams, but unfortunately were not crossed inter se. Captain Hutton reared chickens from the eggs of the Gallus Bankiva; and these, at first very wild, afterwards became so tame that they would crowd round his feet. He did not succeed in rearing them to maturity, but, as he remarks, "no wild gallinaceous bird thrives well at first on hard grain." Mr. Blyth also found much diffi- culty in keeping Gallus Bankiva in confinement. In the Philippine Islands, however, the natives succeed much better, as they keep wild cocks to fight with their do- mestic Game birds. Sir Walter Elliot informs me that tho hon of a, native domestic breed of Pegu is undis- tinguishable from the hen of tho wild csallus Bankiva, and the natives constantly catch wild cocks by taking tame cocks to fight with them in the woods. Mr. Craw- ford remarks that from etymology it might be argued that the fowl was first domesticated by the Malays and Javanese. It is also a curious fact that wild specimens of the Gallus Bankiva, brought from the countries east of the Bay of Bengal, are far more easily tamed than those of India; nor is this an unparalleled fact, for, as Humbolt long ago remarked, the same species sometimes evinces a more tameable disposition in one country than in another. If we suppose that the Gallus Bankiva was first tamed in Malaya and afterwards imported into India, we can understand an observation made to me by Mr. Blyth, that the domestic fowls of India do not re- semble the wild Gallus Bankiva of India more closely. than do those of Europe.' • We have given at length these particulars respecting Gallus Bankiva, for, whether the opinion that all our domestic breeds do not owe their origin to this genus ever becomes an established theory or not, it is certain that the great majority of our varieties are its descen- dants, and, therefore, it claims from us the greatest share of attention. That which has brought doubts into the minds of students has been the habits of the heavy feather-legged races from China—Brahmas and Cochins —which are altogether different to most other breeds of poultry. It is true that poultry breeders have held this opinion always, but their ideas have been disregarded by naturalists as unscientific. The differences of habit were described in the Field newspaper by a swriter as follow :—" After a year or two of preliminary 'examina- tion (this refers to 30 years ago, when Cochins were first introduced), I adopted tbis method of managing the Cochin Chinas: As soon as a brood was as big as thrushes it was taken with its nurse and put into one of the fields. The hen was cooped until she was settled to her range, after which the coop was removed, and an ordinary tea chest, laid upon its side, was put in its place, an old door or some loose boards being leaned over its mouth. When the birds got as big as partridges even this shelter was removed; for it was noticed that, unlike other poultry, which in similar circumstances seek the hedge- rows and trees for shelter, the Cochin Chinas preferred to jug,' as partridges do, in the middle of the fields. This habit is in itself quite unlike that of any other variety of poultry, all of which are, when free to choose, arboreal in their habits. The next distinction was seen when the pullets began to lay. If there were any coop accessible which had been used for a lodging, they would deposit their very abnormally-coloured eggs therein; but if there was not, the descendants of some imported birds ' never sought for a place of shelter under a bush or some hidden spot as other poultry do, but always chose some heap of mould or small elevation, and laid on the top of this, quite indifferent to the eggs being exposed to sight, so that they were above the ordinary level of the land. This peculiarity is strongly marked. "From these idiosyncracies I have inferred that this variety of fowl could not be descended from the tree- roosting, bush-haunting ancestor of the game cock, &c. . . . All the indications, slight, perhaps, in themselves, yet not without weight when taken together, go to show that the ancestors of the Shanghai must have been found by the humans' who annexed them in quarters unlike an Indian jungle, i.e., in some dry desert with scant vegetation, and watered—when watered at all—by rivers fed at a distance •by melted snow, which came down in force when the birds were sitting on eggs.' The extreme stupidity of the Shanghai proves it could have had, in its native habitat, few enemies to contend against, as does its readiness to accept the protection of man. . . When both were free to range at will, the game fowl always 'cut' the Cochin most persistently; and for the most part the game cock, when at liberty, will refuse to accept the advances of the widowed Shanghai hen. He will generally drive her away."

PADDY Mc SPLINTER AS KING OF , 4 ri,; ; IRELAND. BY PADDY HIMSELF. Ye mast know, dear friends, that me name is Paddy Mc. Splinter, th' son iv as dacint a man as iver crack't th' skull iv an Irishman at th' fair iv: Ballycum-Smahum, County Tipperary. Och ! an' sure it's motel that reminibers th' day when I fur-rst saw th' be-u-tiful light o' day. Sure, easn't it th' day iv the grate storm in Ireland when the wind blew so mighty fierce that it tuk—th' divil a lie I'm tellin'—th' roof iv our cabin clans off, an' carried it fall half a mile away, dhroppin' at last upon th' top iv a cabin where. so I was towld afther, that had a tnnderin' big hole In It, an' which our runaway roof jist covered. No wondher, thin, that I have sich a long remimbrance iv th' day on which I was born! It's not th' lasts iv ma intin- tion to tell yez all about me any life beyond this, that th' rayson we left owid Ireland was owin' to a wakeness me father—th' Hiving be his bed this blessed day!—iv not payia' his debts when due—nor either, for th' matter e' that. Th' agint kern down several times for th' rint, but all in vain; an' so at th' lag th' agint towld him that if he—me father, not th' agint, ye mind—didn't pay his rint mighty soon he would be compelled to chew me father th' enthrance out iv his farm. Well, th' beginnin' iv th' end was that we wor all turned out iv our home, pig, cocks, hens, an' ivery mortal thing, one cowld winter's mor- nin'. Me father an' mother, an'th' childer, meself among th' number kern over to Englasd,an'here we have stayed until now, wid th' exception iv me parents, who died from shortness o' breath a couple iv years ago—God bless thim ! Havin' towld yez so mach iv me history, I will now tell yez why I've taken th' liberty iv redhresain' yea upon the question of Home Rule. Sure, whin I think iv th' wrongs iv Ireland I feel all .th' blood iv th' Mc.Splinters rnshin' through me body—a feelin' that makes me wish that I cud , lay down me life in her defince, an' scatther th' blood iv her innimles far an' wide--faix I do! Sure, Ivory wan knows Of wrongs iv Ireland have been cryin' out for redhression for ages, without much attintion bein' paid to thim ; but now, I'm proud to say, th' overflowin' pot has been filled at last, an' justice will have to be given to th' owld counthry. One night I had kern home fram me wark wid me mind filled wid th' thoughts iv Ireland ; amongst others what a grand patriot Parnell must be to persuade me aufferin' connthrymin bow much betther it was to give him their money than to kape it for thimselves an' their starvin' families—when all at wanst I foend meself transported fram Holyhead to Dublin. Everywan seemed to know me, an' everywan wor askin' to shake bands wid me—an' for why, think ye ?—because Home Rule had bin given to Ireland at last, an' I, Patrick Mc.Splinter, th' ancestor—l mane , th' descendent if th' Mc.Splinter, wan iv th' ancient Irish warriors who got his title iv "Splinter" through th' cliver way in which he exthracted a thanderin' big splinther out iv th' foot iv th' Prince he was , sarvin' undher at th' time—was to be th' King iv Ireland! Bands war playin' an' banners flyin', while now an' thin a mighty shout would be given—" Long live Patrick Mc. Splinter, King iv Ireland!" Parnell kern up to me, but inatid o' th' caed mule fadthe (hundred thousand welcomes), I expected fram him, he gev a scowl, an' said, "Ye think ye have got th' whole iv th' .counthry wid ye, Patrick, but yell find yerself mistaken, see if ye don't, now." "An' for why, Mr. Parnell? " I axt him. "Well, for wan thing," said he, "yez'll take th' livin' out iv me an' me party's mouths if ye mak th' counthry prosperous, as ye say ye mane to do." "Well," said I, surprised, I can tell ye, at th' way he wor spakin', "Isn't th' prosperity iv th' connthry what yez have bin agitatin' for all these years ? " "Maybe, it is, an' maybe it isn't," was me gentleman's mysterious reply. "But," he wint on, "I can tell ye wan thing, Patrick, unless yez do all me friends want, yez'll get no money fram over th' wather." Wid that partin shot Parnell left me. I began to see that me path wud not be. altogither strewn wid roses—more like wid blackthorns an' bul- lets. But I had med up me mind to do th' best I cud for Ireland, aven though they shot me life out o' me, still wud I go on strivin' to advance th' intherests if th land o' my birth. Och ! but it was a glorious day, I can tell you; the crowd o' paple in Dublin bein' somethin rayley wondherful ! Parlymint House in Collidge Green was hung. out wid banners iv all kinds, while th' bands that tunin' up filled th' air wid lovely strains iv music. Well, to make a long story short, I was crowned King iv Ireland, wid a goolden crown upon my hid. Parnelll med me Prime Minister, an' though he didn't look as plazed as he might ha' done, he made th' best o' sarcurnstances, an' wish me ji in that cowld-blooded way he has o' spa.kin'. Sure, I thought whin I had settled Mr. Parnell so comfortably, I'd ha' ne'er a difficulty to rule th' whole iv Ireland; but bedad, I soon found meeelf mistaken. I hadn't been long King whin th' mimbers o' me Parlymint began to gie me throuble. One mimber fram th' "black north' had th' impidince to ax th' Prime Minister how much money had been resaved by him out iv th' National Lague Funds. Up jumped Mr. Healey, who, prodacin' a shelalagh fram his pocket, threatened to test th' stringth iv th'" honourable mimber's" skull iv he dared to ax sich a question agin. Mr. Biggar seconded Mr. Healey's threat, an'so yez needn't be supprised whin I tell yez that a free fight all round ink place, a clans sweep bein' made iv moat iv th' chairs about th' place. Th' maythin' (meeting) was adjourned in order to enable th' mimbers to buy stickin' plasther for their faces! Th' next maim' that tuck place Mr. O'Brien said he'd like to bring in a bill for th' " Abolition iv Landlordism in Ireland." Boded, yen should ha' seen th' look Parnell goy whin wan mimber in an ennicint sooart iv a way, wanted for to know if th' Bill included th' Prime Ministher ? Parnell jumped up, an' said th' cloture ud be dhropped npen th' hid iv th' lasht spaker if he wasn't careful what he said. Human nature is human nature as ye know, an' sure it wasn't likely that Parnell, either havin' his fine property down in Wicklow cleared iv debt, taken fram him, an' divided amongst his friends—not at all. Well, what betune th' minabera flyin' so to peke, at each other's throat, an' th' throuble I had to kape th' pace, I began to wish I'd stopped at home in England; but as I'd taken upon mesel to govern Ireland, there was no help for it to but to do th' hist I could, an' betther if I knew how. Bat no sooner had I got things in what I thought fair workin' ordher, thin I found to me sorrow that I'd mod a mistake in my calkilations. Wan day Parnell kern to me, his face as troubled lookia' as if his fortin had been taken tram him. "What's th' matther now, Parnell, me boy ?" seri I. "I've come to give ye my resignation," says he, at th' same time throwin' down forninst me a rowl o paper. "What for, me boy?" "Sure, yet majesty," says he, "things is too quiet for me enthirely, an' not only that, th' boys fram th' wather lint me word that if we don't keep up th' agitation, so as to compel England to make us a prisint iv Ireland altogithar, they'll came over in a body and tear th' whole iv us to smithereens." "Is that th' game ?" Buys I; and sure It's no lie I'm tellin' whin I say that I began to wish mesel a thousand miles away from where I stood. Just as we were spakin , in tubed th' whole iv th' Irish mimbers, yellin' an' shoutia' "Down wid Paddy MaSplinter !"—" Down with Paddy MaSplinter—he's takin' th' brid (bread) out iv our mouth& by his slow-goin' ways!" So sayia', th' rascals med a dash at me, an' though I med a few black eyes wid me shelalagh iv a sceptre, I was no match for the whole iv thins. Down I was nulled tram me throne, and Parnell was fetchin' me a thunderin' blow upon me hid whin—l wakened, an' found mesel safe an' sound in me arm-chair be th' fireside. I was some minus afore I could persuade mesa it was only a dhrame I'd bin either harm'; but yez may be sure that whin I found it was rayely so, there wasn't a more thankful man than yen humble sarvint, Paddy Mc.Splinter, that I was where I was, safe an' sound !—From Ben Brierley' e Journal.

A HORRIBLB TALB or THE S&L—The ghastly details of the Mignonette tragedy—doubtless still fresh in public recollection—have just been paralleled on an American fish- ing vessel. Four fishermen were cast adrift in a dory, off the western fishing banks, and the horrible sequel was far- nished many days afterwards by the craft reaching one of the wharves, containing only two emaciated men and the partially-devoured corpses of their companions. The party when cast adrift were absolutely without provisions and water. On the fourth day one of the number succumbed to cold and hunger, and the day afterwards one of his com- panions cut his throat and drank some of his blood, the others following his example. A second man eventually became a victim to starvation and exposure, and the ghou- lish feast his comrade had furnished was again partaken of. The one redeeming feature of the gruesome story is that the end of both men was the natural result of their hardships and privation. THE IRISH LAND The Purchase Act, in tined by Premiel Pricey night, has just been issued to mem bers of 4rliament. It is in five parts and oomprises 53 clauses, and the backers are Mr. Gladstone, Mr. Childers, Mr. John Morley, and Sir Chas. Russell. The first part deals with with the sale of estates, the second ptovides for the constitution of the Land Commission, the third is occupied with the financial arrangements, the fourth part contains supplementary provisions dealing with the registry of title and conditions annexed to holdings while subject 1 to an annuity, and the fifth part defines the various terms used in the Act. Clause 2, which deals with the sale of estates, sets forth that "On and after the appointed and within the time limited by this Act the immediate landlord of any tenanted estate in Ireland to which this Act applies may apply to the State authority to buy such tenanted estate at the statutory price, and the State authority shall cause his application to be registered, and the applications so made shall be dealt with according to priority of time. In the event of the purchase of the estate from the land- lord being completed, the tenants of the several holdings of which such estate consists shall, except as in this Act mentioned, become as soon as may be in manner in this Act mentioned the owners in fee simple of their holdings for such consideration as in this Act mentioned, and where the tenants do not become the owners of their holdings under this Act the State authority shall become the owner thereof, and dispose of the same in such manner as the State authority may think fit.' The statutory price of an estate according to clause 3, shall be "measured by the amount of the net rent of the estate. The net rent of an estate equals the gross rent of the estate after deducting from that rent the tithe rent charge, if any, payable to the Land Commission, and the average percentage for expenses in respect of bad debts, rates, or cess allowed or paid by the landlord, management, repairs, and other like outgoings, if any. Tithe rent charge shall be ascertained by the books of the Land Commission, and the average percentage for such expenses as aforesaid shall be ascertained, in the case of each estate, by taking the average percentage on the rent for the time being of such estate toi which such expenses have amounted, during each of the ten years immediately preceding the last gale day in the year 1885, as ascertaired by inspection of the rent rolls and books of the estate,and by other evidence if necessary." Clause 4 stipulates that the "amount of the statutory price of an estate shall, except as in this Act mentioned, be equal to 20 times the rent roll of the estate ascertained as aforesaid, and such price shall, subject to such option on the part of the person entitled to receive the same of taking other annuities or debentures as in this Act men- tioned, to be paid by Three per Cent. Perpetual Annui- ties, issued under this Act at par. There shall be added to the statutory price of an estate a sum equal to the amout of any such arrears of rent coming due after the last gale day in the year 1885, and before the date of purchase, as the Land Commission may certify that the landlord has duly endeavoured, but has been unable to collect, and such sum shall, subject to the said option, be paid in permanent annuities to the person entitled to such arrears ci rent."
Irish r last P-
Land

The consideration payable by a tenant for his acquisi- tion of the fee simple of his holding, according to Clause 5, shall be the payment to the State authority of a capital sum equal to twenty times the amount of the gross rent of the holding, and such sum may either be paid down in whole or in part, or may be paid by an annuity during a period of 49 years, equal to four per cent. per annum on such capital sum, or so much thereof as is not so paid down, but such annuity may be at any time redeemed as in this Act mentioned. Provided that where the landlordis legally liable to pay for any repairs or pay any county cess, or the whole of a poor rate in respect of a holding, the average annual amount of such poor rate during the ten years next preceding the last gale day in the year 1885 shall be deducted from the gross rent of the holding in calculating the consideration payable by a tenant in pursuance of this section. Other important clauses provide that applications by an immediate landlord should be referred to the Land Commission, who would decide on the validity of the claim and fix the price. The Land Commission would also distribute the purchase money, meeting all charges and encumbrances. All landlords" rights would be dealt with. in a manner to be afterwards settled, and all ten- ants' rights would be secured before the State authority consented to purchase the estate. The important clause referring to the issue of annuities required for the pur- poses of the Act is the 29th. It provides that bank annuities for the purpose of the purchase ?of :estates under this Act shall be issued, provided that their nomi- nal capital amount shall not exceed £10,000,000 in respect of applications for purchase received from landlords during the financial year ending on March 31 after the appointed day, and £20,000,000 in•each of the next two financial years, the aggregate capital not to exceed £50,000,000, and not more than £20,000,000 to be issued in any one financial year.

div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

CHLERY.—Some of the early batches of this should be now ready for pricking out of the seed quarters into a frame or boxes, and the latter will need the protection of a frame or greenhouse. Pricked in boxes, they require more attention as to watering; consequently these con- trivances are only used when it may be desirable to occupy but a small portion of the frame, and that only till the plants are established and the weather admits of their being turned out under the shelter of a wall or fence. At this time of the year, and more especially as the weather is now, we like to supply the plants when pricked out with gentle bottom heat, provided by placing a frame on any kind of fermenting material. To prevent drawing the plants should be close up to the glass, and in order to insure this the interior of the frame should be filled, within six inches of the top, with similar mate- rial to that which forms the bed, and on that 2in. of de- cayed manure, which should be covered over with another 2in. of rich, friable soil; and, if not moderately fine, pass some through a i-inch riddle, and cover the surface with it. This fine soil will fill round the roots and facilitate the operation of pricking. Insert the plants so that the lower leaves will be touching the soil, or they will not be able to stand upright. Water will be required as soon as the work is completed, and it should pass through a fine spreader for a time or two, or plants will be knocked down and the soil disturbed. The light should be placed on at once, but they should be kept close and shaded should a hot sunny day or two follow. The plants must be about 3in. distant each way, ori,hy the time they have filled the space the trenches should be ready to receive them. SnaLLoTs.—The planting of these, like that of many other classes, has been delayed in consequence of the dampness of the soil, and it was only at the end of last week that we managed to get them in. On wet, heavy soils the shallots should be planted on raised beds about four inches above the ground, in rows about 9in. distant, and 6in. between the sets in the row. If the soil has been well manured for a previous crop, it is preferable to that which has had fresh manure during the present year, as in the latter the bulbs are apt to decay. The bulbs will occasionally push themselves out of the soil, and last year we had to cover ours over with about 3m. of short manure till sufficient roots had been formed to secure them to the soil.

THE FRONT GARDEN.—ROSO pruning may be pro- ceeded with in all localities now. Tea roses only require the weak and inferior wood removed, and some ot the , longest growths made last year might have one-fourth of their length cut off, as it must be noted that these produce the best flowers. This section is rather too tender for most localities in Lancashire, but we learn that the Rev. C. H. Wood, of this town, grows them suc- cessfully in his garden near Bamber Bridge. Moss roses should be pruned similarly ta the teas, and not reduced to stumps, as has been the practice of many. growers. At the same time, overcrowding must be avoided, and severe thinning must annually take place; and a tree that has made, say, half-a-dozen healthy young shoots last year must have the same number of inferior ones removed, and at no time should there be any growth older than three years. All long shoots should bo pegged within a few inches of the soil. Some will be so obstinate that they will require coaxing to get them within a foot. More especially is this the case with hybrid perpetuals, which may be pruned and treated like the above when grown as dwarfs. Since we advocated this method et i culture in this column many have followed our advice, and we have reason to believe are perfectly satisfied with the results, as they assuredly should be when they get a dozen roses for one which they got under the close prun- ing system. With standard roses we have no choice but to cut the past year's growth within three or four eyes of the base. TRH WINDOW.—One of the obstacles in the way of cultivating plants successfully in rooms is the accinnu- lation of dust on the foliage, which impedes the due per- formance of the functions of respiration and perspira- tion, and when the periodical dusting takes place every- thine, receives attention but the plants. Smooth leaved plants might be kept clean by sponging, and those with woolly or hairy surface should be set out of doors and the dust removed with a pair of bellows. At this season of the year all would be benefited if set out during showery weather, but some provision should be made to prevent them from being blown on their sides which would most likely destroy the pots as well as damage the

div.p: LECTURE ON PUDDLING BY MR. T. MORRIS.

--- On Monday evening week, Mr. T. Morris, F.G.S., of Dallam and Bewsey Forges, Warrington, delivered a lecture before the Polytechnic Society, Royal Insti- tution, Liverpool, on "Paddling and the Puddling Furnace, and the influence of oxygen during and after the process." The lecture was illustrated by diagrams, tables of chemical analyses, and a large number of specimens of iron, slag, and puddled bars. Puddling, the lecturer explained, is the process by which pig or cast iron is converted into malleable or puddled iron, and this cannot be done without mechanical applications and chemical changes of a most intricate nature. Puddling is the most trying and laborious work for the toilers, and the most in- teresting to the metallurgist and the analytical chemist, in all the iron industry. So long as this ' work is done in the present slipshod way, we can never come in sight of perfection ; but what is re- quired is that every manager of a puddling furnace should hold certificates f examination in metallurgy and inorganic chemistry, so that he would under- stand the nature of the metals and the fuels he works With. A puddling furnace to-day consists of two chambers. one called a "grate," the other the "hearth" or working chamber. The bottom of the working chamber is covered with "fettling." com- posed of metallic cinders, covered with a sort of stiff , paste to give it a smooth surface. On this is placed a layer of slag and iron scales, two or three inches thick. The fuel is then placed in the "grate," and the furnace heated and the slag melted. The furnace is then allowed to cool, so that the cinders may form a plate over the iron floor,-and cover it up entirely. By this time the furnace is ready for the "first charge," and about 160 to 180 pounds of "hammer slag" is placed in it, and 10 to 16 pounds of iron scales and about 500 pounds of pig iron. When this is in, and the fire in the grate going, every crevice is stopped up, and the ° melting process begins. In about 15 minutes the top part of the iron becomes fused, and the assistant puddler inserts a long bar through a small hole in the door, and rakes the surface off, so as to allow the heat to reach the lower part. In 35 minutes the iron will lie on the hearth in a sheet of liquid metal, covered with the melted slag. The molten mass is stirred (puddled) with a long iron "rabble," and in a few minutes the elements seek their affinities, for now all are free. The carbon of the iron combines with the oxygen of the slag, or silicates, and as the carbOn is given off the atoms of the iron expand until the specific gravity of the iron is no greater than that of the slagg, the whole mass having a thickness four or five time greater than when first melted. Now the blue frame of the carbonic oxide is given off, and the master puddler watches the white fiery mass through a little hole in the door of the furnace, while he stirs it all the time with a long bar, so that every atom of Iron shall get its n‘ledful share of the life-giving oxy- gen. The iron is decarbonised and assumes a spongy appearance, rising from amidst the now heavier silicates like an iceberg from a white sea. The p.ttd- dler gathers this spongy mass into balls of convenient size to carry to the hammer, and works out a :wonder- ful chemical process, all ignorant, most likely, of what is going on. The slightest carelessness on the part of the puddler in allowing the air to reach his gleaming metal will make the iron " coldshort," or I a " hotahort," to be cursed by the blacksmith when it comes to him in future day!. Here comes the critical part of the work on which will depend the strength of chains and girders, the • toughness of a great steamer's propeller, or the. strength of an iron bar, to which is committed the life and limb of multi- tudes in remote places. Two pieces of puddled bar were shown, both obtained from the same charge; but one was rolled from the first ball, which had been rightly puddled; it was tough, strong, and bright as a new shilling, bearing the most extraordinary strain in the torsion test. The other was rolled from a second ball, which the oxygen of the atmosphere had been purposely allowed .to reach. This one was a miserable scorbutic-lookthg piece of metal, unfit for use in any place where. life, limb, or capital were at stake: yet the only difference between the two was that one was.allowed to remain were it could get a little of the. air the puddler was breathing, and thus ' became afflicted with the dreadful disease of rotten- ness. The imperfection in iron rails has been hitherto put down to chemical defects in the metal, such as too much sulphur or phosphorus, but, on analysing the broken shafts or broken bars, these ele- ments never seemed to preponderate at the fracture. Too oft, the trouble is caused by the presence of oxygen in the puddled iron, and this will arise from carelessness on the part of the puddler, and not from any chemical defect in the pig iron. To obviate all the diffi- culties involved in puddling, there has been no end of sehemts floated, with great flourish of trumpets, but each one has come to an early and untimely end, and the puddling process of fifty years ago is the process of to-day. Hundreds of thousands of pounds have been invested in the attempt to disestablish the poor puddler, but even after the invention of the Bessemer process of steel-making, and after all the other processes which have come into the world of late years, the puddler still lives, and there is as much puddled iron turned out now as ever there was. The only improvement that has really come to the puddler's lot during the century was the invention of the Nasmyth steam hammer; but the human hand is still master of the business of converting an immoral pig into a malleable bar. The trouble with puddling is caused by atmospheric oxygen, anfi. machines have not been invented yet to guard it. This oxygen forms nearly one-third of the earth's crust, a fourth of the atmosphere, and eight-ninths of the water surround- ing the globe; and nowhere is its influence more greatly felt, for good or evil, than in the puddling process. Themore thoroughly the effects of oxygen are studied—both theoretically and practically—the better will it be for both employers and employed. The time that has been spent in grumbling over depression must now be spent in improving our methods and our products, and if we do thie, our lost laurels will be , regained, and fresh ones won; and so long as Eng- ; 1 tnd has a lump of ironstone, a piece of limestone, and a cob of coal, she will command the respect of all the buyers and users of iron in the world.—An ani- mated discussion followed, and the full weight of Mr. Morris's lecture was admitted by all.—A vote o- thanks to the lecturer closed the proceedings.

The French Minister has made certain proposals Wnich have been favourably received by the Hellenic Go- Vernment. ATHENS, MoNDay.—The ultimatum was delivered to the Greek Government this evening. The document, which is !gfled by all the Powers except France, calls upon Greece to give assurance that orders for disarmament will be issued Within a week. It further contains a clause stating that mild France ultimately join the other Powers the fact will ~•,"e communicated to Greece in a separate note by the French Government. It is stated on the best authority that Italy a term of 48 hours within which the orders for disarmament were to be issued, but that this condition was reerded by the other Powers as too peremptory. v 'ENNA, TIIESDAY.—It is asserted here in political circles that France, having failed in her enokeavour to .settle the reek difficulty by friendly mediation, intends to propose a conference of European Powers, with a view of obtaining territorial compensation for the Greeks. Anmes, WEDNESDAY.—The Government has telegraphed ti the Greek representatives abroad that the assurances Riven to France should be considered sufficient by the .ewers• It is expected that unless the ultimatum be with. a Ministry will resign. _A large meeting was held last night at the Town Hall. at ch resolutions were passed strongly protesting against gc foreign pressure put upon Greece. SIR RICHARD CRi)§B 'AT FABLES- TO wzi. - The Conservatives of the Newton Division of South West Lancashire held a demonstration in the Viaduct Institute, tarlestown, on Thursday night. There was a crowded attendance, and the proceedings were of an enthusiastic Character. The chair was occupied by Mr. M. B. Westhead, chairraan of the division, and there were also present, in addition to Sir Richard A. Cross, M.P., Lord Gerard/ Messrs. R. Houghton, J.P., W. F. Gooch, J.P., J. Pearson, H. Arnott (Golbernel, T. D. Grimke, B. B. Glover, ve.pmiingfoio.r. (Itoby Hall), Dr. Mackie (Warrington), W. Valiant (Ashton), Rev. G. Carson (Liverpool), Rev. T. 11- Matthews (Earlestown),4o. The Chairman said numerous letters bad been received ,aDologising for non-attendance, including One from Sir A. B. Walker, T. C. Moss. M.P. for Widnes division' T. B. '4°Yden, M.P. (Liverpool), Arc. He remarked that Sir Richard Cross had availed Limself of the first opportunity. ot coming amongst them to thank them personally for that Which he considered so high an. honour by their election of that gentleman as their representative. He thought it was a sad and lammtable fact that a party like the Liberal party Should by a force of circumstances, as it were, be breaking IEO pieces. Speaking of the recent secessions from the -taberal Guernment, he salt that when gentlemen like Lord liartingtor, Mr. Trevelyan, and Mr. Chamberlain could not Support aty measure which they were asked to support and endore that they would not be wise or consis- tent for Mt nation. (Applause.) He concluded by moving " That thismeeting begs to tender its thasks to Sir Richard Cross for ha attendance here this evening to address us, and trusts he mill be long spared to add his weight and influ- ence in Parlament to preserve, as heretofore, the best inter- ests and higtest welfare of the peoples of Great Britain and Ireland." applause.) Mr. J. Person, J.P., in seconding the resolution, said the Conservative of the Newton Division felt proud to have such a repreentative as Sir Richard Assheton Cross. (Ap- plause.) E paking of Irish affairs, he said Mr. Gladstone had become me of the most servile supporters of Mr. Par- nell, and he nit sorry that a man of such ability as Mr. Gladstone shtuld have brought himself into the position he shad done, bvtuse he had pandered to his own vanity, and not to the we tire of the British empire. (Applause.) The motionwas supported by Mr. J. Catherall (Vulcan), and carried wih enthusiasm. Sir Richard ross was warmly received. After thank- ing them for the'ionour the division had oonferred upon ilhn by electing 4m their representative, he said he knee/ Perfectly well thenind of everybody at the present moment waa set upon nothig but the Irish question, and he was quite certain if the rish question had been brought forward and they had fouglnthe election upon it at the end of last Year his majority wold have been five or six times greater than what it really was. •They all knew that the late Government was turne out upon the Irish question, for on the very day on whim they were turned out they boldly declared their policy, anl said in the Queen's Speech that it was a fundamental law lf this country that the two kingdoms should be unit, and they would do nothing that in any possible Vy could shake that union, because they were pektly of opinion that any breach of that union would e of incalculable mischief to the whole kingdom itse but more particularly to Ireland. They were deterrtled to put down that which at that time, and he (Sir Ride' Cross) believed at the Present moment, was the great tile of Ireland itself, that system of terrorism of the leagnwhich existed and which allowed no single human being a, freedom from one end Of Ireland to the other. They sa clearly enough that so long as that league existed no freekm of action, happiness, or confidence conld exist in the ttntry. Mr. Gladstone had taken a new departure in mem politics, and had brought forward bills for practically -eaking up the union Of the United Kingdom and separatinghe legislative body of Ireland from the Imperial Parliaent brought in another bill for the PuirP. He had also o of buying up the Whole of the landlords of Ireland, and heir Richard) ven- tured to say that if any other person than 'r. Gladstone had brought forward those measures they 'told have been laughed out of the House. (Hear, hearand laughter.) It was quite impossible for the Conservativ party alone to fleest these bills. The Liberal party was ividedat p„.

• sent, and the Conservative party, with 252 members, was the strongest party in the House, and were united by one mind, one heart, and one soul, to act as one consistent body for the purpose of preserving the State from danger. (Ap- plause.) Lord Salisbury had promised support to Lord Hartington in the stand he had made against this bill, and had said that if he could form a Government the Conserve- J tive party would give him an independent support. By the bill they were going to give Ireland a legislative body and a national independence, and on this ground alone it ought not to be passed, as it was not a constitutional bill. They were also degrading the people of Ireland by placing that country in the position of a colony that might be at the other end of the world. If the Prime Minister's proposals were carried the result to the English taxpayer would be that no less a sum that £1,400,000 would have to be annually raised by means of fresh taxation, and if that sum were capitalised they would find they would have to pay the large sum of a 2.-000,000. Then it had been estimated that it would not take less than £150,000,000 to buy out the Irish landlords, and, therefore, in credit and hard cash. if this iniquitous measure were carried out, more than £200,000,000 would be required from the British taxpayer. (Applause.) It depended upon the people of England whether they would new speak out. If they did, he believed their voices would be heard in Parlia- ment, and these iniquitous bills would never be allowed to pass. (Applause.) Lord Gerard afterwards moved, and Dr. Mackie seconded the following resolution, which was carried with applause : —"That this meeting is of opinion that any legislation tending to destroy the union between Great Britain and Ireland %mild be detrimental to the peace, trade, and gene- ral welfare of the United Kingdon, and pledges itself to sup- port Sir Richard Cross and the other Conservative leaders in their determination to maintain the integrity of the em- pire." (Applause). The proceedings subsequently concluded with the cus- tomary votes of thankP. •

THE HOME RULE CRISIS. Lord Hartington has intimated that it is not un- likely that he may move the rejection of the Government Home Rule Bill. Mr. Chamberlain has given notice that on the mo- tion to read the Irish Land Purchase Bill a second ; time, he will move as an amendment that it be read that day six months. Mr. Chamberlain, replying to a Welsh correspon- dent, says he will not take part in any Tory coali- tion ariainst Mr. Gladstone, but will content him- self with making clear his own position. Mr. Chambeilain sincerely hopes the Government will he willing to make modifications in their bill which will enable him to give it his support.. Lord Iddesleigh, replying to a correspondent on the Irish question, says he thinks that Mr. Glad- stone's bills are fraught with much danger to the empire, while they will do no good to Ireland. A number of Liberal members of both Houses of Parliament, chairmen of Liberal Associations, and others have joined the Liberal Committee for the maintenance of the legislative union. At an Orange demonstration on the Maze Race- course, county Down, on Monday, resolutions were passed condemning in very strong terms Mr. Glad- stone's bill for the future government of Ireland, and stating that the Orangemen would not acknow- ledge the government of those who had been their bitterest enemies. The Archbishop of Cashel (Dr. Croke), speaking at Thurles on Sunday, said: We owe the successful progress of our national spirit to the truly great, thoroughly sincere, and wonderfully able and hitherto more or less unappreciated, but now thor- oughly approved of and universally admired man who stands at the head of Her Majesty's Govern- ment. I meax, of course, Mr. William Ewart Glad- stone. I always admired him. I believe he has an English head and an Irish heart. No English- man's picture ever entered my house. I have now in my most prominent room the life-size picture of Mr. Gladstone. He is, I believe, Ireland's great- est friend. A Liberal M.P., who has good means of knowing the actual state of affairs and who has been at some pains to check his calculations, thinks that, in the coming division on the Irish Government Bill, 5 per cent must be taken off the maximum number of Liberals and Conservatives to get at the number likely to vote, but that every 'Nationalist will be present. His figures come out thus : Liberals likely to vote Less Seceders (minimum) ..... 68 ...(max.) 7B Liberal vote for the Bill 215 Irish vote Total for Bill -332 -322 gonservatives likely to vote- 240 ......... 240 Li Jeral Seceders (min.) Total asrainst -303 -318 In each case it will be seen that the bill would be carried. The number of members on the Liberal side understood to be definitely pledged against the Irish Government Bill is put at 48. Lord Houghton, who holds a subordinate place in the Government, spoke on Monday night at a large Meeting of Liberals at Barfield. near Barnsley. After references to the scheme of Mr. Gladstone for the government of Ireland, and to the "four other sets of views" put forward by opponents.and can- did friends, his lordship said that to carry into logical effect Mr. Chamberlain's federation ideas would involve the abolition of the present House of Commons, a step for which he did not think any section of Englishmen were ready. Mr. Osborne Morgan writes that he believes the Home Rule Bill, to be not only the best but the only solutidfti of the problem. Mr. Mellor, the Judge Advocate General, thinks it is plain now that the country will support Mr. Gladstone in his endeavours to solve the greatest problem of the time. Mr. Hobhouse, Liberal member for East Somerset, has informed his constituents that he cannot sup- port either of Mr. Gladstone's bills. This announce- ment was made at the annual meeting of the East Somerset Liberal Association, at which a resolution in support of Mr. Gladstone's proposals was carried, with but few dissentients. An address on the Irish question was delivered on Tuesday evening by Mr. R. Leake, M.P., at a Liberal meeting held at Farnworth, and a resolution was adopted expressing the opinion that the proposals of the Government contain the basis of the settlement of the Irish difficulty. Mr. T. B. Potter, addressing his constituents at Rochdale on Tuesday night, expressed approval of the Irish proposals of Mr. Gladstone, and said it was his intention to support the second reading of the Government of Ireland Bill. A meeting promoted by the Irish Loyal and Patriotic Union was held on Wednesday night in the Free Trade Hall, Manchester. The hall was about half full. The chair was taken by the Duke of Norfolk, and among the speakers were the Earl of Dunraven, Dr. Hans McMordie, Mr. T.W. Russell, and Mr. J. F. Hutton, M.P. A resolution was passed affirming that any proposals tending to in- validate the legislative union between Great Britain and Ireland would prove disastrous to the 'interests of both countries. There were present a large number of persons who were opposed to the objects of those who had called the meeting, and the proceedings throughout were very disorderly. Mr. 3lundella addressed a mass meeting at Shef- field on Wednesday night in support of the Irish proposals of Mr. Gladstone. He ridiculed the idea of separation, and stated his belief that every farth- ing advanced for the acquisition of land would be amply and religiously secured. The only alterna- tive policy was one of coercion, and he would never vote for that until every other resource was tried. A vote of confidence in Mr. Gladstone was passed. The Liberals of Radcliffe met on Wednesday night and expressed their confidence in Mr. Gladtone's Irish proposals in a resolution which was supported by Mr. R. Leake, M.P. Mr. Mellor, Judge Advocate General, writing to the Grantham Liberal Association, says that it is plain now that the country will support Mr. Glad- stone's scheme. Lord Clifton writes that as a Home Ruler, if he seriously thought that the Irish Purchase Bill would ruin Irish property in land and form a sure prece- dent for ruining English, Scottish, and Welsh pro- perty in land, he doubts whether he could in honour continue to support Mr. Gladstone's twin mea- sures of Home Rule and Land Purchase, but not taking that view he shall continue to support both bills. At a Liberal meeting held at Melbourne. Derby- shire, on Wednesday night, the Rev. W. H. Tetley, a prominent supporter of Sir Wm. Harcourt, declared that Mr. Gladstone was determined to carry the Irish Government Bill "to the bitter end," and if defeated lit would dissolve Parliament and appeal to the country. LORD HARTINGTON AT RAWTENSTALL. The Marquis of Hartington on Mondaypaid a visit to his constituents. In the afternoon he attended a private meeting at Rawtenstall of the Liberal As- sociation for the Rossendale division, and explained the grounds which had induced him to oppose Air. Gladstone's Irish policy. He also intimated that he had no intention to enterinto any coalition with the Conservatives for the purpose of overthrowing Mr. Gladstone, his desire being to maintain a perfectly independent attitude. In the evening ,his lordship addressed a crowded meeting of Liberal electors in the Co-operative Hall, Rawtenstall. Mr. Thomas Brooks presided, and

read letters from Mr. R. N. Philips, the Earl of I " Derby, Mr. John Bright, and others, approving of the course which Lord _Hartington has taken in re- gard to the Irish policy of the Government. Lord Derby said he was glad to have the opportunity of expressing his concurrence in the opinions to which Lord flartington had given utterance on the Irish question, which he regarded as the most important that had arisen since the Act-of Union was passed. The noble earl added a strong protest against the proposal to create an Irish Parliament in Dublin. Mr. John Bright in his letter referred to the divi- sion in the Liberal party on the Irish question, and said that in his opinion Lord Hartington had acted in a manner at once consistent and courageous, hav- ing done in the House of Commons exactly what his constituents might have expected him to do from his speeches during the election. The Marquis of Hartington, in his opening re- marks, said he saw that there was a division of , opinion in that meeting, but at the same time he ! hoped he should receive a fair and attentive hearing. He was in a peculiar position on that oc- casion, because, for the first time, he was not in unison with the Liberal party generally, nor with I the leader of that party. It was painful for him to, have to separate himself for a time from other mem- bers of the party, and to see the party so greatly divided in its own ranks upon a question of so much importance to this country; still he felt that the propbsals on which lie differed from some of Ins friends were matters on which he was bound to take the course lie had pursued. The measures proposed by Mr. Gladstone were opposed to the .past traditions of the Liberal party. and were not only not called for as matters of urgency, but were not likely to promote any real good to the sister country. He thought it not unlikely that before long the opinion of the country would be asked' on these matters, and when that time came he should willingly bow to the opinions of that constituency. He must, however, sAy that there was nothing in the two schemes now before the country that would induce him to acoept them. They were too much opposed to anything he had said on the subject to meet his approval, and he should be ashamed to appear before his constituents if in doing so he had to strain his opinions. He had all along stated his resolve to support the ad- ministration of the law in Ireland; he and others, moreover, accused the Tories prior to the general election with having entered into an alliance with the Irish party. This they did because they thought the conduct of the Conservatives unworthy of any great English or Constitutional party. Under those circumstances, he would be ashamed of himself if he were now to come forward and admit that the charge was only made as a party manoeuvre and for the mere sake of securing support at a particular ! moment. He valued the unity of the Liberal party as much as any man, but he valued the union of the British Empire more, and would do all he could to maintain that union. It was said that the Irish measures of the Government were not intended to destroy the legislative union between Great Britain and Ireland but only to enable the Irish to manage their own affairs. He controverted these proposi- tions as being equally fallacious and misleading. The people of Ireland were not in reality one people. The Protestants of the North were as much opposed to the Catholics of the South and West as were the English and the Scotch, the differences being of race, religion, and ideas. Great Britain had done much in times past to embitter those differences, and now that the Protestant ascendancy had been done away with he asked whether the English people ought to do that which would create a Catholic ascendancy in the sister country. One of his greatest objections to the policy now proposed was that it would be in the future a cause of greater disturbance than had hitherto occurred. As to the exclusion of the Irish members from Westminster, he admitted that it was a dilemma from which there was no escape. Ile acknowledged the force of Mr. Gladstone's argument for the exclusion of Irish members, but he held that if they were ex- cluded and England insisted on the payment of the Irish tribute, that fact would be the opening up of a series of difficulties and troubles between this country and Ireland. The financial arrangements also provided a store of future difficulties. Beyond these was the land scheme, of which he might safely say no one had been found to approve. If ! the vast mass of the Liberal party adopted the pre- sent measures, not because they were convinced of their merits but in deference to the opinions of ! Mr. Gladstone, it would be useless to ask him or any one else to propose an alternative. If, on the other hand, the Liberal party applied an independent judgment, to the Government pro- posals and passed a calm and fearless verdict on them, then he believed it would be possible not by the genius or inspiration of any one man, but by ! the collective counsel and help ot the many. that an alternative policy for the future government of Ire- land would be proposed such as would be safe, honourable, and beneficial to the people of Ireland than the policy which had just been put forward by the present Government. At the private meeting of the Cou&,il and at the public meeting the audience made it clear that they were not in sympathy with Lord Hartington's views. At the evening meeting the resolution passed thanked his lordship for hi 's address, but avoided an expression of confidence in him, or giv- ing an opinion on the Home Rule scheme. Addressing a meeting at Birmingham on Wednes- day night, Mr. Davitt said that Mr. Gladstone's scheme for the government of Ireland was accepted unanimously by those of the Irish race who were entitled to speak on behalf of the Irish national sentiment. A great meeting in support of the Irish Ineasures of the Governnient will be held in Manchester on Wednesday next. Lord Granville has promised to attend and deliver an address. The Attorney-General (Sir Charles Russell) will also speak. Mr. Jacob Bright will preside. The annual Meeting of the Council of the National Reform Union was held on Thursday in the memo- rial Hall, Albert Square. Mr. W. Summers, late member for Stalybridge, moved, and Mr. C. 11.• Hop-, wood, Q.C., late member for Stockport, seconded, a resolution expressing unabated confidence in Mr. Gladstone and his colleagues, and regarding the Governmet proposals as an excellent basis for the settlement of the Irish difficulty. After considerable discussion, the resolution was carried by a very large; majority, only thirteen voting for an amendment in favour of withdrawing the Government mea.4! sure.—The secretary read a list of seventy branches of the union, all of them pledged by resolution to Mr. Gladstone's scheme. There were no resolutions against.
