RUGBY RULES. RUNCORN V. LITHERLAND.—PIayed at Runcorn on Sat- urday, when the home team won in an easy fashion by three goals, two tries, and five minors to three minors. Davies. Andrews, W Hughes, and Lewis got the tries, Hughes and Riley,eewis kicking the goals. Rraeconer V. WIDNES.—On Easter Monday these rival teams met at Runcorn, when a very pleasant and stubbornly fought game was played, the home team winning by two tries and five minor points to Widnes two minor points. During the first half of the game Davies ran in, also man- aging a similar feat in the second half, his playing through- out being quite a feature in the game. The minor points scored by both teams were the result of long kicking. The play was fast and exciting, each good piece of play receiv- ing its merited applause from an impartial crowd of specta- tors. The passing tactics of the home team went a long way towards their victory, the backs without exception do- ing their fall share in this line, whilst the forwards played a grand game. The Widnes men pl.yed a capital game, though much was lost through sticking to the ball. Bing- ham did well at three-quarter, Farrell being the best of two good half backs. Hardman and Smith took the lead for- wards, being well supported by Purvin, Ridyard, and Mea- gher. Teams :—Widnes : Wilkinson, back; Harding, Bing- ham, and Parkinson, three-quarter backs; Farrell and Barker, half backs; Smith, Fogg, Brown, Hardman, Wright, Wilkinson, Purvin, Meagher, and Bingham, forwards. Run- corn: Wood, back; Davies, Speakman. and Riley, three- quarter backs; Hughes and Andrews, half backs; Hughes, ' Wright, Lewis, Dean, Barnes, Gatley, Clarke Faulkner. and Dolan. forwards. Mr. G. W. Vickers, Salford, was referee. WARRINGTON "A" TEAM V. SOUTHPORT OLYMPIC.— An excellent game was witnessed between these- two teams on the Warrington ground, on Monday, by a large con- course of spectators including an unuseal number of the fair sex. The "A "team men were in first-rate form, and though considerably over-weighted by their opponents in the scrimmages, they proved themselves to be more than a match in the all round game far the Olympics. The result was a decisive victory for Warrington by two tries and two minors to two minors. Whittle won the toss for Warring- ton, and elected to play with the wind in their favour. The home team soon began to press the visitors, and for the first quarter of an hour scrimmages were very freqaent in the visitors' half. Price, who in the course of the game made several splendid runs, obtained possession of the bat), but was brought down after a smart run by Webster. Unsworth dribbled the ball back, and Appleton gaining possession kicked into touch near the visitors' 25. From the throw out Price relieved his side by a capital run. Molyneux then gained possession and had hard lines in not scoring, being brought down within half a dozen yards of the goal line. By some capital passing the visitors brought the ball up the field; but Appleton seized the leather and kicked a ,dead ball. From the kick off Walsh passed to Webster; and after an admirable run the latter succeeded in obtaining a try. amidst lend cheers. The kick for goal was entrusted to Walsh, who as usual made a first-rate attempt, the ball fall- ing just outside the posts. From the drop out Unsworth ob- tained a free kick. Some give and take play ensued, but the visitors succeeded at last in working the ball up to the home 25, Telford relieving by a short run. Price obtained possession, and compelled the home team to touch down. Appleton kicked off, and Robinson returned in fine style. The Warrington captain (from a free kick) kicked the ball well up the field. The visitors failing to return, Price again obtained possession, and made a capital run up the field. Appleton relieved his side, and Bashford following well up amongst others obtained a second try for Warrington. Walsh failed to improve the point, the ball just touchieg the outside of the post. At the commence- ment of the second half Whittle kicked off for Warrington, and following up his kick collared Marshall. The game was of a give and take character until near the end, when some very tine play was witnessed on both sides, Price hav- ing very hard lines in not scoring. Just before the call of time Appleton was compelled to touch down for Warrington, the game ending in a victory for Warrington by two tries and two minors to two minors. For the visitors, Price and Lund played a splendid game, and for the home team Ap- pleton, Telford, W Dillon, Acton, Bashford, Molyneux, Whittle, and Webster were noteworthy. The teams were as follows :—Warrington: Hewitt, full back; Acton, Ap- pleton, and Webster, three-quarter backs: Whittle and Walsh, half backs; Bashford, Jones, Nevins, Forster, Molyneux, Dillon, Littlewood, Telford, and Unsworth, for- wards. Southport: T Holder, full back; Price, Lund (captain), and Robinson, three-quarter backs; Craig and Summers, half backs; Marshall. Toole, Banghan, Neville, Binks, Hankinson, Jones, Webster, and Bell, forwards. Messrs Whittle and R Parry were the Umpires, and Mr Wil- cocks, of Wavertree, referee. VirarteruaTote v. WIDNES.—Tbat a keen interest was taken in the meeting of these two clubs by the patrons of football was evidenced by the very large attendance of spectators on the Warrington ground on Saturday afternoon. It was clear from the determined and spirited manner in which the Widnes men played throughout a very exciting game that they had come with the intention of making , amends as far as possible for their somewhat marked defeat in the cup competition. On the other hand it seemed as Ithough the Warrington men were rather disposed to rest upon their laurels, as they took the game somewhat easily. Ihe result was indecisive, though in favour of Widnes by ' one try and two miners to one try and one minor. Ashton won the toss, and Farrell kicked off. , After some smart in- terchanges Barnes obtained possession of a pass which Far- rell intended for Parkinson, and by a strenuous effort he overcame his opponents, and got over the line; but through an infringement of the rules it was ruled back. Farrell afterwards put in a grand run to the Warrington 25; but was brought down by Buxton. A pass by Farrell to Parkinson lost a lot of ground, owing to Barnes collaring the latter player before he could get the ball away. The Warrington forwards now got the sphere into their own hands and took it down the field, passing grandly. Hough and Hayes were next prominent in the collaring department, and a pass by Speakman to Appleton gained a lot of ground, and Hough and E. Dillon took the ball on to the Widnes line; but Barker relieved. The Widnes forwards at this point came away with a rush; but Hayes put an end to progress. Parkinson then took a pass which was intended for Barnes. and kicked to Buxton, but this player returned to the Wile nes quarters. H. Boardman now handled the ball for the first time, and put in a good kick, the play being stationed in front of the Widnes goal. The Widnes forwards, how- ever, worked the ball to their own. quarter flag, where it went into touch. The ball having been thrown out Bing- ham was forced to save. From a kick out it went again into touch, and on Gilbert throwing it out, Appleton gained possession, and kicked it to Harding, who handled it. Frank Turner cashed up, and dribbled to the line, where Speakman took the ball up and scored a try. The same player failed at the goal. This brought about half-time. Soon after returning a free kick was acceded to, Plumpton and Barnes returning centre. H. Boardman then came to the front wiah a rimming kick, bat Harding returned, play being next confined to the Warring- ton goal line. Speakman was forced to touch down in self- defence, and Parkinson returned Speakman's drop out, and Appleton was collared with ttie ball. From a scrimmage the Widnes forwards rushed the ball over the line and oh- Stained a try, Farrell failing at the place. Fair Turner ' kicked out and charged down Harding's return, and the .Widnes forwards took the ball into the Warrington quarters, but Povey relieved by a grand dribble to half-flag. Plump- ton again came to the front with a good kick to Barnes, and the ball was taken to the Widnes 25. H. Boardman fol- lowed up, and collared Harding before he could get the ball away. Speakman obtained possession and passed to Barnes, who kicked to the Widnes line. Fair. Tur- ner prevented a return, and Plumpton claimed another free kick; but he did not gain much ground, owing to Bux- ton returning the ball. Fair. Turner and Davies now , rushed the i ball te the Widnes quarters, where Davies, 1 Plumpton, and Turner came into collision, the play being stopped for some minntes. Hostilities next toek place in the Widnes quarters, where they remained until the referee blew his whistle. On behalf of Warrington, Buxton had the pick of the play, and played a safe and reliable gains, , his grand tackling and kicking being much admired. Barnes and Gilbert played in their usual good form, whilst in the forward ranks Hayes, Ashtoo, Fair. and Frank Turner, Davies, and Hough were the pick. Of the Widnes contin- gent, Plumpton at back played a grand game, he being well seconded by Barker and Farrell, whilst for scrimmages i Smith, Brosn, and Hardman exhibited superior form. Teams :—Warrington: Full-back, Buxton; three-quarter backs, Boardman, Barnes, and Appleton; half-backs, Gil- bert and Speakman; forwards, Fair. Turner, Frank Turner, Hayes, E. Dillon, Molyneux, Hough, Harry Ashton (cap- tain), Davies, and Povey. Widnes: Full-back. S. Bingham; three-quarter backs, Plumpton, Parkinson, and Harding ; half-backs, Farrell (captain) and Barker; forwards, Marra Fogg, Ridyard, Wilkinson, Wright, Smith, Hardman, )Brown, and Perom. WARRINGTON v. HULL. . This match came off on Easter Monday, on the Holder- •ness-road Ground, Hull. In Warrington a good deal of ex- citement had been evinced during the previous week as to the result of this meeting, as the Hull men are known to be one of the hest clubs in Yorkshire. It was generally thought that the seaport lot would be too strong for Warren's lads, but a few of the supporters of the W.F.O hoped that their lot would play them a tight game. Such proved to be the case as the home lot only managed to beat them by a try, the score being—Hull 0 tries and 4 minors to Warrington 1 try and 4 minors. Through the kindness of the Cheshire Lines Company a saloon carriage bad been provided to convey the players to their destination. The train left Warrington at 9 a.m. on Monday, and after a very pleasant journey, which was en- livened by the singing of songs, &c., and the jokes by Messrs. Fair. Turner, Rigby, Plimpton, and the noted J. R. C., they arrived at Hull about 1-35, where they were met by the members of the home club, and a waggonette being in waiting they soon arrived at the house of Mr. Thompson, Queen's Hotel,who very carefully looked to their comfort as far as catering, &c., was concerned. Jolley, through some reason or other, was left at Doncaster, and did not arrive on the field until half time. After partaking of a splendid repast, which reflected great credit on the host and hostess, the team were driven to the scene of ac- tion, and on arriving there the players fromWarrington were ; taken by surprise at the sight of the ground. DARING BURGLARY AT GOLBORYE. At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, before Mr. Robert Houghton and Mr. T. J.Gillespie, John Johnston was brought up on remand on a charge of burglary and theft on the premises of Mrs. Martha Harrison, pawnbroker, Gol- borne. The value of the articles stolen was set down at £s.—Superintendent Heywood remarked that Mrs. Harrison carried on business in Heath-street, Golborne, and stated the circumstances of the burglary.—Mrs Harrison was then called. She said she recollected Thursday, the 15th April. She locked the doors about eleven o'clock at night, and all was then safe. She went to bed about twelve o'clock, and after sleeping some time she was awakened by hearing] something moving on the stairs. She sat up and listened,l and she then saw the prisoner enter her bedroom door, with his hands shading his eyes from the gas which had been left lighted a little. She screamed out very loud and got out of bed. The prisoner then turned round and ran oat of the room. He had his clothes on, but had no cap or boots. She knocked against the room wall with a timepiece, which she to.k from the mantlepiece, and she again screamed for at sistance. She opened the window and saw the police-officer bringing the prisoner back. She and P.C. Ratcliffe after- wards examined the house and shop. They found a piece of damask, a coat, two pairs of trousers, a table cloth, and a cape in a bundle at the top of the stairs. They had been taken from a large box in another room. Near the door in the kitchen she found a coat, a towel, twe jackets, a shawl, two pairs of boots, a pinafore, an apron, and a tablecloth, all of which articles had been removed from the shop. She found that one of the windows had been broken near the "catch," which was undone, but the window was closed The " catch " was fastened when she went to bed. The back door was found open. The drawers in the shop had been opened and some of their contents removed. There was no cash or money left in any of the drawers. She did not know the prisoner.—P.C. Ratcliffe deposed that at twenty minutes past one on the morning of the 16th April he was on duty in Heath-street, Golborne, when he heard Mrs. Harrison scream. He went to the front door of her shop and heard someone inside. He heard someone run- ning as if out of the back door, and he went towards the back door, when he saw the prisoner rushing out with his clogs in his hand. The prisoner got away, but witness fol- lowed and caught him. He afterwards charged the prisoner with the offence, and be replied "That's right." He was afterwards speaking to a constable in the presence of the prisoner about the breaking of the window, and the prisoner remarked: "I broke it with a stone. I made a good bar- gain, but I was caught napping."—The Bench committed the prisoner for trial at the next Liverpool Assizes.

A good scrimmage next took Place in the centre field, and the ball being passed wide to Mor- phitt he had no difficulty in getting over. Steel again fail- ing at goal. From this time to the end of the game War- rington seemed to have the advantage, but failed to qualise matters, the game resulting in a win for Hull by two tries and four minors to Warrigton one try and four minors. It is only fair to state that the Warrington men got over twice, the tries being disallowed `by the referee' who seemed rather inclined to lean to the home team. On behalf of Warrington, all the backs played a good game, considering their long journey to Hull. Barnes played a very deter- mined game, being well seconded by Buxton. Plumpton also showed very creditable form, as did Speakman and Gil- bert. Jolley was absent until half time, and whea he came be did his little in a praiseworthy manner, one of his runs being the beat of the day. In the ranks of the scrimmagers Ashton, Davies, Hayes, Turner, and Pevey were the pick; but no fault can be founi with any of the players in this department. For Hull, Morphitt, Steel, and Roper (backs), and Iveson, Teal, Bell, and Pattisoa (forwards) showed some good play. On coming back to the hotel the home players gave the visitors a dinner, and again it was seen that Mr. and Mrs. Thompson were fully competent to look after the wants of a lot of hungry football players. The Warrington players this season have had a good•many opportunities of judging about matters of this sort, and if the Hull players possess a good ground they also know where to entertain their visitors to a dinner equally as good. After the tables were cleared, the Hall contingent invited the visitors to partake of some bowls of punch, complimentary speeches in the meantime salting place. The Hull captain spoke of the Warrington Football Club in praiseworthy terms. In his speech he said that until very lately he had never heard of such a club, but hoped that day would not be the last that he would see of ;hem, but at some future time he hoped to meet them on the hid with a good team. He coupled with the toast the name of H. Ashton, the captain of the players.--Mr. Ashton, in replying, said that he was sure that the Warrington team Oad enjoyed the game, and endorsed the first speaker's opinions as regards meeting at some future date.—After a few songs were sung the visitors were shown the sights of Hull by some of the players, and spent a very enjoyable evening, the fan reaching its height when bed time arrived. The team, after partaking of an excellent breakfast, made tracks for the station (Plumpton being very loth to leave), in order to catch the train which left Hull at ten o'clock. After a hearty band-shaking with the proprietor of the Queen's, they were soon out of sight of the noted seaport, and on the way to Warrington. A delay oc- curred at Penistone, owing to the rails being out of order, but home was safely reached about four o'clock, every- body being hiehly delighted with their pleasant visit and reception at Hull, which will be remembered for years to come.

ASSOCIATION RULES. EA.ELLESTOWN (2ND TEAM) V. HAYDOCE Si. JAMES'S (IST).—This match was played at Haydock on Saturday afternoon, and resulted in a clever victory for the visitors hy three goals to none. STUBSEAVI CROSS WANDERERS (iST) V. EARLESTOWN (2ND TEAM).—The Earlestown second team journeyed to Stubslatm Cross on Good Friday, and met the first team of the Stubshaw Cross Wanderers on their own ground. There was a large attendance of spectators. The match tesulted in a well-earned victory for the Earletdown Juniors by two goals to none. _

EA.RLESTOWN WHITE CAMELIAS T. EARLESTOWN CLUB Commtrese AND NON•PLAYkRS. The most amusing " match " of the season in local football circles was played on the ground of the Earlestown Club, the Mesnes, on the forenoon of Easter Monday, when teams representing the local troupe of minstrels known as the White Camelias and the committee and non-players of the club met in a friendly contest. The spectators were greatly delighted with the performance, the amusing antics of the players causing con- siderable diversion. When time was called the result was a victory for the committee and non-players by five goals to four. The white camelias appeared with " blackened " faces. The following were the teams :—White Camelias : Walker, goal; E. Williams and Turner, half-backs; R. Thompson, W. Walton, J. Williams, J. Harrison, Jarrett, Hudson, and E. Corlett, foretards. Committee and Non- players : J. Riley, goal ; H. Roberts and E. Gosling, backs; W. W. Owen, W. Fearnley, and D. Ferguson, half-backs; T. Ferguson, L. Morris, G. Owen, J. Muscroft, S. Lambert, and W. Blair, forwards. EARLESTOWN Y. EARLESTOWN WANDERERS.—The meet- ing of these teams on the Mesnes, the ground of the first- named, on the afternoon of Easter Monday, caused great excitement in local football circles. As the Wanderers have latterly shown good form, whilst it was thought by many the Earlestown club was going "down hill," many thought that the Wanderers would secure their first victory over the late Liverpool cup holders. There was conse- quently a very large attendance, many ladies being present. From the commencement to tha end excitement ran very high, and considerable partisan feeling was ehowm. Each team was loudly cheered by its supporters. The play was ! much in favour of the home team, who pressed their oppo- nents during the greatest part of the time. From the cor- ner kick by Rich, Bowker scored the only goal of the match for Earlestown during the first half. On several occasions the play was of a very rough character, and an unusual amount of " charging " was witnessed. The Earlestown team, after having the best of the game, were declared the victors by one goal to none. Teams :—Earles- town : J Harrison. goal; R Green and J Green, backs : J Duxbury, J Whalley, and G Clough, half backs; W Rich and J Ellison, right wing; R Bowker' centre; J W Sims and T Siddeley, left wing. Earlestown Wanderers: J Tay- lor goal; W Lord and H Selbie, backs; T Goulding, T Philips, and B. Johnson. half backs; J Lowe and W Allison, right wing; T Thompson, centre; J Shaw and J Ogden, left wing. EARLESTOWN v. LOWER DARWEN.—TheSe teams met at Earlestown on the afternoon of Good Friday, and as the weather was beautifully fine there was a vast concourse of spectators, numbering at least 2,000. The proceedings were considerably enlivened by the presence of the Viaduct Insti- tute Brass Band, who rendered selections of music at half- time and also played a selection of dance music after the , match. Beth teams were very strong and representative of the two clubs, who met for the first time. During the first half the Earlestown team played down hill with a strong sun in their faces, but notwithstanding this the play was of a very even and exciting character. When ends were changed

div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF

GUARDI4.NS. The annuel meeting of this Board was held in the Board- room, at the Workhouse, on Wednesday morning. There were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts, Messrs Blackhurst, Brown, W. Houghton, J. Houghton, Foster, A. Woode, Kil- shall, Humphreys, Gibson, Ratcliffe, Greening, Harrison, Mackie, Isherwood, Bonnell, Owen, Voisey, Strange, Pen- nington, Swinton, Jones, Heaton, Clarke; J. C. Sutton (clerk), and S. Sutton (assistant clerk). ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN AND VICE-CHAIRMEN. The CLltint, who was nominated to the chair pro tern, mentioned that the first businees of the Board would be the election of chairman.—Mr. GREENING said he rose with very great pleosure to propose that the Rev. G. F. Roberts be re-elected chairman forthe ensuing year. (Hear, hear.) As chairman during the past year he thought Mr- Roberts had conducted the business in the most satisfactory man- ner, and he did not know that he had ever sat under a chair- man of the Board who conducted the business in a more gentlemanly or business-like way than Mr. Roperte. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. BROWN seconded the proposal.—Mr RATCLIFFE supported the proposal, and said he endorsed all tbe remarks of Mr. Greening. It was true that Mr. Roberts, as chairman. and he i-ad not always agreed, in fact they had agreed to differ—(hear, bear, and laughter)—bat he cordially sup- ported the proposal. He should act independently, and if the chairman trod on his toes he would try to tread on the chairman's toes. (14 aughter.)—Messrs. Harrison, Jolley, and Foster also supported the proposal, which was agreed to unanimously.—The CHAIRMAN, who was received with applause, thanked the Board for the high compliment they had paid him, and trusted that the experience he had ac- quired during the past year of office would prove useful to him and serviceable to the Board. He felt sure that he had the confidence of every old member of the Board, and he trusted that as soon as they knew each other better he would be able to win the confidence of the new members. (Hear, hear.) Last year was an uneventful one, unmarked by any particular questions, if they excepted the matter of Penwortham Bridge, in which the clerk rendered them such useful services. (Hear, hear.) In conclusion he ad- vised them to avoid discussions on abstract questions.— On the motion of Mr. BLACKHURn, seconded by Mr. RATCLIFFE, Mr. Balharry was se-elected senior vice-chair- man ; and on the motion of Mr. JOLLEY, seconded by Mr. GREENING, Mr. Brown was re-elected junior vice-chairman. THE DAYS OF MEETING, ETC. Dr. MACKIE suggested that some re-arrangement as to the time for administering relief to the Warrington poor might be made. The country Guardians, he said, found Wednes- day to be the best day, but to expect Warrington Guardians, some of whom had besiness connections of a close nature, to come from ten o'clock to two or three in the afternoon, was to expect more than oczlit to be expected, and it was this Tatter which caused so much difficulty in finding Warrington Guardians.--The CLERK said they were legally bound to deal with relief cases at the Board meetings, and he mentioned that twice in the year the Beard meetings were adjourned till the Thursday to deal with chronic cases, and be was sorry to say that on these Thursdays the attend- ancp were worse than on Wednesdays, the work generally falling upon three or four gentlemen—the chairman, and Messrs. Greening, Brown, and Jolley generally being pre- sent. He was sorry also to tell Dr. Mackie that the attend- ances at the committee meetings held on Tuesdays, Fridays, and other days, were not nearly so good as at those held on the Wednesdays. For some years it had been a standing fight whether the Board meetings should be held on the Wednesdays or Tuesdays, and it was agreed that for six months the meetings sheuld be held on the Tuesdays, and for other other six months on the Wednesdays; but unfor- tunately for the town Guardians, who had fought for the Tuesdays, there was a worae attendance of town Guardians ' on Tuesdays than there had been on Wednesdays. The Tuesday meetings were then dropped, and they had no dis- putes about it. The School Fees Committee was also left to two er three persons; but the Pad- gate Schools Committee, which met en Tues- days, was, he must say, excellently attended. .(A Member: By country guardians.—The CHAIRMAN said it had always been considered that Wednesday was the most convenient day on the whole.—Mr. BROWN suggested that a committee should be appointed to deal with relief .cases in Warrington as at Newton; but the CLERK mentioned that relief cases could only be dealt with in this way at a distance of four or more miles from the place of meeting of the Board.—Mr. BLACKED:IRn next suggested that the relief cases might be taken in the morning before the general bus- iness of the Board instead of after.—Mr. PENNINGTON said that that system had formerly been adopted, but had not worked well.—The CHAIRMAN thought the best plan would be for the Board to meet in some place nearer the centre of the town. There was sometimes pressure for room in the Workhouse and they could give up that office for the use of the inmates.—Mr. GIBSON : More expense.—Mr. VOISEY supported Dr. Mackie's remarks.—Mr. BONNELL was in favour of the relief cases being taken before the general business.—Mr. GREENING said relief was always better ad- ministered by three or four people than by the whole Board. He was of opinion that Wednesday was the proper day of meeting inasmuch as it was the most convenient day for the country guardians who were the large majority there and deserved consideration. (Hear, hear.) And until some eh - solute necessity arose he would be opposed CO remeYing from that Boardroom. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. GIBSON did not see that the Warrington Guardians had anything to complain of, seeing that they had the least distance to come to the Board meetings. He was surprised that anyone should allow themselves to be nominated Guar- dians if they could not attend to the duties of the office. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. RATCLIFFE did not think they ought to put the ratepayers to the expense of providing new offices; the rates were already heavy enough.—Mr. JoLLEY was also in favour of continuing as they were, but if they. were afterwards forced to remove he would go in for an office in the centre of the town.—Mr. OWEN thought that if any , gentleman thought he would not be able to attend to the business of the Board he should not allow himself to be nominated.—The subject then dropped. WARRINGTON RELIEF CASES. Mr. Jo HN HOUGHTON moved that No. 1 Relief Committee be constituted of Warrington township Guardians. He did not think that the country Guardians ought to do the relief work for the town Guardians.—Dr. MACKIE seconded this proposal. It had been said that they ought not to accept office unless they could discharge its duties—(hear, hear)—but he would like the gentlemen from whom the" hear, hear "came to know that there was an extreme difficulty in Warrington te get men to stand who were in any sense fitted for the work. Dr. Mackie was
Rae-

prooeeding to speak further on this subject when ha called to order by the chairnaan and resumed his seat.—Mr. owEw said the committee meetings held in the town which should be attended by town Guardians were the worst attended of all the meetings.—Mr. Houghton's proposal was then agreed to. •

JISSESIIIINT COMMITTEE. '4 a The business of appointing committees VMS then pro- ceded with.—The CLBRIC suggested that Mr. Broadbent :If who was now an ex-officio member of the Board be appoit-• ted an ex-officio member of the Assessment Committes;rP He understood, he said, that Mr. Z. Armitage, one of the present ex-officio members of the committee, found it dirE-1 rp eult to attend the meetings of the committee owing to 71- business arrangements.—Mr. BLACKER:7E2ST, however, moved that the former ex-officio members. viz. :—Messrs. Z. Armi- tage, W. Lone, A. C. McCorquodale, and J. Rylands, be re-elected.—Dr. MectuE seconded this proposal.—Mr. Fos- TER moved, and Mr. HARRISON seconded an amendment that the ex-officio members of the Assessment Committee, be Messrs. C. Broadbent, Long, McCorquodale, and Ry- lands, and the amendment was carried. The following gentlemen were appointed elected members of the Assess- ment Committee :—Messre. W. Ballaarry, G. Blackhurst. J. Greening, J. Houghton, Dr. .Mackie, Pennington, Ratcliffe, and the Rev. G. F. Roberts.

RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The name of Mr. C. Broadbent was tilled .to those of the ex-officio members of the Rural Sanitary Authority and the following were appointed elected membetv, viz.: Messrs, Foster, Gibson, Grange, J. Houghton, W. Houghton, Humphries, Jolley, Mall, Owen, Roberta, Swinton, Ren- nington, Greening, liestAn, and N oods.

MISCELLANEOUS. The School Attendance Committee was constitnted as for.-- merly with the substitution of Mr. Gibson in place of Mr. Darbyshire. Mr...roisev's name was added to the Finance and Geaeral Purposes (-3ommitreo. and that of Mr. Hum- phreys to the Committee of Visitors to Asylums. The House Committee was composed as follows : Messrs. Bal- harry, Bonnell, Brown, Grange. Greening, Jolley, Kilshall, litstcliffe, Swinton, Strauze, Voisey, Houghton, Clarke. Gibson, Jones, Eckersl,y. Woods, Wright,. and Isherwood. Messrs. Voisey' Jones, Gibson, Woods, Clarke, Owen, Houghton, and Isherwood were added to the Schools Com., mittee ; and Messrs. Blackhurst, Brown, Voisey, Greening, 0.. Harrison, Jones, Jolley, and Dr. Mackie formed the District School Fees and Poor Removal Committee. Newton Relief and School Tees Committerl r- Messrs. Eckersle3-, Clarke, Ratcliffe. and Wright, and also the ex-officto guar.- diens resident in the township. THE COST or THE ELECTION. The accounts submitted to cover the costs of the recent elections throughout the whole Union amounted to £ll6. -

lICEOOL INSPECTOR'S In the mirutes of the House Committee it was stated that Mr. J. R. Moseley, the Government inspector, had inspected- the schools and found that the children were well taught,- but from the nature of the case they could not be very pro- ficient.

VACCIN'ATION, The following letter from the Local Government Board to the Clerk was read, viz. :—" Sir, ;I at directed by the ,Local Government Board to state that they have had under consideration the report made by their inspector, Mr. Collins, after his recent inspection of public vaccination in the Warrington Unime. The Board find from this report that Mr. Holford, the vaccination officer of the Warrington district, has failed in several reTects to carry out his duties with due diligence and accuracy. It appearsahat his per- iodical returns, on whose unsatisfactory character the Board have frequently had to write to the Guardians, do not repre- sent the actual state of vaccination in his district. This is due to the fact that be has entered eases as vaccinated where he did not possess a certificate to that effect, and other cases as postponed by medical certificate" where the certificate had lapsed some time. Further, he has disre- garded the instructions in several respects in that he ha& . nealeoted, in some cans for a period of two I,,cnths, tmend to persons in default the notices vfllich are requiredlo be issued immediately upon the default arising ; that he rarely obtained the renewal of medical ' certificates in cases of , postponement. Havini; regard to 'these irregularities the Board are clonbtfial whether Mr. Holford should be allowed to continue in office, but Work. coming to any decision on the point they will be prepared" to coneider any explanation he may have to offer. Mr. Collins also reports with reference to Mr. Cooper, the vac- cination officer of the Newton district, that he has in several instances failed to obtain the renewal of certificates- of postponement where they have lapsed; and in this con. nection I am to point out that a certificate of postponement uncle- section xviii. of the Vaccination Act, 1867, remains in force only for a period of two months, or until the next periodical attendance for public vaccination after such period. lam therefore to request that the Guardians will require Mr. Cooper to perform his duties properly in thift- respect. lam at the same time time to forward to you to I be returned to Mr. Cooper the accompanying certificates- originally received by him, an to point out that certificates signed by unregistered practitioners are invalid, and shoul& not be accepted.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, ALFRED DE ADRIAN, assistant secretary."—ln reply to Mr. Rat- cliffe, the CLERK said he had received no further informa- tion with regard to the case of the Newton registrar.—lt was decided that the clerk should communicate with the two vaccination officers referred to in the above letter, and request Mr. Holford to send a copy of his reply to the Local- Government Board to the Board of Guardians. A SURCHARGE. The CLERIC stated that the auditor at his recent audit sur- charged Mr. Brown with an account for .£3 7s 7d from Mr. Hedgcock, plumber. The auditor had noticed that the data "Jan." on the account had been altered to June, and it was_ found that the wore charged for had been done in January, 1885, so that the statutory time for payment had elapsed.— Mr. BROWN said he did not know why he should be sur- charged, because the account had been signed by both the workhouse master and the Clerk —The matter then dropped, it being understood that Mr. Brown would appeal against the surcharge in the usual manner. The relief cases were then proceeded with.

- DROWNED IN THE MERSEY. ii The boat accident on the Mersey, by which a man 4.1 named John Garnett (35), joiner, was drowned on the • afternoon of Good Friday, formed the subject of an inquiry by Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, at the ii Red Lion Inn, Penketh, on Tuesday afternoon.— '4O Richard Garnett, brother of the deceased, said he last saw him alive at haif-past one on Good Friday,44-1 when he was going home, and was quite sober.— William Johnson stated that he found the body or deceased on Saturday, on the Cheshire side of the. ; river, two or three yards from land. Wittifess went 11 with deceased into Cheshire on • Friday Morning.. They had some drink, but were not drunk. When ja he pulled the body out of the water the coat was turned up. He pulled it down, and a gill bottle of beer fell out, which he threw into the river.—Evan Thomas, 29, Wakefield-street, Warrington, said he ,0 was taking part in the boat race on Good Friday, from - Runcorn to Warrington, in the boat Annie. They were about 120 yards ahead of the Little Fred when. he heard a shout, and turning round he saw that the boat, the Little Fred, was upset. There were four men on board the Annie. They turned back, ran against the tide, and picked up two men, John. Boscoe and Bentley. Four were sitting on the boat when it was turned keel upwards. Seeing another boat going to the rescue, they turned round and went on to Warrington. The Little Fred seemed to be sailing all right. At the time there was a strong head-wind blowing, and they were running with the tide. He thought the Little Fred ought to carry ten men with both sails. His boat passed tho other on the right hand side.—John Boseoe, Bank-yard, Pen- keth, and Thomas •Kenwright, Penketh, the owner of the boat, gave confirmatory evidence, the last- named adding that he thought if the stern of the boat touched the bank and the wind caught the sail at the same time it would turn the vessel over.— Richard Bentley and George Handles were after- wards examined, Bandies stating that he thought 4, the deceased was drunk and all the others "fresh." 7; I —The jury returned a verdict of " AccidentaL death." ,

Beetham and Son, chemists, Cheltenham —Advt. a FATAL COLLIERY ACCIDENT.—On Thursday afternoon, Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest at the Griffin Inn, Peasley-cross, St. Helens, on the body of John A Birmingham, twenty.two years of age, who died in the Cot- , tage Hospital, on Tuesday, from a broken back and other ~ injuries received in the Nt. Helens Collieries on the sth .3 , January. Mr. Hall, Her Majesty's Tnsrector of Mines. was , present; and Mr. J. 0. Swift appeared for Mr. Francis France, certificated manager of the collieries. Deceased for about four years had been employed. as a gang-rider, and en the night in question was working in a roadway nine or ten feet wide, four and a half or five feet high, and 500 yards long, with an incline of one In three and a half. Joseph Naylor, a fireman, said he. was in a level forty yards front the deceased, who was riding on the front box, when he heard a noise af.i of some dirt falling. Deceased shouted, and witness went to the plane. The rope was at a standstill. The deceased was lying on his side near the top box. He was seriously hurt. He said the box bad got off the road and thrown him off. Witness saw three boxes off the line. He had examined the road and found nothing wrong. It was in good order. He could - not say what caused boxes to get off the line, but they fre- quently got off.—Peter Bridgham, engine-driver, said he felt a twitch at the engine, and immediately stopped it for a signal. Sometimes boxes got off a dozen times in a week; sometimes not at all. A rail out of its place, or a piece of stuff on the road, would cause them to get off.—Mr. Hail thought that gang-riding was always a dangerous kind of occupation, and that in many cases it might be dispensed with altogether. He considered it would be much more to- the advantage of colliery owners if they would employ the men who acted as gang-riders to keep the roads in repair instead of riding up and down the front to very little par— pose,—The jury returned a verdict of " Aocidental death."

SATURDAY, MAY 1, 1886.

LORD HARTINGTON has had a trying time of it in meeting his constituents; but he has undergone the ordeal in a manner alike be- fitting the occasion and the views he holds. It was known that the majority of the Liberal electors were hostile to him in the position he has taken up as an irreconcilable opponent of Mr. GLADSTONE'S Home Rule measure; and this was soon made manifest at the pri— vate meeting of the Liberal Three Hundred which his lordship addressed at Rawtenstall on Monday afternoon. But he held his ground; and held it in such a way that those who were most stronzly opposed to him were constrained to acknowledge that, while sharply differing from him, they could not but admire his courage and consistency. In answering the various questions that were put to him, he showed himself most patient and courteous; but he made no attempt to court favour, or to soften the fact that there was DO likelihood of Mr. GLADSTONE'S scheme being modified in such a way as would enable him to give it his support. Indeed, when asked what he thought of a Liberal like Mr. BRAND giving notice to move the rejection of the Home Rule Bill, without allowing it to go into Committee, Lord HARTINGTON inti- mated that so far from condemning Mr. BRAND, he might feel it to be his duty to ' take upon. himself to move the rejectior of the measure. It was thus bit by bit that the Liberals of Rossendale, who in the main lave decided to stand by Mr. GLADSTONE, cane to see that there was no hope of inducing ,heir representative to change his attitude with changes that might be made in the bill. On the other hand Lord HARTINGTON musthave felt how completely estranged he was from those who so zealously supported him t few months ago when he saw that, while tianz- ing him for his address, they abstained from' passing the customary vote of confiden,:e. At the close of the evening meeting, his l•rdship took note of the colourless nharacte of the resolution which had been passed, and was careful to make it clear that he vpuld have preferred that a direct issue shouldaave been raised even if it had gone against urn. That it would have gone against him tiere can be little doubt; and when the county is appealed to, as it will be, on the Hoine .tule scheme, we venture to predict that LON'HARTINGTON will not be returned again is qe member for Rossendale, unless it be by te aid of Con- servative votes. It is not p?.asant to think that the Liberal party may b so long and so much divided, but it is as well to recognise that we are at the parti4of the ways, and be ready, therefore, to fae the facts of the situation.

It is curious to note tat, although, when it comes to a question cdestructive criticism there is a good dealn common between : Lord HARTINGTON ad Mr- CHAMBERLAIN, the two statesmen stt asunder when they are asked—What ouht to be done? Mr. CHAMBERLAIN thins the Home Rule Bill may be cut and prved so as to meet his tastes; but he is At and out opposed to the Land Purchase ,ill. Lord HARTINGTON objects to both ills' but, contrary to Mr. • CHAMBERLAIN, e has "no hesitation in - saying that if t, Government of Ireland Bill
passes in its ,esent forth, or anything ap-

div.p: Dlt'aaariz to its present form, it is in his opinion a simple matter of justice that the LIM Purchase Bill should also be passed." It is this divergence of views among the op- Ponents of Mr. GLADSTONE'S measures which is the least satisfactory feature of their posi- tion. What they say as to the terrible risks of failure, if the Government should go for- Ward on the path they have marked out for themselves, may well "give us pause ;" • but nn the other hand, as they are not agreed as !_c) what course should be taken, no one need Fe surprised if they have a following which Is small and irregular. It begins to be more and more clear that, surrounded by difficul- ties and dangers as is Mr. GLADSTONE'S Sehelne, it at any rate least divides • the tion; and this being the case, Liberals and Irish Nationalists should rally to its support With a view to its having what the Americans "aall fair show." As we have all along We attach great importance to the kind -I).t reception which is given to the two puills by the representatives of Ireland. Mr. 'ILUIBERLAIN last wcek very properly called .tention to the fact that Mr. MICHAEL rANITT had spoken of the scheme as a break- Which should not preclude his thinking i" dinner and supper. If this be taken as Plying that Ireland will accept Home but will not be content until there is `it,t!solute separation, we are certainly with °se who urge that we must be careful t„ to put weapons in the hands of Ire- which will, at the first opportunity, Used against us. But we rather sus- Peet that MT. DAVITT, with the pro- lierbial license of an Irishman, has been telltPloying a bit of mixed metaphor Which too much importance must not be ttached, particularly as a speech he made at vberdeen, on Monday night, points in quite u,e,..oPposite direction. He said : ki;neY accepted the principle of the Gladstone Ile eine' as a recognition of the rights of the Irish Ql°Pl.5. After a few years of peace in Ireland had. °"ivn how needless safeguards were, these safe- r:lB:l'dg would bp removed and a full measure of thglatsl.ative liberty would be granted. As to the cry it meant separation, it was separation to pillll wastider two parties who were quarrelling, but it hie a, Peaceful action, and might tend to closer 11.`tship for the time to come. The scheme would cepted subject to the amendments proposed by ' fallen as a final settlement of the difficulty. he erring, later on, to an argument pressed trae both by Mr. CHAMBERLAIN and Lord ARTINGTON he met the issue full front, as I follows 01111 e denied as a Catholic that the Catholic people ,I,,,r,eland. hated their Protestant brethren. We did ths!!ve in an age of religious persecution. But if .tliolics were dastardly enough to attempt per- the people of Great Britain, would not tol- ire it for 48 hours. DAVIIT, on Wednesday evening, ad- , t'ff`essed a meeting in Birmingham to the same 1" ect• It may, of course, be contended that ege Irish will say anything in order to gain their 011,,ds but as to this we must judge, as we do in u`,l4er matters, by all we see, hear, and know. t 7. p have no sympathy with those who discuss d question as if there was not a single re- rYieraing feature in the Irish character—as if ng, theft, and assassination were the natural products of the Sister Isle. We would rather 'aY with the poet— Probe nature to her inmost core There's more of good than evil, And man, down-trodden man is more Of angel than of devil. "e hold that Mr. GLADSTONE'S scheme IS a peat one, because it embraces all the known b'ets of the case; and it is a good one in the tr!°ad sense of the term, because it appeals 0" the common heart of man. It proceeds b 4 the broad Liberal lines of trust in the °Ple, when the people have made their :Lee clearly beard. While Lord HARTING- titCI)4 iS coldly sceptical and will do nothing, r• GLAUrSTONE is full of the faith that fears ;::Ithing; and if he is supported by the nation, 111- we trust he will be, his faith will be the 4;ePis of removing some of the mountains of euvelty which at present separate Great ritairt and Ireland.

other respects, though there is still plenty of room for improvement. The population is now estimated to exceed 63,000 ; and with a birth rate very much above the average it would seem that there is no likelihood of a decrease in the number of the inhabitants. Unfortunately the death rate is also above the average, though it is due to St. Helens to say that it will compare favourably with many large towns. The death rate is 23.93, while the average for England and Wales is 19-0. Warrington, which is less by about one-third than St. Helens, makes a better show as to mortality, the death rate being 1845 only, the lowest yet recorded for that town. The death rate from zymotic diseases is 1-2 in Warrington, as compared with 3.41 for St. Helens, and 2. ro for England and Wales. The authorities of St. Helens should look to this, and we are glad to observe that Dr. 111‘lircoLL urges the desirability of adopting the system of noti- fication of infectious diseases. . He is right in saying that where it has been adopted it has been followed by the best results. The low death rate of Warrington is undoubtedly j owing to this and other precautionary mea- sures. We may mention that there is com- pulsory notification at Aeading, where the death rate does not exceed r 8.0 ; and at Bur- ton-on-Trent, where it is as low as 15.49. It is not, of course, to be inferred that notifica- tion of sickness will carry a cure with it, any more than ringing the fire-bell will put out the flames. It is a reasonable means to a desirable end; and when men fully realise that disease, like fire, spreads from small beginnings, they will be as anxious to stamp out one as to put out the other: Dr. iNl‘Nrcou, is to be congratulated in the pro- gress that St. Helens has made; and it is to be hoped his recommendations will have due weight with the Town Council.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
The cuckoo, tempted by the warm weather of Tuesday, came along crooning—" Hail, smiling morn." But what a change there was next day! It didn't exactly " hail"—it snowed. _

Whatever a certain section of railway men may think, the miners of this district are in no doubt as to the Employers' Liability Act; they are emphatic in affirming that it should be made compulsory in its application.

The National Press Agency, 13, White- friar's-street, London, is doing good work during the political crisis. Following on Mr. Gladstone's speeches, at a penny each, it has this week issued, at the same price, a capital pamphlet by Mr. Sydney Buxton. The title is—" Mr. Gladstone's Irish Bills; what they are, and arguments for them."

There is, we regret to see, some sign of abater feeling arising amongst Mr. Gladstone's sup- porters against such politicians as Lord Har- tington and Mr. Chamberlain. This ought to be held in check; Liberals must not show themselves illiberal; those who piead for tol- eration should endeavour to practice it.

The Loyalists of course are loyal. One of them proposes that Mr. John Morley should be tarred and feathered, if he ventures to pay a visit to Ulster. They would show their loyalty to the Queenby assaulting the Queen's representative. But they had better not try it on, or they may be treated to something worse even than tar, and feathers.

The Liberals of Widnes met on Wednesday night and passed a resolution heartily support- ing Mr. Gladstone's policy. Mr. E. K. Mus- pratt, who was in the chair, made a weighty speech, which the Irish electors present loudly cheered. They are wishing now they had sent him to the House of Commons, so that he might give a vote for the Widnes Division on the right side. But they have eaten sour grapes and their teeth are set on edge.

In the letter Mr. Bright sent to the chair- man of Lord Hartington's meeting, he plea- ded for a fair heating for his lordship, but he was careful not to express an opinion on the merits of the Home Rule scheme. Some Tory journalists who, unlike Mr. Bright, are not careful, have referred to the letter as con- demning the Government bills. Perhaps, when they have misrepresented Mr. Bright for a week or two, they will take the trouble to read his letter.

" 'Tis but a little faded flower, but oh how fondly dear!" That is what they used to sing;. but it is all changed now. Choioe flowers have become as cheap as—as old china. Baron Schroder got an orchid the other day for 165 guineas. The times are out of joint, and no wonder, when orchids are being "given away" in this fashion. • • •t-t•,,..t Members of Boards of Guardians are not all hard-hearted. At the Prescot Board, on Thursday, the sum of £3 zs 6d was collected on behalf of a poor woman who has been left with four children.; her supposed husband— a county court bailiff—having proved to be a bigamist of the very worst type. It is to be hoped that a subscription will now be opened outside the Boardroom, for the Clerk, who is familiar with the facts, describes the case as a most heart-rending one.

The Mayor of Warrington, in opening a sale of work at Hollinfare, on Monday, did what will be regarded as a shocking thing —for a Churchman. He positively urged that there was need for reform in the Church, when in one parish there was a rector enjoy- ing £3,000 or £4,000 a year, while in another close by the clergyman was left to struggle on with a remuneration that was a mere bagatelle. Alderman Harrison must mind what he is about, or he will be told that he had better join the Liberation Society.

The " Dzily News " of yesterday says— "Sir Richard Cross, who addressed a meeting of his Lancashire constituents at Earlestown, declared, with the accuracy and sobriety which always distinguish him, that no human being in Ireland was at this moment free from the domination of the National League. It is this scrupulous fidelity to truth and care- ful abstinence from exaggeration which make the Conservative leaders the pride and glory of their more intelligent fellow-conntrymen. This is "kinder sarcastic" on the member for Newton, but it is not undeserved.

To be umpire in a football match is usually regarded as a post of honour; but it is also at times a post of danger. William O'Hara was acting in this capacity the other Satur- day, on behalf of the Sankey Refiners, when a dispute arose about a free kick for "hands." The umpire gave his decision, and was re- warded by Patrick Touhey, a supporter of the opposing team, with a blow on the head with a pick shaft. This was more than the umpire bargained for, and he consulted the magis-

THE WIDNES FREE DINNER movement terminated yester. day. It has proved of great value to the ill-clad ill•fed school children, and a suggestion has been thrown out that the movement small continue every winter. RUNCORN PARISII CHURCH.—Miss A. Rougier has just presented a handsome pulpit desk of brass to the Runcorn Parish Church as an Easter offering. Miss Barclay has also given two maniples for use during the caehration of the Holy Communion. NELSON-STREET BAPTIST CHAPEL, WIDNES.—On Easter Sunday morning a sermon en "'lnt Resurrection of Christ" was preached in the above place of worship, by the Rev. R. Yeatman. In the evening the same gentleman peached on 0 the subject •• Resurrection and Judgment." WIDNES VOLUNTEERS AND THE LIVERPOOL EXHIBITION. —ln accordance with orders received from the ufficer corn-

I The vestry meetings this year have passed off, on the whole, quietly. At the Runcorn Parish Church meeting an interesting discus- sion took place on free and open churches, in the course of which it transpired that " there were several cases where pews were rated at Li and Lez, and the owners were sub-letting them for iz and £3." So there is traffic in church sittings as well as church livings—mer- chandise in the Pew as well as the Pulpit. These people need reminding of Him who said something about a house of prayer be- ing made into a den of thieves.

rnanding the Sth and 40th Regimental District, the Widnes battalion of the 21st L.R.V. will take part in tbe parade to be held on the occasion of the Queen's visit to Liverpool on the 12th inst. Asserta AT W IDNES.—William Jones and Ann Jones, keepers of a lodging-house in Lugsdale-road, were each charged at Widnes Police Court with assaulting Mrs. Keena- •gban, a married woman, on Sunday last. Mr. Knowles prose- cuted, and Mrs. Jones was tined 53 and costs. The case against her husband was dismissed. ST. PAUL'S CHUIICH INS MOTE, WIDNES.—A social gathering of the members of St. Paul's Church Institute took place in the Mission Room, Alforde-street, on Tuesday night. About 35 pers.ous sat down to a substantial tea, and subsequently an entertainment was given under the presi- dency of the Rev. A. P. Hamilton Wilson. THE WIDNES WOUNDING CASIC—At Widnes Petty Ses- sions on Thursday Joseph Houstey, a Pole, was again brought up charged with unlawfully wounding Charles Meitchencavisb, also a Pole. Superintendent Barker said the injured man was still confined to bed at Whiston Workhouse Hospital. The prisoner was remanded for a week to Preseot.

A FARMER'S MISTAKEN NOTION.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, INtiliam Longton, an extensive far- mer, was charged with having, on the 21st April, killed one fowl belonging to Wm.Whalin, of Appleton. Mr. Knowles re- presented Mr. Longton, and pleaded guilty. It appeared that fowls were continually tresp tesing upon defendant's fields of oats, ckc., doing considerable damage, and he thought he had a right to shoot them. He was fined 2s and costs, 12e, and ordered to pay 49 for the fowl. BURNING FATALITY;AT WroNEs.—About half-past two yesterday afternoon the infant daughter of John Faulkner, labourer, of 11,'Bridge-street. Widnes, tt et with a terrible death from burning. Whilst the mother was out in the yard, wringing clothes, she heard the child, which was 18 months old, screaming in the kitchen, and running into the house she found the child in flames. She removed what clothes remained on the child, and Dr. McCatnbridge was quickly in attendance. The child, however, shortly after. wards succumbed to it injuries. ASSAULT BY A GIRL AT WIDNES.—Sarah Murphy, a well dressed girl, who lives in Gossage-street, was charged at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, with assaulting Ellen I . .

Francis, 14 years of age, daughter of Thomas Francis, fish dealer, Siinin'e Cross.—Mr. Knowles appeared for the com- plainant. A number of witnesses were examined, from which it appeared there was a quarrel between the parents of the girls with regard to the tenancy of a house. The ill- feeling had animated the children, and on Sunday, the 25th April, as Francis was walking along Slum's Cross Murphy struck her on the face, knocked herdowu, and kicked her.— The defendant was fined 103 and costs, 16s, or seven days' imprisonment. ROBBERY FROM A WIDNES BUTCHER'S SHOP .—At Wid-

nes Police Court, on Monday, Stephen Scalley and John Walsh, young men, were charged with stealing 4Mbs. of beef, worth 2a, from the shop of Hannah Thomas, widow, Waterloo-road. About 11 o'clock on Saturday night Mrs, Thomas at the request of the prisoners weighed Olos. of beef, and wrapped it in paper, when Walsb snatched it out of her hands and ran away. Scalley followed him. P.C. Thompson in the early morning apprehended the prisoners. Walsh pleaded guilty, and Scalley alleged that he was in a beerhouse at the time. The Bench sentenced each prisoner to three months' hard labour. Scalley had been 15 times and Walsh 5 times before the Bench for felonies and minor offences. WOUNDED BY A. WOMAN AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, before Mr. J. Brock, Bridget Mullen, wife ef a caustic finisher, living in Grove-street, was charged under a warrant with unlawfully wounding Ellen McCabe, of Mill House Lodge, Appleton. Mr. J. W. Knowles ap- peared for the prisoner.—P.C. Bruce said on Sunday night about a quarter past eleven he was in Warrington-road when Mrs. McCabe came to him and asked him to go to a house in Grove•street, where she had been assaulted by another woman. He went and knocked at the door, which WAS opened by the prisoner, who at once turned round, took a tumbler off the table, and sent it in Mrs. McCabe's face. She had a terrible gash on the cheek, and a number of cuts on the forehead and about the eyes. The doctor was called in and stitched the wounds.—As the injured woman was un- able to appear, the prisoner was remanded. WOMEN DRUNKARDS AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, Rose Kelly WAS charged with being drunk and disorderly in Elizabeth-street—Superintendent Barker said this was the prisoner's 50th appearance, her offences having commenced in 1872.—The prisoner: I only came out on Saturday, your worship. They always have me in. If I get one glass of beer, the police would have that I am drunk whether I am or not.—Mr Brock; You are a perfect nuisance to the town. You are perpetually in this court. I don't know how many times I have seen you myself. It is quite clear that something must be done; we cannot have you here perpetually. You will be committed to gaol for a month.—The prisoner: Thanks, your wor- ship. You are one of the best magistrates in the whole of them.—Sarah Ann Taylor, of Ditto°, was charged with being drunk. This was her 22nd appearance, and Mr Brock said the remarks make to Mrs Kelly would apply to her. She was fined 20s and costs, or one month. LOCAL MINERS AND THE EMPLOYERS' LIABILITY ACT.—The council meeting of the Ashton, Haydock, Whiston, Prescot, and Thatto Heath miners passed the following resolutions on Saturday:—" We de- sire most sincerely to thank our 'agent, Mr. Samuel Woods,for the excellent and candid manner in which he gave expression to the views of the miners in giving his evidence before the Select Committee now sitting on the Employers' Liability Amend- ment Act." That this council regrets to learn that some employers in this district are using means to get the men's views on the Employers' Liability Amendment Act, which is entirely unfair, by put- ting false issues before the men, by canvassing, under the officialism of the colliery, and thereby rendering it quite impossible fer the men to give an unbiassed opinion on the subject." "That this coun- cil considers the men have given repeated. expres- sions of opinion on this Employers' Liability Act— to wit, in 1881, when 60,600 miners struck for it in Lancashire; in 1883, when the miners of the king- dom petitioned Parliament in favour of Mr. Burt, M.P.'s bill; and since then have expressed only one opinion in meetings all over the country in favour of the action now being taken." MARRIAGE OF Mn. IL GREENALL.—OR Thursday the marriage of Mr. Henry' Greenall, son of Mr. E. Greenall, Grappenhall, was solemnised at Holy Trinity Church, Southport. The bride was Miss Edith Eckersley, of 27, Leyland-road, Southport, daughter of Mr. Wm. Eckersley. The ceremony was performed by the Rev. C. S. Hope, vicar of Holy Trinity, who was assisted by the Rev. Canon Green- all, of Warrington, and the Rev. T. Rigby. The bridesmaids were ltfiss Davies, of Adlington ; Miss Cope, of Malvern: and Miss Queenie Greenall, daughter of Sir Gilbert Greenall, of 'Warrington. The bride was "given away" by Mr. James Eckers- ley, her uncle, of Burnt House, Adlington. The principalguests were—Sir Gilbert and Lady Green- all, Warrington; The Rev. and Mrs. Cope, of Mal- vern; Mr. and Mrs. Peter Greenall, of Warrington; Mr. and Mrs. J. Ainsworth, of Freshfield ; Mr. and Mrs. Davies, of Adlington Hall; Mr. and Mrs. Jones, of Preston Brook; Mr. and Mrs. Bardswell, of ' Southport,; Mr. and Mrs. Appleton, of Warrington; Mr. and Mrs. Edward Greenoll, of Warrington. Over 100 presents were given to the bride. At the wedding breakfast over 70 guests were present. The bride and her husband left Southport at half- past two for London, onitheir way to Paris. THE NEW BISHOP OF. MANCHESTER.—The Arch- bishop of Canterbury has fixed Tuesday next for confirming Dr. Moorhouse, the new Bishop of Man- chester. The ceremony will take place at St. James's Church, Piccadilly, London. Bishop Moor- house preached on Sunday morning at Paddington Parish Church, London, of, which he was formerly vicar. Selecting. as. his text the words "Wily should it. be thought a thing incredible with you that God should raise the dead," his lordship, in a sermon of half an hour's duration, examined the historical evidence against and in favour of miracles, and showed that in the ease of Jesus , Christ there was irrefutable evidence that he rose froi?. the dead. He declared his belief that the apoltles were not under an hallucination when they wrote their Epistles on the resurrection, and as-. ,Serted that it was high time that somebody lifted;utp his voice against the dogmatism of unauthorised scientists. The knell of the Materialistic philosophy had been rung in Europe • but though it would not die at once because it had been discredited its doom was sealed. On Thursday Dr. Moorhouse arrived at Manchester, by the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire line, from Spilsby, Lincolnshire. The Bishop, since he left London has been spending most of the time with his brother-in-law, the Rev. Thomas Walker Sale, rector of Halton Holgate, near Spilsby. The Bishop, whose visit is of a purely private character, and was only known to two or three friends, was met at the station by the Arch- deacon •of Manchester (the Ven. G. IL G. All 7 son), and Mr. E. P. Charlewood. Dr. Moorhouse, upon his arrival, drove to Bishop's Court, Higher Broughton,

, SANGER AND 4ON'B CIRCIIB.—From our adver- tisement columns it will be seen that the hippo- drome circus and menagerie of John Sanger and -Son's will pay a visit to Warrington next Thursday, when the tent will be erected on the piece of vacant ground _near the GeneralrPost Office. On the fol-

lowing day the establishment will be open at Wid- nes, on ground adjoining the Grapes Inn. At each place, at one o'clock in the afternoon of each day,, a free novelty procession will take place, which will no doubt be of so attractive O. nature as to induce
large numbers to visit the after performance. Next Saturday the establishment proceeds to St. Helens.

A vioLENr MARRIED COUPLE AT WIDNKS. Before Mr. J. Brock and Mr. T. S. Timmis, at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, William Wilkinson, a flatman, of James-greet, Widnes. was charged with committing an Aggravated asfault upon his wife Esther. Mr. Knowles was for the conaplf nant and Mr. J. 0. Swift for the defendant. Mr. Knowles said on Sunday, the 11th April, Mrs Wilkin- son had boiled an egg for the baby "as it would not take pebs." The defendant complained of eggs being given to the baby, on which the wife retorted that it was not as bad as putting a sovereign on a race horse. He then knocked her down, kicked her on the aide and on the stomach, and otherwise abused her, causing her mouth to bleed. She screamed" murder," and two women named Mercer and Houghton burst open the doer. Although only married two years, it was alleved that the defendant had been in the habit of thrashing his wife. He had threatened to kill her and she was afraid to live with him. Mr. Knowles therefore applied for a judicial separation.—The complainant gave evidence of a confirmatory character. In cross-examination she admitted that on several occasions she had struck her husband in the face, which had been dis- figured with a black eye, and that he had not struck her in return. They then lived at Northwich —Emily Mercer and Eliza Ellison also gave evidence.—Mr. Swift contended that-the defendant had had great provocation, and that there was not evidence to prove an aggravated assault or to jus- tify a judicial separation. Amongst other witnesses he called Mrs. Turton, of 39, James-street, whose husband was a sulphur refiner. She had seen Mrs. Wilkinson pull her husband off the sofa by the end of his nose, and also by tbe hair of his head. She had shook her hand in his face and said he would see who would be master. She was a woman of very violent temper. If she would behave herself she would have nothing to fear from the defendant. On the occasion when she pulled her husband off the sofa by the nose, he and Mr. Turton were talking about race horses, and she supposed the complainant did not like it.—The Bench considered there was not sufficient evidence for a separation, but bound the defendant over to keep the peace for three months, himself in £lO and two sureties of .-S5 each.

RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The annual meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians was held on Tuesday at the Union Workhouse Dutton. Present:Colonel Ashton (chairman), Revs. John Lock- wood, J. W. N. Tanner, and Thomas Whitley; Messrs. W. Whittaker, John Weir, P. Speakman, W. Fisher, S. Taylor, W.Farrell, James Warburton, T. Lewis, J. Mclntyre, E. Aaron, P. Hall, W. Pickering, J. Brandreth, J. Parr, J. E. Hamilton, W. Whitlow, T. Hadfield, Joseph Knowles, Jos. Stokes, Thomas Hewitt, John Davies, Joseph Smith; Charles Mounfield, U. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk.) APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN.—The Rev. J. W. N. Tanner said he had great pleasure in proposing that Colonel Ash- ton should be re-appointed chairman for the ensuing year. Colonel Ashton was well acquainted with all the business of the Board, and was able to transact it with efficiency and despatch. He was a man of business, and had conducted the work to the entire satisfaction of the Board,—Mr. Speak- man seconded the motion, and it was carried unanimously. , —Colonel Ashton, on taking the chair, thanked the Board for the honour they had done him. They all knew the ability of Mr-Linaker and the great assistance he afl arded to the chairman. (Hear, hear.) The assistant clerk bad a great deal of work to do and if it were not for the help he rendered the work would not be got through so quickly and so well. Although they did getthrough their work quickly they did not sacrifice effioiency for that consideration. (Applause.) APPOINTMENT OF VICE-CHAIRMAN.—Mr. Hadfield pro- posed that Mr. Weir be re-appointed vice-chairman. 11ft. Weir had been very attentive to his duties, and they could not do better than retain him.—Mr. Warburton seconded the motion, and it was carried unanimously.—Mr. Weir suitably replied.

WARRINGTON LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.—A special meeting of the General Council is to be held in the Committee-room of the Liberal Club, on Wednesday evening next, "to discuss Mr. Gladstone's proposals relative to the future government of Ireland,rand to pass resolutions thereupon or otherwise:" The 'chair will be taken at eight o'clock by Mr, MeMinnies, J.P. A large attendance is anticipated. THE BIRTH A.ND DEATH RATE OF WARRINGTON. —For 'week 'ending Saturday, April 24th, 1886.—The mean temperature was 47 Fahr., and therefore 3 deg. warmer than thepreceding week. The maxi- mum temperature 62 Fahrenheit. was recorded on the 20th inst., and tha minimum.temperature. 36 Fahr6nheit, on the. 21St—inst. The rainfall measured-I)9in. The general direction of the wind was E. During the week, which was the 17th of the current year; 24 births and 20 .deatbs were registered. The death rate from all causes. wasequal to 224 per 1,000, s,gaiiist 20.4 the average lof the previous fourweeks, and. against 22.9 the cox, responding .week of last year. The deaths included 1 frora diarrhcea, 1 from tubercular disease, 2 from old age, 2 from heart disease, 8 from lung disease, 4 fxombrain disease, and]. from:scalding. One case of typhoid fever, 5 of measles, and '3 of whooping cough were reported under the requirements of the Act of Parliament.—JNo. 11. GORNALL, Medical Officer of Health.
