div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

NEW PoonRATES.—The Runcorn magistrates on Tuesday signed a poor rate of 10d in the E to realise £35 2s 2d for Stockham, and of lid in the £, to realise £312. for the township of Sutton. FARNWORTII AMATEUR MINSTRELS On Monday even- ing gave an entertainment in the National school, Farn- worth, in aid of the distress fund of the parish. Mr. and Mrs Hunter acted as conductor and accompanist. RUNCORN MERSEY MISSIONS.—From our advertising columns it will be seen that the annual concert in aid of these missions will be given by the boys of the training ship Indefatigable in Runcorn Public Hall, on Tuesday night. ADDRESSES TO WORKING-MEN AT WIDNES. —The subject of the Rev. R. G. Hughes's address to working-men and their wives, in Milton Concvgational Church. Simm's Cross, on Sunday evening, was " The relation of water .to religion." PRESENTATION AT RUNCORN.—The girls prepared for confirmation by the Rev. Robert Edwards, curate-in-charge of Newtown Mission, have presented him with a handsome gold pencil case, inscribed with his name, as a token of their gratitude.

FIRE AT WlDNES.—During the absence of the inmates, a fire broke out at the house 74, Oxford-street, on Monday afternoon. A men named Evans first observed the flames, which were quickly put out by buckets of water thrown on by several men. The damage was only £3. Michael Fallon, labourer, is the occupier of the house. SUDDEN DEATHS AT WlDNES.—William Rosevere, aged. 16 months, son of Thomas Rosevere, chemical labourer, 12, South-street, was found dead in bed early on Monday morn- ing. Annie Griffiths, aged one month, daughter of William Griffiths, labourer, 17, Bridge-street, died in a fit about nine o'clock OH Monday morning. The coroner has deemed in- quests unnecessary. BANK HOLIDAY AT RUNCORN AND WIDNES.—The first Bank Holiday of the year was observed on Menday by the tradesmen of Runcorn and Widnes without exception, and the railway traffic to Liverpool, Frodshane, and Chester I was very heavy, upwards of 1,000 were booked to Frodsham. The football match between Runcorn and Widnes attracted I about 4,000 spectators. PRESENTATION.—The blacksmiths, fitters, and labourers employed at the Widnes Alkali Company's works recently met at the Cocoa Rooms, Hutchinson-street, Widnes, and presented the foreman, Mr. John R. Hudson, who has left for another situation, with a beautiful illuminated address, suitably framed. A very pleasant evening was spent in singing, speaking, and reciting. . HARTLAND WESLEYAN CHAPEL, WIDNES.—The anniver- sary sermons of the Sunday school were preached in this am:eel on Sunday. in the morning by the Rev. A.?. Wat- son, of Runcorn, and in the evening by the Rev. G. Wood, of Runcorn. In the afternoon an address was delivered to the scholars, teachers, and friends by Mr. R. Shaw, of Run- corn. There were good congregations at each service, and the colleetions realised about £35. STREET ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—Late on Good Friday night a 'bus and a spring cart laden with bay belonging to the landlord of the liridge Hotel came into collision near Hutchinson's crossing, Waterloo-read. The driver of the cart was thrown out, but luckily escaped without injury. A labourer who was passing was knocked down and rendered unconscious, but after being attended to by Mr. P. Smith, druggist, of Runcorti, who happened to be passing, he was able to walk away in care of a conetable. A Reneawer PONY AT RUNCORN.—On Saturday night a pony belonging to J. Moores, fish dealer, Trinity-street, took fright in Halton-road and dashed over Dolph Bridge aud along Bridge-street at a rapid speed. The street was thronged at the time, and people rushed wildly in all directions. An old woman, named Mulaney, and two girls were knocked down. The latter escaped Aniujured, but the old woman sustained a severe wound on the temples and was carried away in an unconscious state. The animal was brought to a standstill in Trinity-street. A HORSE PRECIPITATED DOWN AN EMBANKMENT AT WIDNES.—A brickmaker named John Proffitt, who lives off Moor-lane, met with a serious accident the other day. He I was driving a team of horses on the embankment of chemical waste on the Liverpool arrival platform side of the Centra Station, when one of the animals slipped, and rolled down the embankment into the field below, taking Proffitt with I it. The animal was little worse for its fall, but Proffitt sustained a serious fracture of the leg, and was cenveyed to Liverpool. The limb has been set, and he is now progres- sing favourably. RUNCoRN CRICKET Cern.—This club opens the season to-day, when the first eleven travel to Sutton. An improved lot of fixtures have been made, several old members, who have a reputation with the willow, have rejoined the club, and a successful season may be anticipated. The officers are as follows :—President, Mr. J. U. Frith; hon. treasurer. Mr. J. M. Frith; hon. secretary, Mr. J. J. W. Potter; cap- tain Ist eleven, Mr. E. A. Chorlton sub-captain, Mr. W. Heap ; captain 2nd eleven. Mr. James Green; committee, Messrs. F. Bibby, R. Gorst, E. Gregory. A. G. Haddock. W. Haddock, W. Hodgetts, John Kuowles, %V. Newton, J. Pick- thall, and Speechley. DAUGHTERS OF TEMPERANCE, RUNCORN.—The quarterly conference of the Manchester Grand Union of the Daughters of Temperance was held in the Bethesda Lecture Hall, Runcorn, on the afternoon of Easter Monday. There was a large number of representatives present from Man- chester. Salford, Cheater, and. Runcorn. The officers' reports were read and adopted. Afterwards tea was pro- vided for the members and friends, to which a large number sat down. The following ladies assistad at tea : Mrs. Boyle, Mrs. Jones, Mrs. Jabez Stubbs, Miss Peck, Miss Rowlands, and Miss McLeod. Subsequently a public meeting was held. Mr. Thomas Cooke occupied the chair, and explained the objects of the society. He invited the ladies present to become members of the "Lifeboat Union," which had been established in Runcorn. Addresses were also delivered by Messrs. C. Booth, W. H. Lowe, and R. Shaw, and Mrs. Gregory and Miss Walcroft, all of Man- "cheater. After the meeting was over a variety of social games and pastimes was indulged in. FUNERAL OF Mn. J. P. MOREWOOD, WIDNES.—The funeral of Mr. J. P. Morewood, the Widnes representative of the "Liverpool Ceurier," took place on Sunday afternoon at Farnworth Parish Church. The cortege left the late residence of the deceased in Widnes-road at three o'clock. The chief mourners and several friends, inclqding Dr. Edwards, Mr. James Foley, and the reporters of local news- papers, followed the hearse in four mourning coaches. The body was preceded by about 80 members of the Order of Good Templars, the deceased sometime ago having taken a very prominent part in the work of the order. The burial service was conducted by the Rev. George Bond. M.A., vicar of Farnworth. Several wreaths and a floral cross were placed on the coffin, which bore the inscription:—" John- son Pomerett Morewood, died April -21st, 1886, aged 46 years." The body was interred in the presence of a large number of spectators, who exhibited many signs of sorrow, and the last scene was touching and impressive. At the elm the Rev. George Bond delivered a brief address, in which he alluded to the respect in which Mr. Morewood was held by a large circle of 'friends. He spoke of the *Witty with which he had followed his profession, and said Ithat he had visited him on many occasions during his last illness, and was glad to be able to say that the deceased said he had no fear of death. His end was peaceful, and the closing scene was brightened by the hopeful words of. the deceased. He had suffered under many vicissitudes, but notwithstanding all he had reared a family respectably, and had earned the esteem of his many friends. ET. Joan's AMBULANCE ASSOaIATION, WlDNES.—Dur- ing the past winter a' "St. John's Ambalance Class" was Isuccessfully conducted in the Widnes National Schools, and as there was a desire that a wider circle should have the benefit of the useful instruction a public meeting was held last night in the Baths Assembly-room to discuss the ad- visability of terming a centre in the town. About fifty persons assembled, and in the absence of Mr. F. H.Gossage, J.P., who had been announced to preside, Mr. H. Wade Deacon occupied the chair. In his openng address the 'Chairman explained that the secretary to the association in London had written to the Rev. J. Right Williams that it *mild not 'he desirable to form a centre in Widnes unless they could be certain of not less than three or four classes per annum, and in dare time form an ambulance corps. Mr. 'Beacon doubted whether Widnes was quite large enough to support a centre, and he favoured the idea of working under the Liverpool or sotne other centre, He drew attention to the fact that they were assured of the aid of the medical men of the town, and paid a tribute of praise to Dr. McLennan for his labours in teaching in the class during the pact winter. (Applause.) He had pleasure • in moving "That this meeting is of opinion that it is desir- able that some centre or organisation in connection with 'the St. John's Ambulance Association ehould exist in McLennan seconded the proposition, which wan supported by the Rev. R. Burdon, who said if we could do anything to lessen the sum of human misery we should Ibe conferring a great benefit on our fellows. He promised I to do all he could to promote the success of the association. ' The resolution was carried unanimously.---Mr. E. Carey moved a resolution appointing Messrs. Gossage Deacon, !Morrison, and the Revs. B. Bunion and J. Wright-Williams la committee, with power to add to their number, to ascer- tain wheeher such an organisation he practicable, and, if ! found to be so, that the committee be authorised to take all steps necessary to form such an organisation.—,Mr. Oakcien seconded the motion, and it Was carried unauimously after. I•some renierks by Mr. H. A. Wharton, who had acted as secretary to the class. The certificates obtained by the 22 students of the rea.ent class were then distributed by Mrs.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER;
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER;

LONDON, TIIURSDAY. When on Monday Parliament meets to resume its work it will find the ,politiCel situation :consider- ably cleared up. The position alike of Lord Hort- ington and Mr. Chamberlain has been so clearty defined that little is left for. conjecture. -Lord. Hartington, we may take it, is irreconcileable. He will not have the Home Rule Bill at any price, and will indeed be satisfied with nothing less than moving its rejection himself; This is news which has carried great joy through the Conservative camp. It was the very thing they wanted, and. justifies the leaders in that policy of self-effacement • which has excited-indignant comment among some sectiOns of the. rank and file. That Sir M. ll. Beach. or Lord Randolph Churchill should have moved the rejection of the Bill in the House of Commons would have had a tendency to cloge up the ranks of the Liberal party.. That Lord Hartington should take such a course will widen the breach through which the Conservatives hope to rush in and take possess ca of office.

- Mr. Chamberlain, on the contrary, has plainly in- dicated that he is open to an arrangement which, 'concluded, would enable him to give his sup-. port to the second reading of the ,Home itule Bill. He has intimated this in his speech at Birmingham. Rut I happen to know that the matter has been carried a little further through private correspondence. In the odd way in which these things are done Mr. Chamberlain does not call at Ilawarden and have it out with the Premier, nor does he correspond with him directly. He writes to a well-known member on the Liberal side and. frankly states his views. The member then writes to Mr. Gladstone, who replies in a letter, the pur- port of which is communicated to Mr. Chamberlain. Mr. Gladstone declines before the second reading of the Home Rule Bill to give the assurance Mr. Cham- berlain demands. But he has, I believe, gone so far as to intimate that the question shall be regarded as an open one to be settled in discussion in Com- mittee.

This does not on the face of it seem much. But really it is a good deal, and may end in a settle-. ment of the difficulty between Mr. Chamberlain and. the Premier. In introducing the bill:Mr. Gladston% gave it to be understood that the exclusion of the Irish Members from 'Westminster was a vital point. If it were objected to it would be regarded by him- self as fatal to the bill. If now he will let it be understood that the question is an open one, upon which. the sense of the House of Commons may be declared without affecting the existence of the bill or the ministry, a very Important step will have been taken.

Whilst • the recess has • served. to make clear the • personal positions of some of the principal•figures - in the political world it has also supplied opportu- nity for the declaration of opinion throughout the country. Lord Ilartington learned somethink of , this, at the great meeting at Rawtenstall, which was distinctly hostile to his views. At Binning- ' ham Mr. Chamberlain's bolder tactics averted a similar repulse. • There is no doubt that if, when the question of adjournment was raised with the object of postponing decisionon the resolution sub- mitted, Mr. Chamberlain had not come to. the front, and-passionately -urged that a vote 'should forth- with .be taken the adjournment *would have been Carried:: I think I,have seen , it. somewhere stated that Mr. .Schnadhorst, .who 'knows public opinion in Birmingham even better than Mr. Chamberlain, is at one with his old chief in his opposition.to Mr lir,' Gladstone. That is I believe, not the version - of facts given by Mr. Schnadhorst himself in private .• conversation. Birmingham would after all stand by: Mr. Gladstone if it came to a persOnal conflict with Mr. Chamberlain.

This feeling in the country has manifestly,growrt within the last ten days and is likely to grow, but it Would be a Mistake to 'misinterpret its precise meaning. The people are stirred not, I believe, so ranch in favour of the Home Rule Bill as in personal. advocacy of Mr. Gladstone. They have known him for fifty years and are not inclined at this time of day to set his councils at nought. Mr. Parnell and his followers are responsible for the deeply seated distrust with which the project of extended Home Rule is regarded by the great majority British elec- tors. We must have Home Rule now. The stone has been set rolling and no power on earth can stop it before it reaches its natural goal. But if Mr.. Gladstone were to disappear from the scene before the work were accomplished, the end, still inevit- able, would be long postponed, and the interval would be filled up with dire doings in Ireland. A hearty support of Mr. Gladstone at the present juncture would see the question settled off, sparing the waste of time and the peril to public peace that would follow upon delay. This is a feeling which daily grows throughout the country, and will, I be- lieve, make itself felt at Westminster when the division on the second reading on the Home Rule Bill takes place.

The directors of the annual show at South Ken- sington have profited by experience. They have got everphing in a forward state, and the opening on Tuesday is expected to be completed .without a hitch. The presence of the queen crowns the cere- mony with the last touch of dignity and splendour. It is not only that her Majesty will be there,'but that her presence will draw all the great inert of the • 'State. The poet Laureate hiss written an ode which is to be sung instead of recited, whilst :Madame Albani will sing "Home sweet horae." Of the ex- ,hibition itself 1 can say, having had an. oppertunity Of seeing it in its almost 'Complete state, that it will . excel in varied interest allits predecessors. I ven- ture to predict that it•will be the most popular of the series. lip to the present time no one has sue- :ceeded in giving it the necessary name. The Fisheries and the Healtheries were easily hit upon. 'The Inventories was ratlier a clumsy shot, but it 'mssed. What is to be ihade out of "the Colonial and Indian Exhibition?" "The Colonies" has been sug- gested, but id only half descriptive, and is also com- monplace. Mr. George Augustus Sala is back from the land of the Golden Fleece. I saw him yesterday at the press view of. the Royal Academy, his deep mourn- ing testifying to the grievous loss that befel him during his visit to Australia. He is so much altered in appearance that at first he was scarcely recognis- able—possibly owing in some measure to this un- usual • apparel, for George Augustus, as a idle, affects white waistcoats and neckties of . glowing colour. Apart from this, however, .he is decidedly thinner, and has aged in appearance more than is warranted hy a year's absence,

Another well-known jourrialist who has just re- turned to town is Mr. Escott. He-comes by easy. stages from Egypt, where-he-has been in search of health. He is better, but will, I fear, never again be well, whereby English journalism will lose one of its ablest pens. With that light heart wherewith , affairs of this kind are settled, people are already beginning to talk of Mr. Escott's successor in the editorial chair of the" Fortnightly Review." The name of Mr: Frank MU is freely mentioned, and the appointment would be an excellent nue. But happily the chair is not yet Vacant, and a further period of rest may bring Mr. Escott back to it.

This has been a week of private vitifivs—Mr. Whistler's yesterday, the Academy to-daY;:and 'the Grosvenor to-morrow. What the Whistler exltibi- tion was to bring forth we have been leafing for - weeks. Great things were expetted. At- all great shows there is much 'trumpet playing in front before the public are admitted into the tooth. To- dayithe public were admitted. The booth is not very large, but it has been specially designed to show off J the performance. The pictures. were small " blots " of colour, landscapes, and seascapes, nude females and females in diaphanous attire, all very sketchy, some almost childish, others very clever; still the kind of things an artist would keep by him as hints or studies of greater work coming on, and wokild hesitate to summon a public to inspect as Rerious• completed works. Mr. Whistler has a great deal of cleverness and of true artistic' feeling, but he has collected round him a small adulating clique who' become hysterical over all his trifles. It wiqild be better for him if his admirers Were more liensible.

EASTER AT WARRINGTON. - Ifonda.S was very generally observed as a holiday in Warrington, and a general inclination seemed to prevail to take ad- Vantage of the beautiful weather with which the Easter of this year has been favoured; ' Between twelve and thirteen hundred persons loft the town front he Central Station for Liverpool; Manchester, Southport, Matlock, &c., and 1,500 people bOokkel at Bank Quay. BeSidesthese numerous brakes and other vehicles were requisitioned by pleasure- Seekers to 'carry therm to less distant resorts. In. the town a football match between Warrington 't A'- 'teanatind Southport Olympic was a 'great source of attraction, drawing together some two or three thousind si)ectators • and 'cricket and other gatnes were largely indulged in. The park and recreation grounds are now looking their best, and these were resorted to by a very large number of juveniles, and of the more stay-at-home adults. Altogether the Easter holiday seemed to pass very pleasantly,

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.

SATURDAY.—Before Aldermen Chandley and Burgess. MiscistwrEous —Ellen Connor was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Scotland-road, and with haying assaulted P.C. Taylor on the previous evening. P.C. Mono- elan apprehended the prisoner, an-I she behaved violently on her way to the bridewell, and when there assaulted P.C. Taylor by crushing his hands with a door.—She was tined lete and costs, or 14 days.—John Hewitt and John Mullen were each fined 5s and costs for drunk and disorderly be- haviour on the previous day.--Mary Ann Holmes, a middle-aged woman with a child in her arms, was charged with drunkenness. She was found by a constable in the middle of the night drunk and asleep in an empty house, the child being running about the floor in a very dirty state.— Chief Constable Hunt stated that the woman had formerly been in a good position on a farm at Burtonwood, but she seemed to be coming down to beggary.—She was discharged on promising to go to work on Monday. A DESERTER.—WiIIiam Faulkner, a young man, was charged with being a deserter from the West York Regi- ment stationed at Mcllinglr, Ireland. He was apprehended in Buttermarket-street by P.C. Monoghan.—Committed to await escort. . _

WIFE Assaurr.—Robert B. Cook was charged with as- saulting his wife on the 22nd tilt by striking her on the face. Mr. A. Browne defended and pleaded provncation. The Bench ordered defendant to find two sureties of £lO each, or go to prison for 14 days. aarNKENNESS.—Je, hn Mannion, for being drunk and disorderly in Winwick-street, on. Saturday afternoon, was fined 58 and costs; George Hopkins, for a similar offence committed on Town Hill, was fined 20s and costa, or one month's imprisonment.—Thomas Waterworth was tined 5s and coats for being drunk and disorderly, and Bryan Fla- hertY was fined 108 and costs for the same offence.—Henry

Wilson, who said he was a solicitor's clerk out of employ- ment, was charged with drunkenness in Church-street. and WM allowed to go with a reprimand.—Edward Healy for drunkenness in Bold-street, was ordered to pay is, the lockup fee. SLEEPING OUT. James Babbitt, charged with sleep- ing sot in a shed at Old-road, Latchford, was dismissed. TREATING A VAGRANT HANDSOMELY.—John JORE-s (85), of Wigan, was charged with begging in Orford-lane. The magistrates discharged him and directed that his fare to Wigan should be paid. TUESDAY.—Before Councillor C. Broad'aent and Mr. E.
J. Guest.

POLICE ASSAULT.—Mary Lockett and Margaret Burns were charged with assaulting P.C's. Corbett and Johnson, and with being drunk and disorderly in Bridge.street, on the previous evening. Prisoners were stated to have be- haved in a very violent manner, one of them having bit Constable Johnson, but as the Chief Constable said that of late they had kept out of trouble, the Bench dismissed thinn with a caution. FILIDAY.—Before Mr. R. Garnett. _

DESEETER.—Thomas Fay was charged with deserting from the 3rd Battalion Royal Lancashire Fusiliers, stationed at Bury. He was remanded. A WOSILN'S QUARREL.—Ann Eagan and Catherine Glee- son summoned each other for assault. Mr. A. Browne ap- peared for Eagan. The two women quarrelled about a clothes line. The Bench dismissed the case.

div.head: DARESBURY PETIY SESSIONS.
div.p: DARESBURY PETIY SESSIONS.

TCESDAY.—Before Messrs. E. Greensll. J. Marson, C. Broad- bent, and H. Nield. UNWEIGIIRD BREAD.—James Allwood was summoned for delivering bread without carrying scales to weigh the same on the sth inst. Defendant said it was his custom to send the weights and scales with his servant; but on the day in question they were undergoing repairs—A fine of 28 6d and costs was imposed. REFUSING TO QUIT —John Highfield was fined 58 and costs for being drunk on licensed premises at Stretton, in the occupation of Mr. Hindley, on the 2nd inst., and with refusing to quit when requested. AN UNLICENSED HAWBEE.—William Lomax, Warring- ton, for hawking at Walton Superior. on the 18th inst., without a license, was fined ss, including Cost,. GAME TRESPASS.—Thomas Swift, Abel Grimshaw, Chas. Forster, and Samuel Rustage, were charged under the Poach- ing Prevention Act with coming from land where it was suspected they had been in search of game, en the 2nd inst. Prisoners were seen at Walton Superior by Sergeant Booth and P.C. Dutton, under suspicious circumstances. Op be- ing searched they were found to be in possession of nets, hares, and rabbits. Prisoners were each ordered to pay £5 and costs.

A VIOLENT IBISHMAN.—John Mitchell, an Irish labourer, was charged with being drunk and disorderly, and with wing malicious threats towards Charles William Phillips, landlord of the Ring-o'-Bells Inn, Daresbury, on the 25th inst. Defendant was very drunk and was behaving in a dis- graceful manner at Daresbury on the day named. The people living in the neighbourhood were going to church at the time, and were insulted by the defendant. When Mr. Phillips opened his house defendant attempted to enter; but was prevented from doing so. Defendant became exas- perated, pulled out a knife, and threatened to inflict serious injuries on the landlord. He also said he should mark him. Defendant was sent to gaol for one menth with hard labour. ATTEMPTED SUICIDE.—Mary Taylor, or Bostock, de- scribed as a widow, of Stockton Heath, was charged with attempting to commit suicide on the 22nd inst.—James Davies, a young man who works at Bank Quay chemical works, saw the prisoner on the banks of the river about nine o'clock on the morning in question. His attention was afterwards called to her being in the water. Be got a boat and went to her. She fainted when she jumped in, and although the water was only about three feet in depth her head was below the surface. He secured her, and took her across to the Lancashire side of the Mersey, where she re- ceived every attention, and was afterwards taken to the lock-up. When charged with the offence by Sergeant Booth she said that a man who had been courting, and who worked at Crosfield's soapery, told her she would be better in the river than anywhere else, and she thought she would go to the spot where she did in order that he might see her. Pri- soner's mother said her daughter bad had a great deal of trouble lately, and the magistrates bound the nrisoner over in the sum of £lO to be of good behaviour for ihree months, and ordered her to pay the costa.

Peck, John Doogan, and Ellen Atkinson were each fined for drunkenness.—Thomas Hart, of Stockton Heath, was fined 5e and costs, 10a od, for permitting his horse to stray in Brook-street, Runcorn. The deferdant said the pony had strayed from the stable at Stockton Heath.

NEWTON PETTY SESSIONS. SATIIRDAL—Before Messrs. R. Houghton and T. J. Gillespie. Dm:manorEss.—Martin Touhey was summoned for drun- kenness at Earlestown. The summons was dismissed.— Thomas Williams was summoned for being drunk and disor- derly at Earlestown on the 17th April. P.C.'s Lloyd and Hunt gave evidence. The defendant strongly denied the charge, said he was never drank in his life, and called two witnesses, both of whom swore that the defendant was sober. The magistrates considered the case proved, and fined defendant 5s and coats.—Michael Costello, for drunkenness, was fined 5s and costs.—Cain Edwardson was fined 5s and 'costs for drunkenness at Golborne, and William Heyes (Gol- borne) was fined a like amount for a similar offence.—Jas. ' McHugh, for being drunk and disorderly at Golborne was fined 105 and Costs. —Patrick Hallyhan and Richard Blower were summoned for drunkenness at Haydock, and were each fined 5e and costs. street, Ear- CHIMNEY ON Noden, Nelson. lestown, was summoned for having the chimney of his dwelling-house on fire on the 19th April, and was fined 3s 6d, including costs.

div.head: LIBERAL MEETING IN WARRINGTON.
div.p: LIBERAL MEETING IN WARRINGTON.

ADDRESS BY MR. JOSEPH LEICESTER, M.P. On Wednesday evening a largely-attended and entl siastie aggregate meeting of the Liberal Ward Committees was held in Wycliffe Hall to hear an address by Mr. Joseph Leiceeter, M.P. (labour representative for West Ham), en "Mr. Gladstone's proposals relative to the government of Ireland and the Irish Land Bill." The chair was taken by \ Mr. F. A. Roberts, and amongst those present were the Rev. R. Pilcher, 8.A., Rey. E. Moore, Dr. Gornall, Councillors W. Pierpoiat, Fleming, Broadbent. J.P., and Roberts ; Messrs. E. J. Guest, J.P., F. Monks., J.P., J. Walker, C. S. 1 Burgess, G. Plumpton, &c. , The Chairman, who was received with applause, said that he knew they were all sorry for the unavoidable ab- sence of Mr. .McMinnies, who was unfortunately again troubled with his old complaint. He would have very much liked to have been there to welcome Mr. leelcester. (Hear, hear.) To remove any misapprehension about the objects of that meeting he might say that it bad been called suddenly owing to their bearing that their old towns- man would tas in the neighbourhood and that there was a possibility of inducing him to come and say a few words to the Liberal committees in Warrington. It was not a meeting to formally take into consideration Mr. GI .aistone's pro , posals now before Parliament. At the proper time the ' Liberal Council would take those matters into their con- sideration, and it would be in their province to deal with them by resolution or otherwise. That night they were met to welcome lelr. Leicester to Warrington again—(ap- plause)—and to hear what be had got to tell diem of his recent life in the House of Commons. He did not suppose Mr. Leicester would regale them with anecdotes as to the court dresses he had been wearing or anything of that sort —(lataghter)—but he would tell them something of the weightier matters of current politics. (Applause.) Mr. Ismcessine, M.P., was received with loud applause. He said it was 42 years since he left the good old town of Warrington. He left it under very distressing circumstances; he was houseless, homeless, friendless, and nennilese, and he did not think any man could be in a worse condition than he was at that time. He had discovered this, that no man ought to depend upon a special providence for his success in the world. He believed that in a great measure they were masters of their own destinies. (Hear, bear.) During the whole time he had been away from that town he had been on the side of all that was progressive and on- ward. (Applause.) He had not, like certain gentlemen, affected the company of lords and dukes. He attributed his own success in the world to that perseverance with which God had endowed every man, and he sometimes taought he held his present position because of his t mperance princi- ples. (Loud applause.) He had discovered that the best side of a public-house was the outside—(bear, hear)—and be said to the young men there that if they wanted to get on in the world, if they wanted to be soneethieg, if they wanted to elevate themselves shoulder high above their fel- low men, there were three things they must do—keep outside the public-house, their hands out of their pockets, and the pipe out of their mouth. (Applause and laughter.) Through being a sober man he became a thoughtful man and a reading man, and when they wanted a man for West Ham they sent for him. (Laughter.) West Ham was a constituency of aristocracy—aristocracia—(laughter)—what very nice names these men g ate themselves. (Laughter.) Somehow or other they always used Greek words if there was any difficulty to be met. He read of a nobleman getting drunk and being tried by the Lord Mayor, the other day, and the counsel—those special pleaders and mystifiers of the law who made a lie into a truth and a truth into a lie—said his client was not drunk, it was simply dvresomania. (Laughter.) And if a lady began to thieve or steal they called it kleptomania. (Laughter and hear, hear.) But the aristocracy of West Ham were the real aristocracy ; they were the producers of the world's wealth, they were not the privileged classes, they were working-mac, and they determined to have a working-man to represent them in the House of Commons. (Applause.) They had no small diffi- culty to contend with, but they learned te believe in them- selves and in thorough organisation to the utmost extent of the meaning of that word. They could never win the battle unless they brought about the conditions of success, and what a shame it was for men like them (the audience) to have a suspended piece of animation to represent them in the House of Commons. (Laughter and hear, bear.) Why, their representative could not represeet himself let alone anyboely else. (Laughter.) He sat opposite him some- times, and he felt sorry that Warrington should have no voice to plead its ceases. If they were to have a Tory in the House of Commons, for goodness sake let them send somebody that could do something. (Laughter.) Referring to his electioneering experiences, Mr. Leicester said that n West Ham they had to contend against the fair radars. He thought they had been all dead, but he found they were not. (Laughter.) Ha told them that if they were men they would never take a mean advantage of free trade. They were willing to eat cheap food, to read cheap newspapers, and to wear cheap clothing, which the free traders had fought for. They were like trades unionists who believed in trade unions but would not pay. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) The speaker then men- tioned that there were a large nember of sugar refiners in West Ham whose trade was depressed, but to illustrate the evil consequences of a duty on sugar, be mentioned that he had bad a look round Paltners' large biscuit manufactory, in which about 1,200 men and women were engaged, and he was told that if the price ef sugar were raised those men and women would be thrown out of work. And with regard to the fact that every third man in certain worts was a German, he asked how it was if protection was such a blessed thing in Germany Germans came into England by thousands, and undersold Englishmen. (Hear, hear.) He also Pointed out that whoever raised the price of articles of food dropped the value of a man's wages, and he did not believe in low wages. (Applause.) The population of Eng- land in 1845 was eighteen millions, but now it was between thirty-four and thirty-five millions, and whilst the popula- tion had increased 60 per cent., trade had increased 500 per cent. (Applause.) They had to fight against the fair traders, and then they had the ladies of the Primrose League. He boned God would forgive them for the lies they told. (Laugh- ter.) Coming to the morning of the Bth April in the House of I Commons he said be then saw a scene which he would never I forget. He was there in the morning at eight o'clock— they made overtime in the House of Commons that day if they never made it before. (Laughter.) When he went in the morning at eight o'clock he thought he should be Arst, but be was very nearly last. Everybody felt the impulse of the moment, and when he went out he saw a great living mass of humanity. No great monarch ever rode more tri- umphant to the House than Gladstone did that day. (Pro- longed applause.) Within the HOll3O every seat was packed, and as he came, that man ef 77 summers, his head bleached with age, such a shout rang out, all the Liberals jumped to their feet with the exception of three—and the Irish mem- bers, 86 in number, stood like a wall of fire, and a shout went up as if they were common people. (Loud applause and laughter.) And as the grand old man stcod there he (Mr. Leicester) thought there was a tribute to genius, such a tribute as was never paid to man. There he was, forsaken by some of his friends, frowned on by his Queen, hated by the Tories, and looked down upon by others, but what was he? He was the greatest statesman ever God made. (Applause.) ' Continuing, Mr. Leicester said if he had to describe a Tory he should describe him as a man who never stole anything he could not lay hold of. (Laughter.) The Tory was a man who never acted; be was acted upon. He never moved unless he was shoved. (Laughter.) He did not believe a man ought to be praised for doing what he could not help doing. If it was a question in the House of beer and publicans the Tories were there, but if it was a matter of political rights they were very diffident in coming to the front. The work- ing-man was a felon when he wanted his rights. Mr. Gladstone Kaye Greece her freedom, and was not that an answer to Mr. Joseph Chamberlain, who spoke of Mr. Gladstone having said of Jeff Davis making a great na- tion. But that did not tell in the House, because more than Mr. Gladstone were mistaken. Fifteen millions of money was lent somewhere. Who lent It? The Lancashire men, when they were starving, when children were almost dying at their mother's breasts, refused to support the slave- holders. (Applause.) Proceeding, Mr. Leicester said that he bad no reason to tell them of the Land Bill of 1873, for Ireland. The House of Lords rejected the Land Bill. If that Bill had passed there would have been no more agrarian crime and bloodshed in Ireland. (Applause.) But the Lords kicked it out. What did they do in 1880, when they had another franchise bill? They kicked that out. With regard to the bill now pi oposed by Mr. Gladstone, he thought there were one or two questions they should ask themselves in relation to that matter. The question that first came to his mind was one of common sense, but common sense was not the sense that was common in the House of Commons sometimes. ' (Laughter and applause.) What was the question he desired to ask himself in approaching the subject as a working-man, hr working-men came to it in the rough? The only ques- tion they had to ask was—ls there a justification for this measure? Is there a necessity for ii? If a man's leg had to be taken off to save his life, you must do it, else he die. At the last election the Tories wanted to gain the Irish vote, but when they got it, and were defeated by the farm labourers, when the scales were turned on them they sent that man of paper, that paper man—(laughter)—to Ireland. He Mr. Leicester did not believe he ever arrived at Dublin. —(langhter)—but he came back and said that they would have to resort to the sword once more. Again the Tories acknowledged that nothing but the sword would do, and that they must go back to coercion. There was another question. In Ireland there were 30,000 troops, maintained at a cost of nearly 4i millions per annum, which meant more soldiers to govern Ireland than there were in America. There were also 12,000 armed constabulary-42,000 men to keep five million people in order. That, to his mind, showed the absolute necessity for a change in the mode of govern- ment of Ireland, and he knew that the examination the bill would have in the House of Commoas would not allow any- thing to pass that was prejudicial to England. (Applause.) Did they ever know a nation well governed to reLel ? Such a thing was not knewa in history. They might say that Ireland had stumbled here and there, but what if she had ? If a person were struggling in the water for dear life, and a hand was held out to save him, would be refuse it because it was the hand of a Pirate ? In her terrible struggle for freedom Ireland might have gone wrong, but she had struggled manfully, and had stuck to it for 86 years, and with the exception of two years there had been coercion during the whole of that time. (Shame.) He said that there was a justification for the measure. The death of all sedition and rebellion was good government, and Mr. Gladstone proposed that. (Ap- plause.) The reason Lord Hartington had given for his ‘
thn-

attitude on the subject was like a single grain of wheat hid in a bushel of chaff; they might search all day ..;ere they found it, and when they had found it it was not worth" the search. - (Laughter and applause.) Lord Hartington said that every blessing the Irish claimed in their own govern- ment they could have from ours. But how was it then that rebellion went on? He (Mr. Leicester) had sees the sun set three times for ever. (Laughter.) It set when the Reform Bill of 1532 was passed, when the royal Duke of Wellington said that the sun would never shine again. 3 hat was the argument of the landlord power of that day, and it was the same argument of the landlord power now. When they bad got the Reform Bill it gave political life, political i force and action, and scene and power in every direction. Then it was that they abolished slavery, repealed the bread i tax, and abolished the tax on knowledge. If increased re- sponsibility had so acted in the case of England, what would not it do for Ireland, and Mr. Gladstone's Land Bill gave responsibility to the people and power to use it. (Applause.) They said Irishmen were lazy. Well, he was not lazy when he fought; he was not lazy at Waterloo. The bravest men that ever met on a field of battle were Irishmen. (Hear, hear.) Shiel was an Irishman, O'Connell was an Irishman, Grattan was ap Irishman, and the greatest orator that ever ! stood on the floor of the House except Gladstone, was an Irishman, Richard Brinsley Sheridan ; the late President of America and the late Prime Minister of Spain were Irishmen. (Applause.) Did they tell him that these men were lazy ? Trust them, and see if they were lazy or not. (Applause.) The Irish abroad sent four and a half millions of money every year to their dis- tressed friends in Ireland. and ho was it they could send that enormous sum if they were lazy? He had written to Mr. Parnell and be said that at any rate it was not less than £4,500,0,30. If they bettered the condition of Ireland the results would be better. (Applause.) They had tried coercion in Canada and it failed, and during the last 50 years, with the exception of two, Ireland had been under coercion. ("Shaine.") If they went back to coercion every house in Ireland would be a battleground, and what about the greater Ireland without? (Hear, hear.) At the present tinie the 86 Irish members were factors in tbe destinies of England. They would prevent the Tories doing anything when they felt inclined, and heaven knew that was very seldom—(laughter)—and if the Liberals wanted to take away the death-grip from the the land they would be pre- vented. Ten million acres of land might be cultivated to- day if the land were freed, but if Mr. Gladstone attempted to deal with it the List), if they still wanted freedom, would stop him. The fact that the Irish could turn an election ire the country was one which should be seriously considered by Lord Hartington and Mr. Chamber- , lain. ( sear. bean) They found that out in Warrington at I the last election. ( laughter.) They had got for Warring- ton no representative at all, only the worst of it is tit' Gilbert's vote went as far as his. (Laughter.) Wartington was Litieral, everybody knew that, but the Irishmen would make it impossible to send their own man. He said that the present bill must pass. (Hear, bear.) They talked about bastard oelections but, as Mr. Whitbread had said, their remedies were behind the times, the public was before them, 1 their objections were too late, and what did it mean but mis- trust and want of faith in Irishmen, as though, as Mr. Glad- stone put it, they had been cursed with a double dose of 1 original sin. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) His (Mr. Leices- ter's) idea of tee scheme was this, that it meant confidence in Ireland, faith in Ireland, and faith in the good that was in men and not in the bad. (Applause.) And he said that as sure as they were there that night the bill would pass and what was wrong in it would be righted. (Hear, hear.) What was in it that did not square with their convictions would be subjected to severe criticism, and be had faith in the re- suit, because the sentiment of the people had already gone ' with it. He had been all over the country, and everywhere it was the same. Some of Mr. Chamberlain's best friends ' had told him that if he had left the room at Birmingham 1 the meeting would have gone against him. Mr. Chamber- ' lain was not so popular in Birmingham since be deserted the grand old man. (Applause.) He (Mr. Leicester) was sorry Me old friend Mr. Peter Rylands had gone wrong; but this he would prophecy, that Mr. Peter Rylands had sat in the House of Commons for the last time. (Applause.) This he also knew, that every one of the twelve men who represented labour in the House, from Joseph Arch to Joseph Leicester. would stand up for freedom of right, truth against falsehood, light against darkness, God against the devil. (Loud applause.) Mr. MONKS moved the following motion: "That the members of the Warrington Liberal Association offer- to • their old townsman, Mr. Joseph Leicester, M.P., their heartiest congratulations on his elevation to the House of Commons, and at the seme time thank him most cordially . for his able and interesting address." (Applause.) He was I particularly glad to find that Mr. Leicester was so thorough a Radical. A man of his type would be of great value in the coming struggle with the House of Lords. (Hear, hear.) Tney were not at that meeting to discuss the Irish question ; the proper time for that would be when the council met to which they would all be summoned, but he was quite sure that Mr. Leicester had helped many of them to understand that question much better than perhaps they would otherwise have done. He was not there to thank Mr. Leicester for every word he had said in reference to that question. He yielded to no man in his admiration of Mr. Gladstone and the work he had done for the Liberal party, and he also said this that be had the greatest ad- miration for the tone in which the Marquis of Hartington and Mr. Chamberlain had discussed that question in refer- ence to Mr. Gladstone and his personality. He thought their thanks were particularly due to those men beCause they bad raised the whole level of the discussion. The matter had to be discussed and he hoped the day was far distant wheboLiberals would hiss and boot the men who differed fronrehem. (Applause.) . The Rev. R. FILCHRR seconded the proposal, and said he was one of these who had sprung from the people, belonged to the people, and trusted in the people, and be was .a fop- lower of Mr. Gladstone,not because he was Mr. Gladstone, but because he embodied the great principles of justice to the people. (Applause.) And he was one of those who meant to stick to Mr. Gladstone. (Applause.) He was per- fectly convinced that if the English people faced that ques- tion as it would have to be faced, and when they became convinced of the real justice of the thing they would face it maefully and generously. (Applause). Mr. STIRRUP also supported the resolution which was carried with acclamation, and Mr. larcsrruu suitably ac- knowledged the compliment. The CHAIRMAN said that be thought they should almost get a promise from Mr. Leicester to come again and address a larger meeting in the Public Hall. (Applause.) Novt they had made hi • acquaintance they should like to know a little more of him, and they had been so well pleased that evening that they would like to give the remainder of the party an opportunity of hearing him. (Applause.) The Rev. E. Mooau proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman. He remarked that be had thoroughly enjoyed the address Mr. Leicester had given, and thoroughly agreed with it. ~tp!.,,
Mr. LEICESTER seconded the vote of thanks, which was carried with applause, and the meeting terminated.

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MAY I. 1886.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MAY I. 1886.

AVERY IMPORTANT CONSIDERATION. A most important consideration for all at this season of the year is how best to rid the system of the diseases induced by the trials of winter. In many cases it seems as Ough the seeds of consumption had been planted in the system by the trying weather we have gone through. The symptoms may have commenced with a slight cold, a little sore. throat and hoarseness, then come, perhaps, a feeling of weakness, or chil- liness, ace onpanied or followed by aching of the limbs; now and again a hot, dry, feeling of the akin; general feverishness; tightness in the chest, with diffietilty of breathing; a little cough, short and dry, then soma expectoration; the weakness Increases, and friends become anxious. In other cases various forms of Liver or Kidney Complaints are deveksped ; the lassitude becomes nervous wesknese•; the sleep is uneasy, and troubled by unpleasant dreams; and ne patient, instead of waking refreshed, gets up with a feeling of weight and ,anguor, and every action seems a burden. Others again begin the spring with what appears like con- firmed Indigestion; headsches, bile, loss of appetite, a gnawing sensation at the stomach, a sense of ' fulness and oppression, pains in the breast or bowels, or in the region of the heart, are all so many signs that the stomach is out of order. These are a few only of various form of complaints from which ynt2 may be suffering. YOU need not continue to suffer, as I shall show. The system is more liable to thee at.acks in the spring and early summer, as the bodily powers have been reduced by the trials of winter. It is of the greatest impor- tance to pay attention to the general health at this season. This is why doctors prescribe so generally a good tonic medicine to be taken during the present months. ( Concluded.) , ilisitilffbcas to the distaiice of 'AMlveicli sled to a reply which, to my unaccustomed ears, sounded like " Pemilk an a (pare," with which valuable piece of information I was forced to be content, and, after thanking my obliging- informant, pro- ceeded upon my way rejoicing. There is something delightfully vague about such a reply. It may mean anything; val; riator, or go to Bath. It may be most excellent joke, the delicate aroma of which is utterly lost upon the recipient ; a neatly turned compliment, or a query as to whether your mater- nal parent is aware of your absence from home. But this uncertainty amounts to the appalling when in company with a carriage full of vivacious and loquacious Cambrian nymphs. You can only hope that as they are mighty so they will be merciful. Less ambiguous and more amusing it is to note the vagaries of "English as she is spoke" in Wales. As an instance, which occurred nearer home, a Welshman in charge of a savage-looking dog, whose. plentiful display of calf-rending teeth indicated anything but an amiable disposition, when asked if the dog was quiet, replied "He would not bite very proper.". At Rhosgoch vocally Trusco a dexterous blending of a hosk and a cough, I took train to Amlwych. This little town is irregularly built both as to plan and elevation. It owes its exiStence to the fact that the neighbouring hills afford an abundance of copper ore, and also that here the iron-bound coast has a cleft in the rocks wherein small vessels may find a more or less safe harbour and loading berth. This gorge or cleft, whose precipitous sides at their widest will not exceed 100: yards apart, affords a tolerably secure port in any but very heavy northerly winds, in which case a sort of gate is thrown across the narrow part of the entrance, where it is about 25ft. wide. This gate—or boom as it is called---is composed of square beams of timber, the ends of which are dropped into grooves on the face of the pier and so bar the entrance to the little harbour. By this expedient they only hope to debar a portion of the heavy seas which. thunder upon this rock-lined coast. Occa- sionally, in very heavy northerly weather some of the larger seas over-ride all obstacles and, laughing at the feeble opposition of boom and piers, topple into the little harbour, to the disturbance- of its contents,. the straining of ropes, and the rubbing of sides. However, the place was now indeed a haven of rest. The light breeze was off shore, and what bit of seascape was visible through the mouth of the fissure lay smiling in the sunlight, which served to give just a pleasant sparkle to its surface; A Liverpool speculation gig rowed out and crept along shore towards Holyhead, and a "flat ". was preparing for sea bound for Conway. The "hand," a poor fellow with a wooden leg—but merry withal —went stumping about the narrow decks, setting; things taut and "fakeing "down to a running accom- paniment of jokes and bright pleasantries. Seeing me upon the pierhead suggested a wicked one to be played upon a poor Welshman who, it seems, had been discharging the "flat." He persuade(' thiS in- nocent that I had something to do with thecargo and, therefore, a likely subject from whom, "Slow- ance " or. its equivalent in Welsh might possibly be extracted: Now, the Welshman knew as little of English as I of Welsh, so the fight was a fair and square one. After a severe tongue tussle he de- scended the pierhead to his boat, and if it is pos- sible to, swear in Welsh that man did it! his coun- tenance had volumes of anathema writtenthereon, and doubtless poor timber-toes came in for a liberal allowance, of sinister blessings in his native dOric. In the harbour lay a fine new three-masted, iron schooner, the "Elizabeth Peers," lately built and fitted out here. This job must have been a'weleome one to the place in the depressed state of its-trade consequent upon the closing of most if not all the copper mines in the vicinity, and the consequent ' falling off' of its carrying trade. Copper mining , seems to be unprofitable here owing to cheaper if not better ore being obtained from abroad. From, Amlwych my route lay across the island to Menai Bridge, through some very park-like scenery, many beautiful bits of which I much regret not to have pictures of, except the very fleeting ones of memory. And herein lies the advantage possessed by the "-camera maniac "-- he can verify his- memories by reference to less perishable records, and so share his pleasures with friends upon his return. Reached Menai Bridge in nice time for the steamer leaving here at 3 p.m. for Liverpool. Past Bangor, Garth, and Gallows Point, avoiding the visible dangers of Puffin Island on the one side, and the submerged embarrassments of- the Levan sands on the other, we sped swiftly across the beautiful Bay of Penmaen. Here we sighted our old friend, the flat "John." of Liverpool, last from Amlwych, hanging about the mouth of the Conway for want of wind to carry him in. and the flood tide near spent. Was it the Welshman's malediction had thus reduced my sportive friend to this strait? Anyhow, there he was waiting, whistling, and wishing for the wind that was to carry them to Conway, safety and comfort. What a: contrast she presented to our swiftly speeding steamer cutting the green water into feathers by. her trenchant prow, churning it into effervescence by her dashing paddles, and leaving it seething in a broad white wake 1)s. she rushes with headlong speed from port to port; the one representing the old and more leisurely mode of ocean travel, with its almost entire dependence upon the fickle elements, the other the modern high-pressure,, hot-pressed, and feverish hurry of this eager age. The wall-like Ormeshead soon hid this ancient mariner from our view. Calling at Llandudno, we exchanged passengers on the give and take prin- ciple. And then, overrunning the constable,' we. came abreast of Rhyl about dark; picked up the, Swash buoy after some eager peering through the, binoculars, and ran up the Horse and Rock Chan, nels into the busy waters of Liverpool.

div.head: LIBERAL DEMONSTRATION ON HOME
div.p: LIBERAL DEMONSTRATION ON HOME
RULE AT WIDNES.

A meeting of Liberals was held in the Baths Assembly Room, Widnes, on Wednesday night, for 'Or purpose of considering Mr. Gladstone's Irish Volley. The meeting had been called by the Liberal Association, and the room was crowded with an attentive and enthusiastic audience. Mr. E. K. Muspratt, J.P., who had a most cordial reception, occupied the chair, and he was supported on the plat- fOrm by Dr Commit', M P, Messrs E R Russell. P, T S Timmis, J P, E Carey, S K Mnspratt, J Morrison, F Hayes, and H B Shores (secretary), - The Secretary read a letter of apology for non-attendance from Mr. F. H. Gossage, J.P.,. who said: "1 hope a resolu- tion will be unanimously passed expressing sympathy with Mr. Gladstone in his splendid effott—(applause)—to bring about a lasting peace between England and Ireland—(as- plause)—and confidence that he and his colleagues will succeed in passing a measure which will satisfy the just claims of Ireland without injury to Imperial interests." (Applause.) Captain Henry Brunner wrote: "-I bops it will be a successful meeting, and that a strone resolution in ,fittpport of Mr. Gladstone's noble measure with be passed. The more I consider the two bills, the more satisfied and cm:winced Ifeet as to their wisdom and safety—(hear, bear, and applause)—and commend them heartily to my fellow- townsmen for their best consideration and support." (Ap- plause.)
i succeed

The Chairman, after maintaining that the question of Home Mile was before the electors at the general election, said it was perfectly clear to anyone who gave a single thought to the question that if Ireland returned, as she had done, 86 Nationalists to the House of Commons—(cheers)— that the present Parliament would have ho consider what policy should be adopted towards that country. If we ignored their demands it was clear there was only one policy left, and that was consistent and persistent coercion. (Hisses.) That was after all the only alternative policy before the country, because none of those who ob- jected to the scheme of Government had given us any alter- native policy with the exception of Mr. Chamberlain. (Groans.) As he pointed out at the general election, we ought to endeavour from a Liberal point of view to ask ourselves how much andnot how little Home Rule we could grant to them—(applause):--and that he was glad to say had been the guiding principle of Mr. Gladstone's Home Rule Bill—(renewed applause)—and it was fer that reason that it bad found acceptance at the hands of Mr. Parnell and those who followed him. (Loud applause.) That bill granted full legislative power to Ireland with certain exceptions. There were some who said we ought to define what subjects they should have the right to deal with, and then that the Imperial Government should deal with all the others. He maintained that if we acted in that spirit it woold be an ungracious act, and would sot be likely to earn the gratitude of Irishmen. (Applause.) What ought a great statesman to do on an occasion of this kind? He was reading the other day an address by Mr. Emerson, the great American phileseehier, made before President Lincoln brought in the Emancipation proclamation, and these words were so appropriate to the great occasion with which we had to deal in this country that he would read them:—" Now, in the name of all that is simple and gen- erous, why should not this great right be done? It is very certain that the statesman who shall break through the cobwebs of doubt, fear and petty cavil that be in the way will be greeted by the unanimous thanks of mankind. Men reconcile themselves very fast to a bold and good measure when once it is taken, though they condemned it in ad- vance." He maintained that was the exact position in this country. There were many Liberals and nearly every Tery who had condemned Mr. Gladstone's measures in. advance,

but Mr. Gladstone had brought in a great and bold measure, and it was because it was a great and bold measure that he believed when it was thoroughly understood by the country it would be carried by acclamation. (Loud applause.) A 'truly Liberal policy was a policy of trust in the people (applause) and he said that that included trust in the Irish people. (Applause.) We had not granted the extension of the franchise to the Irish people that we should ignore the demands of their representatives. (Hear, hear.) The Tories did, not object to the prinsiple of the bill, but told us of the dreadful things that wou4d happen if the measures were carried. But had not they told us before of the dreidful things that would happen when j any Liberal measure was brought forward and proposed to Ibe carried. (Hear, hear.) If they sincerely believed what they said, and if they believed that this great empire 'es going to be destroyed if we granted Home Rule to Ireland, did they think they would be content with one or two speeches in Parliament or an opera House, ard then going away and leaving the country to decide for themselvel. Where was Lord Salisbury and Lord Randolph Churchill. (Loud groans.) They took very great care to keep out of' the fray because, as Mr. John Morley—(cheers)—had told. them if this bill were not carried they woeld themselvea cirry a similar measure. (Applause.) He denied that ther granting of autonomy to Ireland would be at all compar- able to the granting of autonomy to the Turkish provinces, because the circumstances were not analogous. Let them do jostice to Ireland. That was the cry of all Liberal!, and he hoped that with very few exceptions all th 3 Liberals in this district would rally round their great leader and enable him to carry these two great measures, which he hoped and trusted would lead to the final settlement of the Irish. question. (Loud pplause.) Mr. T. S. Timmis moved "That this meoting desires to record its hearty approval of the principles- upon which the Government of Ireland Bill and the Sale and Purchase of Land (Ireland) ,Bill are based, believing that these prin- ciplese if carried into effect, will bring peace to Ireland and increased strength to the Empire." (Loud applause.) Per- haps, he said, some of his friends might feel somewhat sur- prised to see him on that platform advocating that resolu- tioneand twelve months ago be should have been equally surprised. But a good many things had happened since then. The general election, he said, had enabled Ireland for the first time to speak its mind as a nation. (Cheers.) We had tried coercion and conciliation, and now we were going to trust the Irish, which we had not done before. (Cheers.) He did not believe that the measures of Mr. Gladstone meant separation, bat rather that they meant in- creased unity and strength to the Empire. From 30 years' experience of Irishmen he felt certain that the Irish were an honest race, and he believed • they would stick to their part of the bargain. t,Cheers.) Mr. F. Heys seconded the resolution with very great pleasure. he had been a Home Ruler ever since he had thought on the subject at all—(applause)—and he was quite sure that if these measures were carried they would conduce to The peace and prosperity of the empire. (Applause.) Dr. Commins and Mr. E. R. Russell supported the reso- lution, which was carried enthusiastically. On the motion of Mr. Joseph Morrison it was decided to forward a copy of the resolution to Mr. Gladstone. It was also agreed, on the suggestion of the Chairman, to send a copy of the resolution to Lord Hartington and Mr. Cham- berlain. (k Voice: Send another to Moss. Loud laugh- ter.) The Chairman said he thought some of the audience might do that as they were his constituents. (Laughter) The customary votes of thanks concluded the proceedings.

Gibbon, A. Fryer, James Baird, T. Dagnall, and Woods (vestry clerk).—The Chair- man appointed Mr. G. Armstrong to be vicar's warden, and Mr. John Baird was elected parishioners' warden; Messrs. James Baird and E. Gibbon were appointed aidesmen ; ,and Messrs. John Baird and E. Gibbon lay representatives.—The balance sheet of the church shows that the income for the past year was £59 Hs sd, the expenditure £5B 2s 4d ;, Warm, ,131 IGs Id.

HOLY TRINITY. WARRINGTON. The vestry meeting in connection with Holy Trinity Church was held on Monday morning. The vicar, the Bay. E. C. E. Carleton, presided, and there were also present Messrs. W. J. Burgess and John Hatton (retiring wardens), and A. Brimelow. Mr. Hatton submitted the churchwar- dens accounts whieh showed that the total receipts had been £221 14e sid including a balance of £l2 18s lad, and the total expenditure £195 Is 10-Id, leaving a balance in hand' of £32 123 7d. there being, however, bills amounting to something like £4O yet to par. On the motion of the chairman, seconded by Mr. Brimelow, the accounts were passed. The vicar again nominated Mr. Hatton as, his warden, remarking that they could get no one to de the work more efficiently than Mr. Hatton did it. On the mo- tion of Mr. Burgess, seconded by Mr. Brimelow, Mr. R. Rowson was appointed parishioners warden. The follow- ing were also appointed :—Sideemen : Messrs. R. Dobson. junr., E. Booth, J. Hatton, and James Harding. Lay re- presentatives: Messrs. G. White and J. Faircleugh. Vestry Clerk: Mr. H. B. White. This was all the business. ST. BARNABAS, WARRINGTON. The vestry meeting of this church was held on Tuesday evening. The Rim. G. Alltoo, N icar, presided, and there were also present Messrs. Roscoe, Kent, Denham, Smith,and Parsonage. The Chairman, in submitting the accounts, tendered his best thanks to the churchwardens (Messrs. Smith and Denham) for the hearty support they and their families have rendered him during the past year. It was a matter of thankfulness that they had been able to tide over the difficulties of another year under the distress and many other hindrances- that prevailed in that large parish. In the past year they had established in the parish every kind of parochial machinery—club, classes, band, chasities4rc., and all these things had been attended with large outlay; but he was happy to sly they were all new all clear and in full working order. The income for the past year in con- nection with tbe church was £7l 153 11d, and the expenses were £B2-9/3 Ohl,but as he wished their church to be out of debt he had again cleared off the adverse balance. He then stated that he would be glad to again nominate Mr:Smith as vicar's warden. Mr. Denham was also re-elected parish- ionerewarden. Messrs. Yeomans, G. Bradburn,,T. Kilahaw, beattergood,. Mather, and Parsonage were appointed sides- man; and Mesas. Brown and Yeomans lay representatives. This was-all the business.

div.head: ST. PAUL'S, WARRINGTON.
div.p: ST. PAUL'S, WARRINGTON.

The annual vestry meeting in connection with St. Paul's Church, Warrington, was held on Monday morning. The chair was occupied by the Vicar, the Rev. S. Wilkinson, and amongst those also present were Messrs-T. Sutton, D. W. Finney, Pbllitt, Asburst, Jeans (vestry clerk), ikc.—Be- fore the commencement of business, the Chairman said that they had bad another year of happy, pleasant work. They had had very few alteratioes during 18854 but they must all deeply deplore the loss of Mr. James Craik,. who took such a deep interest in the work of the church,. though he would never take office; he was one of those modest, quiet men, who would do all the good they couldwithout pushing tkemselves forward. He then paid a well deserved tribute of praise to Mr. Jolley, vicar's warden, Mr. Sutton, people's warden, and Mr. Jeans, vestry clerk. He hoped that in the future year they would be as successful and happy as they had been in the past oae. There had been considerable im- provements in the churchyard during the year, and in regard to that the work of Mr. Finney was prominent.—Mr. Sutton read the annual financial statement. Last year, be said, they commenced with a debt of between £3O ancl£4o. Their expenses, including old debts, amoanted to £lB9 is Id. ; The income from pew rates had been £3l 17s 11d, Sunday evening collections, leaving out those of special objects, amounted to £lOB 5.9 ed, for the annual tea party £24 is 11 was received, making a total, income for the year of £166 Be 4d, and leaving a balance of £22 12s 9d due to the war- dens.. They were, therefore, a little better off this year than last with regard to their liabilities. In addition to the ordinary expenses connected with the church, the war- dens had this year been able to- pay off about £l3O of the debt owing in respect to the alteration and decoration of the church, and also to expend about £l2O on the church- yard. The Chairman considered the report very satisfac- tory. The accounts were then passed on the motion of Mr. Pollitt, seconded by Mr. Ashurst.--The Vicar ap- pointed Mr. Jolley as his warden for the en- suing year, and Mr. Sutton was re-elected people's warden on the proposition of Mr. Finney, seconded by Mr. Pollitt.—Messrs. Ashurst, T. Morris, W. Lawless, J. Smethurst, W. Pollitt, and D. Jones were appointed sides- men, the first two being appointed by the wardens, and the latter four on the motion of Mr. J. Lawtoa, seconded by Mr. J. Lawless.—On the.propositson of Mr. Ashurst, secon- , ded by Mr. Sutton, Messrs. W. Richardson and D. W. Fin- ney were elected lay representatives to attend such confer- ences of the clergy and laity of the deanery of Winwick as may be held during the year.—Mr. Jeans was re-elected vestry clerk and thanked for his services. ST. JAMES', LATCHFORD. The vestry meeting of St. James' Church, Latchford, was held in the vestry ot the church on Monday. The Bev. F. Slater (vicar) presided, and there were also present Messrs. J. Taylor. T. Hutchinson (retiring wardens), J. Worrell, T. Walton, W. S. Abrahams, T. Jackson, and C. S. Burgess. Mr. Hutchinson presented the churchwardens' accounts, which showed that th,, total receipts had been £1.85 17s 3d, and after the expenditure had been met there would be a balance against the churchwardens of £5l lie 2cl.—On the motion of Mr. Worralt, seconded by Mr. Burgess the ac- counts were passed.—The Chairman explained with regard to the adverse balance that the gross amount of the offer- to7ies this year were less than last year by £2O, bat oat of that £2O £l5 last year was for special offertories,. so that as a matter of fact the general offertory was only about £5 less this year than last. There had also been a great strain upon them in connection with the new schools, and no doutt the depression iu trade had something to do with the lessening of the offertories. He also mentioned that their last tea party had not been so successful as it usually was, owing to their not being able to have a pantomime in con- nection with it.—The Chairman then again no.rainated Mr. Hutchinson as vicar's warden for the coming year,. aad Mr. Taylor was re-elected parishioners' warden. Messrs. Won; rall, Walton, Jackson. and Andrews were appointed sides- men; Megsrs. H. N. Houghton and C. S. Burgese lay repre- sentative; and Mr. Abraham vestry clerk. Votes-of thanks to the retiring churchwardens concluded the proceedings.
PREII AND OPBN OIEURCHBS. Mr. Imison moved, and Mr. Whittaker seconded $ motion that the pews be rated as usual for the ensuing year.

- Mr. Moss said as he intended to vote against that two's' tion perhaps he might be allowed to state his reasons for adopting that course. In the parish magazine a short One ago the opinions of the vicar in favour of making the church free and open were quoted. He was led to believe that that extract was intended to prepare the minds of the public for some change being made at that vestry meeting, and be should be sorry and disappointed if they had to go on as before and appropriate about three-fourtbs of the area of the church to certain individuals, leaving the rest of the town- ship of 15,000 inhabitants to be accommodated is 20 free seats. This was one of the greatest abuses in connection with the Church of England. They heard a great dial about church reform, and the Bishop of Peterborough Was doing his best in the House of Lords to put an end to the very abuse which they in Runcorn were seeking to perpetn" ate. He could fully sympathise with those churchmen who liked to have a pew to themselves, because it was very' comfortable. He had a seat to himself and he liked it; but he thought that all churchmen ought to Wel . at this matter not merely from a persons ' point of view, but with reeard to the interests of the Church of England. They ought to rernete- ber that the Church of England was not a private establiehe moot to be regulated simply with regard to personal coca- . fort. Every ratepayer had a right to a seat in the chnteh:, ' I At the eeneral election the cry of "The Church in Danger' was raised, and they saw clergymen and laymen on the same platform appealing to the people to vote in favour Of the church as by law established, and maintain the cennen' tion between Church and State. That was one way of defending the church, but it was not his way. He failed to see what interest, the masses of the people could have In supporting a church from which they were practicallY excluded, and which was kept for tbe benefit of a privileged few. He was one of those Liberal Churchmen who were sometimes accused of betraying their church of leaving the church ata critical time, but he was as anxious for the advance of the church as anybody else. The wa° to advance the church would be to open the doors to the masses of the people and invite them to enter ire!. When that was done they would have a parish church in the true sense of the word, and a worthy branch of the' national church. Until that was done, bow could thee' appeal to the people to defend the church with any hoPe when the time came that the church was on her trial, as assuredly would. He wished, as a humble churehman, to wash . his bands of any responsibility in the matter. bl voting against the resolution. The Chairman : nave no feeling in the matter. lam ill the hands of the parishioners. At the same time, I don't see how you can improve the present plan The church bs entirely free at night, and every morning as soon as the bell stops everybody are allowed to sit where they please. - Mr: Ligbtburn said, the church was to all intents and PS' poses free and open. There was no exclusion; the ',WWI* were not pushed into the obscure corners, they had the veri best seats in the church, and he did net see any reason Why they should alter the present system. The Rev. R. Edwards explained that the opinions-pube lished in the Parish Magazine were from letters published by the vicar 20 years ago. Mr. Edwards argued that every parish church ought to be free and open to all the parishioners alike, but in the present instance there were several things to be taken into consideration. Beveral gentlemen had ex- pressed to him that it would be unjust and unfair to-move an amendment that the church should be free and open, because the sum of £BO or £9O would have to be forth" coming for church expenses from some other source.. The poor man was as much a churchman to him as a rich man, and therefore the poor man had as much right in the church as the rich man. He mentioned instances where visitors to the church had been removed from seats they badoesuoied, not becanime they were filled, but lossause they weae apPr°' priated. . ' ._ _ _

ST. MICHAEL'S CHURCH, BURTON WOOD. The annual vestry meting was held on Monday evening. The Rev. W. Wilson, vicar, presided. The aecoants showed the receipts for the year to be £B3 13i 4d, and the expendi- ture £59 34 Bd, leaving a balance of £24 9s 81 Messrs. T. Hewitt and J. Forster were re-elected wardens, and Messrs. T. Howard and J. Fairclough sidesmen. HALTON PARISH CHURCH.

The annual meetior of the parishioners was held on Tuesday evening under the presidency of the Bay. J. Lock- wood, vicar. The statement of accounts showed that after paying off a deficit of £l6 5s 3d a balance in band was left of £4 Os 10d. Mr. John Rutter was re-appointed vicar's warden and Mr. Joseph Stokes was, appointed people's warden. Messrs. A. Woodier, John Ackerley, Wm. Nickson, and Edward Buckley were elected sidesmen. DITTON PARISH CHURCH:

Tbe annual vestry meeting of Ditt-on—ei";:rch was held on Monday evening, under the presidency of the Vicar, the Rev. C. WooII. The accounts, which showed a deficit of £2 N 11d, were passed. Mr. Joseph Longton, Ditehfield Hall. was re-elected vicar's warden, and Mr. John Lucas, Hough Green, was elected people's warden. The following were appointed sidemen :—Messrs. Kyle, Lewis, Beryl, and Smith. Messrs. Beryl and Lewis were appointed-lay represen- tatives. A vote of thanks was accorded the vicar and churchwardens, and the meeting closed.

Mr. Imisou argued that a meeting of the ctongregation ought to be specially summoned for the purpose og giving their opinion as to whether this change was desirable or not before it was dealt with. He hoped that meeting would show its disapprobatim of any such scheme until the opinion, of the congregation had been obtained. (Heart hear.) Mr. Lake said that in a matter like that it was. perhaps ae great a mistake to exaggerate as it was to underestimate ; and he thought Mr. Moss in saying that only twenty gala ..were sat apart as free seats for 15,000 people. was an oar geration, because he left out a consideration altogether Trinity Church and the various mission-rooms, which pro: vided accommodation for a large number of people. He dia not see how they could manage without the pew rates, and he hoped the vestry would pass the original resolution. Mr. Mellor said before the resolution was passed he shoal& like to say that as long as n pew rate waa necessary some better system of rating should be adopted than the present. He now wished to urge the matter by mowing that all the pews be let at a uniform rate by the wardens. He knew of pews down the centre able which were rated at £2, bang sub-let for £3. The pound was put in the pockets of,Pri- vate persons, which he considered was a great shame. Mr. Lake said there were several cases were pews were rated at £1 and £2, and the owners were sub-letting therO £2 and £3. He mild only say that if the seat-.holdere would insist upon paying their rates to the wardens, who alone were entitled tereceive them, it would break down the system, and it would be a great deal better financially for the church. Mr. Lightburn : From your own knowledge are there three cases of that sort? _
Mr. Lake: Three ! I should say, speaking of the boat that there are 13. Mr. Mellor then proposed that the seats down the south centre aisle be rated at a per annual and the rest at £2.
Mr. hub.= said it was curious to find one who stronglY advocated a free and open church moving that the pews ba rated.

Mr. Mellor observed that the reason he had spoken vial,l because he thought that so long as the pews must be rate(' that they should have a uniform charge. He thought that private individuals should not be allowed to make mono' out of the pews. but that the whole should go towards the church. Mr. Mailer's amendment was not seconded, and the ori* ghaal proposition was carried. tbe The choir were heartly thanked for their services, 1311 motion of Mr. Lake, seconded by Mr. Barker, and the Pr°P. ceedings afterwards concluded.
