On Monday evening a meetinr, of the parishioners was held in the National Schoolroom for the purpose of select- ing churchwardens for the ensuing year. The outgoing churchwardens were Mr. J. Hall and 'Mr. T. Gerrard. The vicar, Rev. A. P. Reynolds. appointed Mr. Seaward. of Peel Hall, Kingsley, as his warden; Dr. Steel, Newton Hall, was elected people's warden. The retiring wardens had a small sum in hand, which it was proposed should be devoted to repair of the chancel of the church. It was suggested at the meeting that all the sittings in the church should be free, but after some discussion it was decided not to adopt such a course at present.. ST. HELEN'S CHURCH, HOLLINFARE. The annual vestry meeting was held in the vestry on Tuesday, and was well attended. The Vicar (the Rev. G. F. Roberts) presided.—The accounts of the outgoing war- dens, showing a balance against them of were found cor- rect and passed ; and the wardens were accorded a vote of thanks for their services,--Mr. Wm. Cawley and Mr. John Higham were elected wardens for the ensuing year, the for- mer by the Vicar and the latter by the parishioners, Mr. John Cawley and Mr. James Arstale being their respective sidesmen.—Mr. William Cawley and Mr. Richard Graham were elected lay representatives at the diocesan conferences. —The Vicar presented &balance sheet to the churchwardens, handing over to them.the church completely restored at a final cost of £214 15s, free from debt e: and a cordial vote of thanks to him for his services was. unanimously carried. This concluded the business of the meetin-

al g. FARNWORTH'' PARISH CHURCH. The vestry meeting at St.,Luke'S Parish Church, Fun- worth, was held on Monday nighta.in the chancel, tntder the presidency of the Rev. George Bond, vicar. The balance sheet showed a total income of £lO3 6s 2y, and expendi- ture £lO9 12s 10, leaving a balance againgt the church- wardens of 46 6s Bd.—On the motion of Mr. Kidd, seconded by Mr:Glover, the•accounts were passed.—Mr. Bond nomi- nated Mr. Longton as his warden.—Mr. Thomas Baker was appointed warden for Bold, Mr. Matthew Taylor for Cuerd- ley, and Mr. J. W: Wareing for Cronton. The whole of the sidesnien and church council were reappointed. Messrs. Peter Longton and J.W.Wareing were appointed to represent the parish at the Ruri-Decanal Conference.—A conversa- tion took place on the proposed,restoration of the church.— The Chairman said they had got nearly £l,OOO towards the work.

ST. MARY'S, GREAT SANKEY. The annual vestry meeting was hel4 on Monday after- noon, the Vicar (the Rev. E. S. Jackson) presiding. • There were also present Messrs. H. Bate (vicar's warden), William John Hatton (people's warden), Kerfeot. Peter Boardman, Richard Boardman, Cook,, D. Naylor, Alex. Thorpe, John Travis, and W. D. Jeans.—Mr. Cook contended that enffi- dent notice had not been given of the meeting, and that, therefore, lb would be illegal to hold it that day.—The Chairman thought three dear days' notice had been given. —Mr. Kerfoot did not think it advisable to hold the meet- ing if what they did could be subsequently upset.—Mr. Jeans said the notice which had been given of the meeting was not sufficient in point of law. But what did it all amount to ? These parochial proceedings had now been re- duced almost to nothing, as they had no church rate to levy. He knew other cases where notice had been giVen in the same way as the present, and the meeting had been held and no one had raised an objection.—Mr. Thorpe: Ia Sunday a dies nem ?—Mr. 'Jeans: Properly the notice ought to have been. put up yesterday week.—Mr. Hatton explained that it was put up on Thursday afternoon, last.—After some far- ther discussion, it was decided, on the motion of Mr. Cook, seconded by Mr. Kerfoot, that the meeting be held that day. —The accounts, which showed a balance in hand, were un- animously passed; and on tbe motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. Thorpe, a vote of thanks was accorded to the outgoing wardens.—The Chairman nominated Mr. Thos. Owen as his warden, and Mr. Hatton was re-elected people's warden; Messrs. Grange, Baker, Davidson,' and Safe, sides- men; and Messrs. Thorpe and Forster the repiesestatives at the ruri-decaeal conferences.
FRODSHAM PARISH CHURCH.

The Easter meeting in connection with Frodsham Parish Church was held in the Kingsley Chapel, at the Parish Church, Overton on Monday morning, when the Rev. H. B. Blogg, M.A., vicar, presided. The accounts of the churchwarelens for the past year were submitted. The total of the receipts was £475 Os 6d., and there was a balance of £l6 3s 2d.—The accounts were certified by the auditors as correct, and were passed.—The Vicar nominated Mr. A. Thomas as his warden for the ensuing year, and Mr. C. E. Linaker was unanimously re-elected as parishioners' warden. The following were appointed sidesmen, viz. :—Mr. H. Linaker, Mr. G. H. Danby, Mr. R. Bate, and Mr. J. Robin. son. The following report was read, viz. :—" The Tower Restoration Committee beg to report to the vestry that they have entered into an agreement with Mr. Thomas Davies, bailder, Frodsham, from the repair of the tower, re-setting the present battlements, cornice, and gurgoyles, and re hanging the bells, for the aim of £1,025, and to complete the same by the 30th November next. He bore up under the annoyance for a long time, but finally turned to her and said,-" That is a very bad cold of yours' madam." "But it is the very best I've gots" replied the lady sweetly. Tux Coox Kusw.--A Henry county farmer came to Clinton on the late cold wave wearing a euon-akin over- coat. A west-side grocer inquired, "Why don't yen wear the hairy aide in. instead outr "I reckon the coon knew which side was the warmest when he wore it, didn't he ?" teplied the farmer. HE KNEW MS_MEW.A minister in Scotland who had

bee—n—ne—wly settled in a rural parish gave great atis- faction to his new flock by reason of his remissness in what they caned " praying for the weather." At leacth a num- ber of them waited upon him and stated their grievance. Elt mceived them courteously, and said he was ye:7 anxiowi to perform all his duties to the best of his ability, but con- f assed that he was rather ignorant .of agricultural affairs and of the kind of weather favourable to the maturing of the various crops in which they were interested. "But," he tdded, "if you will all agree as to the kind of weather I should pray for, I will be most happy to do .so.; and, What is more, I will guarantee that you will get it !" "Who is that at the kitchen door ?" asked Mr. Jollilsin of bis young wife just after breakfast. "It's a beggar; and I'm bothered to death with them," she replied, as she got up to answer the man. "Wait a minute, my dear," &aid her husband; I'll arrange so that he won't trouble you any more." That's a darling!" she said lovingly. yea are always ready to help me." He went out, and in a few minEtes he returned. "Well," asked his wife "did you get rid of him ?" " YeS ; I gave him something to eat." "Oh, you shouldn't have done that! He'll be sure to come back and worry me more than ever !" she said petulantly. "Oh, no, he won't, love! I gave him a piece of that rake you made for breakfast." At a recent school examination such absurd answers as these were given—" Magna Charta was a great man, and he was called Magna Charta because he used to go about Preaching." Second bright boy: " Non." "That's right." First WY', indignantly: "That's just what I said !" div.head: CHURCH RESTORATION AT ROLLIN-
div.p: CHURCH RESTORATION AT ROLLIN-
FARE.

On Monday afternoon a sale of work was held at the school in connection with St. Helens Church, Hollin- _fare, in aid of the restoration ef the church. The Vicar (the Rev. G. F. Roberts), by energetic action, succeeded in raising by private donations about £l9O towards the restora- tion of the church, which is a comfortable and attractive- looking place of worship, and as the sum expended was £214 odd he determined, with the assistance of Mrs.l Roberts, to hold a sale of work to raise the amount required. The principal donors were Lord Winmarleieh, who gave £5O, and Lord Lilford, who gave £25. The Vicar's stall was under the charge of Mrs. Roberts, assisted by Miss Ratcliffe and Miss Allen; Miss Pye and Miss Brooks at- tended to the toy stall, and the refreshment stall was under the management of Mrs. Arthur G. Smith. The Mayor of Warrington (Alderman Harrison) opened the sale, which was not, during the afternoon, as well attended as might have been hoped.—The Vicar, prior to the opening cere- mony, made a few remarks, explaining the cause which originated the sale of work, and cordially thanking Alder- man Harrison for his presence. A year ago, he said, he was obliged to take further steps for the restoration of the church, owing to the fact that the gallery was unsafe, which was an immediate nec(.ssitv for actton being taken. • At the same time he determined to effect the decoratiou of the east end, and he had been well assisted by a number of gentle- men, who gave subscriptions. There now remained a balance to be raised of £l9 odd. As it was proposed to hold a bazaar for the improvement of the church yard and wall, he wished it to be clearly understood why a few weeks ago he determined to get up a small sale of work at Easter, with the understanding that it was to pay off the debt on the the church. He set to work to get up that sale independent of any further effort on behalf of the parishioners generally, in which he should hope to assist, towards carrying out the greater work—the restoration of the present burial ground. He then referred to the dilapidations on farmsteads con- nected with the living, and the money spent in the way of repairs. They were old and wretched buildings, and there was no fund to meet the constantly recurring expense connected with them; he could not, with the small income attached to the living go on defraying the constantly recurring expense, and he thought that from that sale of work if a sufficient sum were raised a nucleus of a fund might be formed. As the sale was to some extent for the purpose of relieving himself, he thought it would be the beet plan for him to bear the expense of getting it up. (Hear, hear.)—Alderman Hauutseme, in opening the sale, spoke of the excellent work of Mr. and Mrs. Roberts, and said that it was highly creditable to the people of that neighbourhood that they had such a church. It seemed unfortunate, he said, that in the Church of England there was a wide dis- proportion in the livings of various churches. Mr. Roberts had spent the best days of his life there, and the remunera- tion to him was a mere bagatelle—not worth talking about had he not private resources of his own. If they went a few miles away they found, perhaps, a rector enjoying £3OOO or £4OOO a year, who was not doing anything like the work of Mr. Roberts, and this they found all Over the country. It was a great pity that it should be so, and it was to he hoped that the true friends of the church, those who were within the church, would themselves endeavour to bring about a more equitable adjustment, a more just redistribu- tion, of the patronage of the church. Those who resisted these necessary reforms were the greatest enemies of the church, and he thought the greatest enemies were to be found within and not without the church. There were people who had ears to hear, and yet they would not hear. They would not take advice, or profit by experience, but went on their own way year after year, not lifting their fin- ger to effect such necessary reforms as would do away with the necessity of a clergyman like Mr. Roberts having to put his hand in his pocket to defray the almost necessary ex- penses of the church.—The sale, which was continued on Tuesday, was then proceeded with, and sufficient money was raised to clear off the debt.

A BIGAMOUS BAILIFF AT PRESCOT• SINGULAR REVELATIONS. At the Prescot Petty Sessions on Tuesday, before Lieutenant-Colonel F. W. Earle and Lieutenant-Col. W. W. Pilkington, George William Hardwick, alias William Roberts, was charged on remand with the desertion of his wife and four children, and he was also charged with bigamy. In the first-named case Mr. S. H. Hartley, clerk to the Board of Guardians, prosecuted, and Superintendent Barker conducted the prosecution for bigamy. Mr. Hartley said: A. warrant has been issued and executed for the apprehension of this man Roberts for deserting his wife and four children. Upon his apprehension it was discovered that he had a wife living in Leeds. He was married to a person now an inmate of the Workhouse in November, 1875, and that woman and her four children are now charge- able to the common fund of the Prescot Union. lam afraid I shall not be able to proceed against the man for deserting his wife and four children, seeing that he had a former wife living, and I believe the police purpose taking proceedings against him on a charge of bigaray. Superintendent Barker.: That is so. I shall have to prefer a charge against the prisoner' whose real name is George William Hardwick, and he is charged with having, on the 22nd November, 1875, at Pam- worth Parish Church, Widnes, married one Agnes ' Gregson, his former wife, Mary Jane Bracewell Hard- wick, to whom he was married at Leeds Parish Church on the .30th January, 1860, being then and now alive. The following evidence was then given : Mary Ann Whittaker, wife of George Whittaker, a horse dealer at Leeds, said she had known the pri- soner for 30 years. His correct name was George William Hardwick. She saw the prisoner married at Leeds Parish Church on 3othjanuary, iB6e, to her cousin, Mary Jane Bracewell White. Witness was invited to the wedding, and she saw the prisoner sign the register. After the marriage prisoner and his wife Bred together at Leeds, and there were five children born. The prisoner left his wife just before the fffth child was born in 1869. Since the prisoner left in 1869 his wife had conducted herself respectably, and had brought up her family respectably.—Agnes Col- line, an inmate of Prescot Union Workhouse, said that in the summer of 145 she went as a servant at a beer. house in Bridge-street, St. Helens, kept by William Tickle. The prisoner then lodged there, known by the name of George Roberts, and he was employed as a clerk. Soon afterwards he begin to court witnese, and on 22nd November, 1175, she was married to him at Farnworth Parish Church. In the register the prisoner signed his name as "George Robertg," and described himself as a "bachelor:" They lived together in St. Helens as man and wife until 3ist October last year, when he left her and her family without a penny. He was then employed as a °meaty Court bailiff, and 'keel been so employed for some time. There were four children born and she was now near coeffueent of fifth child. For some years after the marriage the prisoner treated her well except when he Wa€ " in drink." He often took drink. and she had to ,leave the house several times. She ,had also to pawn the clothes to get food for herself and family.—john Yates, a slater, living at No. I court, Eccleston-street, St. Helens, said he witnessed the marriage at Peen - worth Parish Church.--P.S. Bull said he bad that day charged the prisoner with the offence of bigamy, and: he replied " It's true. It's 'no use telling any liesi about it." Witness had also made extracts from the. registers in the parish churches of Leeds and Yarn-I worth, which he produced.—The prisoner, whO badl nothing to say, was then committed for tiial at-the; next Liverpool Assizes, and an application by tl-.3 pri• Boner to be allowed out on bail was refused.

I beg to protest against such" wickedness law-abiding portion of the community, have been in high places."--1 ours, etc. placed under arrest at different times, the appre- hension of Ope leading to investigations that caused others implicated to be discovered. The robberies have been carried on in a systematic manner for some-timer, and the seizure of about a cart load of goods at a lodging-house in Cloth Hall-yard indi- cates that the operations of the thieves haViii been large .Be4e• • Mrs Madden, wife of the occupant of the house, who was said to be the means of disposing of some stolen': goods,' by litettus of a second party whose- testithorty has been given in evidence., against her,, was ,promptly. put under arrest and the koodf) taken to the Police Station. A number of the articles thus seized proved to be the property of Mr. Joseph thrice, by whom they had been stored in a warehouse in the Eagle and Child yard, Bridge-street. As will be -seen from appended accounts, two youths, named Perci- val and Fleming, were yesterday morning committed for trial for stealing about £l5 worth of goods from that place, the property, sof Mr. Grice, whilst Mrs. ~ Madden was also comm4ted.fo take her trial.as an accomplice in' receiving the .goods. Percival, Who' seems to have taken a prominent part in the.bur7 glaries, was als6 `coMmitted yesterday on two other charges,' and-other- youths are in_ custody oil re- mand, awaiting -a hearing of the charges against them next Week. The police deserve considerable credit for their vigilan-4e, and the smart manner iii which they detected and captured some of the pri= soners. The prosecutions at the Borough Court yes- terday, were conducted by Mr..T. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk) on behalf of the police, and the female prisoner Madden was defended by Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, Warrington. Reports of the various cases are appended : WaIiEHOUSE BREAKING IN THE EAGLE AND CHILD-YARD.' At the Borough Court yesterday, before Mr. R. Garnett, Edward Percival,-atias Fay, alias Philips, described as a rag gethererzenti of no fixed abode; and Patrick Fleming, lanourer, were charged on remand from Monday with break- ing into a warehouse in Eagle and Child-yard, Bridge-street, and stealing a silk dress, a sealskin jacket, and a large quantity of wearing apparel, the whole of the value of £l5, the property of Mr. Joseph Grice, of 73, linutsford-road. Mary Madden, Cloth Hall-yard, was charged with receiving the same, well knowing them to have been stolen. Percival had been arrested on another charge, and Chief Constable Hunt. from i Mort-Intim received, had reason to believe that he was concerned in othe- charges. He was locked up, and, according to a statement made by Chief Constable Hunt at the first hearing on Monday, members of the borough police force went to the house of Mrs. Madden, the wife of John Madden, a labourer, who keeps a registered lodging-house in Clcth Hall-yard. and Mr. Grice, the prosecutor, also went with them. Mr. Grice had a long time previously had occasion to store a lot of goods, principally wearing apparel, which were placed in boxes in a werehouse in the Eagle and Child-yard. On the 15th April Mr. Grice went to the warehouse and fecund that four boxes had been broken open and a large number of articles stolen. At the house of Mrs Madden a considerable quantity of the stolen gee& were found. The police had also get possession of a lot more property that did not belong to him. When the case came on again yesterday Mr. Whittle briefly stated the ' case, and witnesses were then called. It was stated by Mrs Potter that at the request of Mrs Malden she pawned some of the articles produced, which were identified by Mr Grice as his property, and gave the pawn tickets and money re- ceived t,) Mrs Madden. Joseph Henry Houghton stated that some of the at ticles were pledged at his father's shop in Mersey-street, and Mary Ann Leach, a domestic servant, said that Mrs Madden asked her to take charge for her of a I silk dress and sealskin jacket, as her husband might want I her to pawn them, as he had no money. Witness took care I of them for her, and afterwards handed the articles to In- spector Soinks. Evidence was also given by the Inspector, who said that he asked Madden to give up everything Per- i rival and Fleming had brought to her, but she maintained that she bad not got anything. Afterwards she said to wit- ! eeee—e` 1-eew I shall go to prison. I'm quite as had as Teddy for not having turned the things no before" When on the way to the police station the female prisoner said to I P.C. Neill, "This is a bad job; I know I shall get 6 months. I wish I hid bad nothing at all to do with it, or had the I things in the house. I know he could not come honestly I by them. My husband knows nothing at all about them.'" A number of articles were found at Fleming's house. On Fleming being charged at the police station, he said that there was not half of the things the Constable had mentioned taken while he was with him (Percival); he only took a bagful, and some were rags. In ; the bag were two pincushions, a candlestick, pair of pincers, and a lamp, which he took home. Percival, on being charged, said " Yes, yes, that is correct; I toek all the rest," and turning to Mrs. Madden he said " What are you crying at; don't cry, I'll try and get you oat of it." Mrs. Madden said "I only gave Teddy a shilling in money for them, the rest has been taken out in food and lodgings. If I was only out ef here I'd jump into the river. My hus- band knows nothing about them." All three prisoners were committed for trial, and Mr. Browne applied for bail on be- half of Mrs. Madden, who, be said, was recently confined, and had also a child very ill.—Mr. Whittle did not object, and bail was fixed at two sureties in .£lO eech. At the same court, prsoner, Edward Percival, was charged on remand with breaking into the warehouse of Edward Whitehead, packing maker, Eagle and Child-yard, Bridge- street, and stealing twelve reels of sewing cotton, three knives, three pipes, and other articles, value 6s, his pro- perty.—Mr. Whittle said that the offence was supposed' to have been committed between the evening of Friday the 16th April, and Saturday, the 17th April. Mr. Edward Whitehead ha .l .a warehouse is Eag'.o and Child-yard, and on Friday one of his workmen saw the place locked up safely. Next morning it was found that the place had been broken ieto and a number of things missed. Prisoner was appre- hended with some of the stolen articles in his possession, and confessed to the theft. Evidence was given by Eliza. beth Taylor, who ia in the employ of Whitehead, and who spoke to locking up the warehouse on the evening of the 16th April; by Mr. Whitehead, who described the articles missing, and said that on Saturday morning, the 17th April, he found the warehouse very much upset, and saw a place where entrance had been effected; by Inspector Spinks, who said that at about noon on the 21st of April he saw prisoner in Bank-street and, as his pockets appeared bulky, stopped and searched him, finding some of the articles produced in his possession.—Prisoner was committed for trial at the next Liverpool Assizes. THEFT OF AN OVERCOAT. - Prisoner kdward Percival was also charged, yesterday, with stealing from the stable premises of Mr. Edward Con- nor, cab proprietor, Sankey-street, an overcoat, value 20s, the property of Albert Owen, a cab driver. Mary Madden, Cloth Hall-yard, was charged with receiving the same, well- knowing it to have been stolen. Mr. A. Browne defended Mrs. Madden.—ln stating the case, Mr. Whittle said that so far as regarded prisoner Percival it was a simpler one than the last, and be thought they would have no difficulty in committing him. He also thought that the evidence would be sufficient to warrant the Bench in committing Mrs. Mad- den. On the 12th February information was received by the police that the overcoat had been stolen from the stable premises of Mr. Connor, in Sankey-st..Percival was subsequen- tly charged with the theft, and said "Yes, Neale knows where I took it from; it was Connor's yard." He lodged with Mrs. Madden, and it appeared that she, on the 3rd March, gave the cost in question to a woman named Potter, who would be called as a witness' to pledge for her. Mrs. Potter got 5s on the coat, and Mrs. Madden gave her Lid for her services. Witnesses were then examined in support of the charge, and Mr. Browne' in defence of Mrs. Madden, called a youth named Monoghan, who swore that prisoner Per- cival himself rave him the coat produced, and gave him 3d for pledging it. This, however, was denied by Mrs. Potter on her being recalled. MIL GLADSTONE'S BILLS AND THE IRISH I PROTESTANTS Sir,—Much opposition is being raised to Mr. Gladstonee Irish Bills on the ground of the danger which they are said to threaten to the Protestant minority of Ireland. The Tories, the self-constituted defenders of our Protestant faith, who moved heaven and -earth to secure the Catholic vote at the recent election are shouting themselves hoarse in condemnation of Mr. Gladstanes "treacherous purpose" to band over the Irish Protestants to the tender merc:es of the Catholic majority in Ireland. It is true that it what they have done" were "done by" them, Irish Protest- ants might look forward with justifiable misgivings to the revolution which is about to be accomplished. To the ignorant and savage screechings of malevolent Tories, _how- ever, no reasonable, man pays any attention; but it is a fact that men of the stamp of Lord Hartington do see, or fancy they see, a serious menace to Protestaut interests in Ireland in the realization of Mr. Gladstone's proposals. In his weighty speech to his constituents the other day, Lord Hartington laboured hard to impress his hearers with this sense of danger. Indeed, about half of the speech is com- posed of reflections on this part of the question. Now it is to the reasonings of thoughtful men like Lord Hartington that every. Liberal, every Englishman, is bound to give Intl attention. Tory declamations oferleap themselves, with the usual reauli; but to the voice of reason all serious men attend, The question I. wish briefly to deal with is this—Are the privileges—religion!, social. politicel, commercial—now. en- - joyed by the Protestants of Ireland likely to be curtailed or even endangered her 010 whieu te proposed to Con- g...' *bo matt people ? I answer with a simple nega- tive. The fear is a groundless one, as I think will appear front the following considerations :—The clergy and people of Ireland—l mean of course the Catholic population—are practically at one in the demand for Home Rule. But it is a mistake to think that the Irish people seek to be freed from Protestant rale as each,. Doubtless it was so in earlier stages of that rule, eg , the early post-Revolution times. But now the opposition is to-English rule as such; to the domination of Saxony, of Englishmen. The English name is execratei in Ireland. That the :English are Protestants aggravates the discontent Is true, but it is not the prime cause of it. The opposition of the Irish clergy is another thing. In their case I think it Is true that the secret of in- tense dislike to English rule is profound hatred of Protestantism. Bat priests and people are united in the demand for a !separate government.for Ireland. So that on the one baud we have the great majority of the Irish people with their clergy demanding Home Rule; on the other the Protestant minority opposing it. It is therefore argued by Lord Harlington and others that the history of religious parties in Ireland warrants the assumption that the oppressed and persecuted majority will, as soon as it is invested with power, expend the pent up vengeance of cen- turies upon the heads of the defenceless minority. But Lord Hartington assumes what cannot be granted for a single moment. He assumes a perpetually united Row in Catholic Ireland. He ignores the fact that the preeent state of unity is a historical and not an ideal product. Catholic Ireland is united by a cry ; when the cry is listened to and answered the process of party formation will set in. How does Lord Hartington suppose that Ireland will govern itself if not upon nasty lines? He argues on the supposition that in the Irish House of C :lemons the Government will be Roman Catholics, the Opposition Protestant. Now I think an appeal to history settles the question for us. Government by the people and priestcraft have never none together. Priests have often led people in the attack upon aristocratic privi- leges; but, popular freedom and government attained, the privileges and claims of the priesthood have been the next to undergo popular examination. It was so in France at the Revolution ; it has been so in Italy in more recent tia) s. And when the Spanish working classes have anything ap- proaching the franchiee the privileges of the priests will have to stand in the light. So will it be in Ireland. When the Irish people have got their Parliament, into thorough working order, and when they understand how thoroughly they are enfranchised, the complete political union of priests and people will rapidly disappear. Instead of an united Catholic majority in the Irish Parliament there will be most likely a clerical and an anti-clerical party. Now it is in this state of things that the future strength of the Irish Protestants will lie. Each of the contending Catholic par- ties will bid for the Protestant vote, and the Protestants will practically he able to make their own terms. There is no stronger position for any party to occupy than to be the balancing party; and there is no way in which minerities, or clasees, or sects have secured their rights so frequently as by making their help indiepensable to one or other of the great parties in the State. To go no further back than the late Stuarts, we have ample proof of this. The history of Non- conformity is a history of party exigences; Nonconformist rights have been the rewards for Nonconformist help. Statesmen do not as a rule trouble themselves with griev- ances of minorities from a deep sense of the injustice to which those minorities are subjected; but in reward for services rendered, or to still an inconvenient cry, "See what the unjust steward said)." The very question of Home Rule would have been left for a future century to settle but for the obstructive tactics of the Home Rulers and the mas- terly balancing policy of Mr. Parnell. And until these processes of dlfferentiation and integra. tion have been completed the Irish Protestants have innu- merable safeguards. So secure, indeed, is their position that the additional safeguards suggested by Mr. Gladstone are unnecessary. For many years Ireland will be absorbed in mastering her new constitution. The Catholics will be on their best behaviour; anxious to create as favourable an impression as possible in the minds of the people of Europe. The Protestants are immeasurably more wealthy than the Catholics, and history forbids us to believe that the wealth owning few are in a position of disadvantage in a free coun- try; and political economy chimes in "especially in a coun- try engaging in 'Free Trade." Further, the people who entrust their dearest and most sacred interests to a Protestant—Mr. Parnell—cannot be justly suspected of an intention to deal unrighteously with those who profess the same faith. And lastly. I believe that the day of religious persecution is over even in Ireland. England, with her million charities, her enlightenment, her power, is too near and too closely united In multitudinous ways with Ireland for us to look with misgiving upon the coming day. And if all these con- siderations fail to convince us, surely we may find assurance and peace in our knowledge of the Irish character—the warmth of heart, geniality, sterling honesty that mark the simple native of the Emerald Isle. And no man who recalls our past history can deny to the Irishman his fair share of the glory wbih attaches to it. or for a moment doubt the loyalty and patriotism of a people who have so freely given up their sons to fight our battles; of whom it might be said—

Home Runs You SCOTLAND.—A meeting of the Scottish Land Reform Alliance, lately the Fanners' Alliance, was, held in Aberdeen on Saturday, at which Mr. Eselemont, M.P.delivered a speech dealing with the prospects of laisti legislation. The Chairman of the Alliance believed that a Scottish Parliament was the only medium through which Scotland would get her legislative requirements attended to. A motion was put in the following terms :—" That before proper measures can be passed in settlement of the land question, this committee is of opinion that England, Scot- land, Ireland, and Wales, while retaining their share in the administration of Imperial matters, shoild each have a National Parliament for administering its own local affairs." The proposal was carried. TRAGEDY AT NOTTINGRAM—At Nottingham, on Satur- day night, James Walker, a carter, murdered one of his children. Of late his wife had contracted habits of intem- perance and neglected her children. On Saturday, in her &b-' sence, Walker undressed and put to bed his three children, aged respectively eight, six, and three years, and then went out. On returning home shortly before eleven o'clock, he found his wife still away, and thereupon resolved, as he subsequently stated, to murder his children, and then com- mit suicide. Carrying the youngest child to his own TOOIII he cut its throat, but his nerve then failed him, and he raised an alarm which resulted in the discovery of the crime and Walker's arrest. He had, however, inflicted a wound in his own throat, and his conduct at the time of his ape, prehension and since has been violent. Walker is 42 years' of age. See Advt. • DROWNAD IN WESTON CANAL. On Monday, at the Weaver Hotel, Weston Point, Mr. J. E. Worsley, deputy coroner, held an inquest touching the death of John Coran, a native of Teignmouth, and formerly seaman on board the schooner Rare Plant. On the night of the 3rd April the de- ceased was in Runcorn, and at 11 o'clock was seen going in the direction of Weston Point, where the echeoner lay. His dead body was found in the Weston Canal near No. 2 lock on Friday afternoon. A verdict of found drowned was returned. The jury commented in strong terms upon the unprotected state of the canal at the point where the de- ceased fell into the water. It was stated that that was the third inquest which had been held during fifteen months upon seamen who, going down the canal bank, had fallen into the canal at this extremely dangerous point. A rail 20 yards in length would, it was said, provide adequate pro- tection. A presentment was made that the Bridgewater Navigation Company should be asked to protect the canal at No. 3 lock by placing a rail there. A Loc..km RACH FOR £.5O.—A match which appeared to create considerable interest, as it attracted about 700 persons, was decided on Saturday afternoon at the Star Inn Grounds, St. Helens. The men engaged were Peter Anders and Charles Dilliway, both of St. Helens, and their engage- ment was to run 150 yards for £25 aside. They had pre- viously opposed each other on the same track, namely, on the INh December last, when Dilliway, who was conceded one yard start in 120 was declared the winner by a foot. Excitement ran high as the men wended their way to the mark at six o'clock in the evening, each being heartily cheered and encouraged by their respective partisans. An- ders was made favourite, and the betting closed at 6 to 4 on him. A capital start was effected. For about 30 yards the pair ran closely together, when Anders began to draw away. He was well in front at the half distance, and eventuallv won by three yards. The track was in excel- lent condition and the men had a strong wind at their backs.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 1, 1886.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 1, 1886.

DISORDERLY FOOTBALL MATCH AT EARLESTOWN._.. —On Saturday week a scandalous scene was witnessed during the course of a football match between the Earles- town Olympic and Sankey Refiners (Earlestown) teams, and which was being played in a field near Crow-lane Glass Works. The particulars were fully stated at the Newton , Town Hall on Saturday, When before Messrs. R. Houghton and T. J. Gillespie, Patrick Toutity was summoned for as- salting William O'Hara. The defendant, who was repre- sented by Mr. A. Browne, pleaded not guilty. Mr. Knowles I appeared for the complainant.—Mr. Knowles stated that the assault was committed on a football field on the previous Saturday. when the complainant O'Hara was acting as I umpire for the Sankey Refiners, who were playing the Earlestown Olympic. Daring the game some dispute arose as to the ball being "fouled," and the complainant, as um- pire. gave his decision upon it. Two players offered to strike the complainant, and the crowd of spectators rushed on the field. The players in question and the crewd were ordered off and while this was going on the defendant came behind complainant and without any provocation struck him on the head with a new pick shaft, inflicting a severe wound. The complainant had not spoken te defendant, nor had he given any provocation. He produced a medical cer- tificate that the complainant had a wound two inches long. It was a very severe injury, and he ((r. Knowles) asked the Bench to inflict a severe penal ty.—The complainant, William O'Hara, whose head was plastered, then gave evidence in support of Mr. Knowles' statement. He added that the dispute arose about a free kick for "hands." His bead was badly cut, and he lost a great quan- tity of blood. He had been off work for a week. The wound had to be dressed by a doctor.—ln reply to Mr. Browne, complainant said he was perfectly ;ober, and he I did not use any bad language to :the Olympic players, nor did he threaten them. A man named I..emond also struck him, and he (complainant) then pulled his coat off to de- fend himself.—William Jones, labourer, Sankey Sugar I Works, gave corroborative evidence. He said the complain- ant was perfectly sober. Witness was not a player, but a ' spectator.—James Murray, labourer at the Sugar Works, and Thomas Corcoran, labourer at Havdock collieries, also corroborated.—For the defence, Mr. Browne said the defen- dant had lived at Earlestown for about twenty years, during which time he bad never been charged with any offence, nor had any complaint been made against him at that court. Alluding to the dispute on the field, Mr. Browne said O'Hara bad been objected to as umpire because he was drunk, and that when the spectators rushed on the field O'Hara began hitting right and left.—The defendant strongly denied that be wilfully struck the cpmplainant, and said that he was merely pmehing him with it to draw his attention, and ask him to desist, when the complainant, who was jumping about the field, knocked his head against it.—John Turton deposed that O'Hara was jumping up and down the field, using "all sorts of language."—Martin Touhey (brother of the defendant) gave similar evidence.— The Chairman said the defendant would be fined 20s and costs.—Mr. Knowles applied for an order for the defendant to defray the complainant's advocate fee and the costs of the witnesses.—The Bench ordered the defendant to pay the advocate's fee, and also is to each of the witnesses.

div.head: WIDNES VESTRY MEETINGS.
div.p: WIDNES VESTRY MEETINGS.

PARISH CHURCH AND ST. PAUL'S. The annual vestry meeting of the Widnes Parish Church was held on Wednesday night, at the .National Schools, Waterloo-road, Widnes. The Rev. J. Wright Williams pre- sided. Mr. F. Neil, vicar's warden, presented the statement of accounts. He said that at St. Mary's Church they com- menced the year with a balance in hand of £34 3s 7d. The offertories had realised the sum of £99 14e id, making the total income £133 183 6d. The total expenditure was £126 193 2-W, leaving a balance in hand of £6 193 Itd. The largest items of expenditure were in respect to repairs to the organ and to the roof of the church. At St. Paul's they commenced the year with a deficit of £33 33 W. Includ- ing this amount, the total expenditure had been £B9 17s Bid. Ihe offertories had yielded the sum of £B6, which left them with a deficit of only £3 17s 811—The accounts were passed, on the motion of Mr. W. Treacy, sen., seconded by Mr. F. Beattie.—The Vicar mentioned- that since April 30th, 1885, they had distributed to the poor the 9um of £5O 12s 8-.14. The receipts amounted to £43 23 7d, so that there was a slight deficit. They had also collected for the Church Pastoral Aid Society £3l 5s (3d, Additional Curates' Aid Society £lB lOs Id. Curates' Fund £6B is 96, and for the Society for the Propagation of Christianity amongst the Jews £4 4s 9d. The Vicar re-appointed Mr. F. Neil as his warden.—On the motion of Mr. J. Farrant, seconded by Mr. F. Cave. Mr. L. Kilcross was appointed parishioners' warden , Upon the election of Church Council coming forward, Mr. Dickson complained that many persons of the Temperance Society in connection with the church), whilst occupying a good proportion of tbe space of the churches, contributed very little to its support. He thought those who so con- spicuously represented the branch institution should have more care for the maintenance of the church, and should at least sensibly assist in contributing to the funds by taking and paying for seats in the church.—The Chairman said he should like the speaker and everybody else to know that the falling off in pew rents at St. Mary's had only been the legitimate outcome of the conduct of the present Vicar of the parish—an outcome that he expected from the first, and which he was quite content to face—and especially as those who were interested last Sunday made up the offer- tories in one day to over £4O for the Vicar, he thought be would be content to rely upon the efforts of the hearts of his parishioners. (Applause.)—While considering the appoint- ment of the Church Council, Mr. Kilcross proposed the name of Mr. Dickson, but that gentleman declined to stand, —The Vicar then appointed the following sidesmen : Messrs T Hughes, J Williams, T Showan, F H Pankhurst, W Treacey, senior, C Jones, T Atherton, A Edwards, W Lowe, F Beattie, Hewitt, and Pemberton. The vestry ap- pointed the following :—Messrs J Lord, F Cave, John Far- rant, H N Wharton, W Dwerry house, 13 Balmer. T Bruce, C Watson, John Matthews, J Beach, William Chadwick, and D J Brookes —Messrs J B Imison and H N Wharton were unanimously appointed to represent the par- ish at the ruri-decanal conference.—On the motion of Mr. Hewitt, and seconded by Mr. Imison, Mr. W. Chadwick was re-appointed vestry clerk. ST. AMBROSE CHURCH. , The annual vestry meeting was held on Thursday night. The Rev. S. H. Spooner, vicar, occupied the chair, and there were present—Messrs. John Valentine, T. A. Bullough, Jno. Goff, Joseph Williams, Thomas Menton, W. S. Callender, it. Riley, and James Edwardson.—Mr. R. Riley, the trea- surer, submitted a statement of accounts which showed a total income for church expenses of £5B 7s 56, and an ex- penditure of £56 17s 16, leaving a balance of £1 108 46. For the clergy fund there had been received by offertories £56 Os 9d, by donations £45, and by subscriptions from the secretary £2l 16s. There had been collections for many ob- jects. The gross income of the church having been £257 Os 106, against £244 8s lid in the previous year.—The Chairman re-appointed Mr. E. Carey as his warden, and on the proposition of Mr. Minton, seconded by Mr. Williams, Mr. Valentine was eleeted people's warden. The following were appointed aidesmen :—Messrs. T. A. Bullough, S. Kidd, D. W. Hunter, John Goff, R. Riley, Wm. Smith, H. Johnson, R. Mercer, T. Minton, W. Carthe, Wm. Hill, Jas. I Edwardson, S. Upwards, T. Forster, Jos. Williams, Hy. Lea, , and G. I. Neil.—ln answer to questions, the Chairman said the bishop had stated that there was a possibility of the en- dowment of the church being taken into consideration at the end of the year.—Messrs. T. A. Bullongh and John Gaff were appointed lay representatives.

PR,ESCOT. A CRICKET MATCH was played on Easter Monday between the 2nd Eleven of Wavertree and and Eleven of Prescot, on the Prescot ground, resulting in in easy victory for the home team. Tau WAYWARDEN FOR WHISTON--At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, before Lieutenant-Colonels Earle and W. W. Pilk;ngton, Mr. Henry Cross, clerk to the Prescot Highway Board, intimated that at the next Petty Sessions he should apply for Mr. James Sumner to be appointed waywarden. THE SI7PPORT OF A MOTHER.—WiIIiaIII Sumner, labourer, Widnes, was summonei at the Preec.ot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, to show cause why.an order should not be made upon him to contribute towards the support of his aged mother, at present in. receipt of parish relief. Mr. S. H. Hartley, clerk to the Prescot Guardians, prosecuted, and ap- plied for an order of is 6d per week.—An order for the amount named was made. Vicronie PLACE CHAPEL.—On Easter Monday the an- nual tea meeting was held in this school-room. About 80 persons sat down to a substantial tea, to which ample justice was done. The ladies presiding at the tables were Mrs. Mather, Mrs. Johnstone, Mrs. Appleton, the Misses Stockley, and Miss Abbott. After tea a service of song entitled " Dickery " was rendered by the choir in a very efficient manner. Mr. W. L. Duncan's reading of the service was all that could be desired; and Mr. M. Hayes ably conduc- ted. A very pleasant eveniag was brought to a close by the usual votes of thanks.

PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The first meeting of the members of the Prescot Board of Guardians after the recent triennial election was held at the Union Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday forenoon, when there were present the Rev. T. Chambers, Rey. Father Finegan, Rev. C. W. Wool!, Messrs. John Lowe, J. Jackson, W. Birchall. .I. Buckley, W. G. Ashton, J. Griffiths, W. Daine, J. Kenwright, W. Tyrer, J. W. Wareing, C. B. Johnson, J: Leatberbarrow, J. Fisher, W. Gerrard, J. Mat- thews, F. Syder. P. Middlehurst, J. Whalley, R. Tuson, T. F. Hill, W. Swift, J. Ellison, W. Middlehurst, J. Ranson, ' H. Hulme, W. B. Longton, H. Heald, and S. H. Hartley (clerk). APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN AND TIOR-CHAIRMAN.-- Mr. J. Leatherbarrow, the past chairman, was appointed chairman Pro t—The Chairman said the first business was the appointment of chairman be the ensuing year.— The Rev. T. Chambers moved that Mr. J. Lowe be appoin- ted chairman.—Mr. Birchall seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously.—Mr. Lowe thanked them for the compliment, and saki it would be his duty to do the best he could, and he hoped with the assistance of the Board he would be able to conduct the business as it had been hither- to conducted. (Hear, hear.)—On the motion of Mr. Leatherbarrow, seconded by Mr. Bucholey, Mr. J. Fisher was elected senior vice-chairman, and on the motion of Mr. Matthews, seconded by Mr. Jdekse,n, Mr. Wm. Birchall wes elected junior vice-chairman.—Mr. Fisher and Mr. Birchall briefly returned their thanks. Tgg STANDING ONDINS.--011 she MOUOLI of Zdr. Tyre',
Lord Redesdale's condition last evening caused consider• able anxiety.

Stoke Park Mouse. near Stoke, occupied by Lord Clon- curry, has been burned to the ground. Tha Guion liner Wyoming, which arrived at Queenstown on Friday, reports having passed several ilehergs in the Atlantic.
Mr. J. Earnest Groaves, proprietor of the Festiniog Quarries, has been appointed Lord-Lieutenant of Carnar- vonshire.
It is stated in New York that Herr Most. the well-known Socialist, is in hiding in order to avoid being arrested for having in a recent speech advised his audience to take up arms.

Mr. Jefferson Davis delivered another speech to his Southern friends, on Thursday, to an immense audience, in which he jusiifind the secession of the Southern States, and the stand made for their rights and liberties. CtiIIRCH BRAWLING,—The magistrates at Wombourne, Dorset, on Friday sentenced two boys named William Phillips and David Harris each to 14 days' bard labour for church brawling. The boys are said to have diiturbed the congregation by shouting and laughing in the church porch at the village of Talbot, near Poole, last Sunday. The sentence has caused considerable feeling ha the district.

THE HOME_ RULE QUESTION. A declaration has been signed by the Archbishop and every priest in the archdiocese of Cashel expresskg a deep sense of gratitude to Mr. Gladstone for his many signal services to their country—notably for the disestablishment of the Protestant Church, for the Land and Franchise Acts, and for the great and abiding interest he has evinced in everything that can tend to progress and pacification in Ire- land.

A conference of representatives of Scottish Liberal Asso- ciations was held in Glasgow on Friday, when the constitu- tion of a National Liberal Federation for t-cotland was adopted. Mr. Gilbert Beith, M.P., who presided, said they were in the midst of a national crisis. The question for the nation was whether they were to listen favourably to the claim or keep the old road and coerce Ireland into obedi- ence. Mr. Beith expressed himself in favour of Mr. Glad- stone's policy.

GREAT FIRE IN MANDA LAY. The Viceroy telegraphs to the India Office that a fire broke out in Mandalay at daylight on the 29th ult., and, on account of the violent wind, extended a considerable dis- tance. The origin of the fire is unknown. THE POPE AND THE EMPEROR WILLIAM. ROME, FRIDAY.—Tbd POpe yesterday despatched a letter in very cordial terms to the Emperor William, thanking his Majesty for his recent gift of a pictorial cross as a sou- venir of his Holiness s mediation between Germany and Spain in the Caroline Islands question. PRINCR: ALEXANDER.

PIIILOPPOPOLIS, Fatner.—A Te Deum was sung in the Cathedral this morning to celebrate the anniversary of Prince Alexander's accession to the Bulgarian throne. The Prefect, acting on the Prince's behalf, subsequently held a reception. The city will be illuminated this evening.

RELIEF Comstryrszs.—The -reneraalitees for the various townships were appointed. tv"l— HELENS AND WIDNES RELIEF CASES.—The Clerk suggested the new Board should take into consideration the question of allowing :it. Helens and Widnes relief cases to be investigated before the committees in those towns, so as to save poor people the trouble of visiting the Workhouse. He thought a satisfactory system might be arranged though it would incur a little•extra cest.—The Rev. T. Chambers thought it an admirable suggestion--The Clerk: The same thing will apply to Woolton.—Mr. Fisher thought it would be a great advantage.—Mr. C. B. Johnson asked what the I expenses of the proposed alteration would be. In principle it seemed everything that could be desired.—The Clerk replied that the cost would be a matter for inquiry. At Woollen they would have to engage a room which would pro- bably cost about 2s 6d a week, and they would have a little expense in sending the books there. At Widnes and St. Helens they had relief offices, and the applications might be dealt with there.—Mr. Dame: If these arrangeinents are made how long will they be binding ?—The Clerk: The Guardians can put an end to it at any time. After further discussion the Clerk promised to formulate a scheme and bring it before the next Board meeting.

div.head: TEE GREEK-REPLY TO THE ULTIMATUM.
div.p: TEE GREEK-REPLY TO THE ULTIMATUM.

ATHENS, FRIDAY.—The reply of Grsece to the ultimatum of the Powers is as follows :—" The Greek Government, referring to its Note of the 26th inst., despatched prior to the delivery of the collective Note of the Powers on the same day deems it necessary to add the following explana- tions. The Royal Government having accepted the coun- sels of France, as stated in the above mentioned Note, and having thus given before presentation of the collective Note a formal assurance that Greece, yielding to the desire of the Powers, would not disturb the peace, it follows as a conse- quence that the Greek Government will not keep under arms the present effective strength of the army. The Govern- ment will, therefore, proceed to make a gradual reduction of this effective strength in such times as may be required by the prudence indispensably necessary for carrying out a measure of this kind.

The Central News learns that the Note addressed by the Greek Government to the Powers is not considered a reply to the Ultimatum. The Powers insist upon an unconditional promise of immediate disarmament.
WARRINGTON DRAMATIC SOCIETY-

On Thursday evening the first of a series of three performances in aid of the funds of the"Warrington Infirmary giVen by the members of' the War- rington atic Society in the Plitslie Hall:- The ' piece selected for representation was Mr. T. W. Robertson's comedy, "Caste," which proved a very happy selection. 'There was d'good attendance, the., reserved seats being. well filled, tho Ugh in the gal- leries and pit there were some Vacant spaces. The characters were allotted amongst the Members of , the society as follows :—Hon. George talroy,' Mr. w. E. Atkin; Captain Hautree, Mr. T. Manners Smith; Eccles, Mr. J. E. Davies; Sam. Gerridge, Mr. J. T. Picton Dixon (servant to D'Alroy), Mr. A. Browne; and these were assisted, by the following ladies :—Miss Edmiston as the Marqpise de St. Maur; Miss Kate Hodson as Polly; and. Miss Maud Robertson as Esther. Judging from. the suc- cess of the performance, a more jiidicious dis- tribution of parts could not have been made. . As the hero and heroine, of the play, Mr. Atkin and Miss Robertson. had somewhat trying parts to sustain, but both are to, be congratu- lated on the manner in which they acquitted them- selves. Miss Robertson, in particular, was exceed- ingly effecthe on several occask.ns, andi notably so in the pathetic passages in. whicll she buckles on her but lately married husband's sword, and after- wards reads the condoling letter from Captain Hautree on the supposed loss of her husband in his encounters with the Sepoys in India. Miss Robert- son was frequently and deservedly applauded. It is, of course, no discredit • to say that Mr. Atkin did. not altogether avoid amateurishness, his utterances and movements were at times. somewhat hasty, if not embarrassed, but on the whole he filled his im- portant part with much credit. Mr. Smith very happily caught and maintained the supremely non- chalant air and manners of the aristocratic believer in caste, Captain Hautree, whose encounters with the lively and irrepressible Polly were continual sources of amusement. Mr. Davies undoubtedly scored a triumph in his representation of the bibu- lous Eccles. From hoginnin to end he seemed to thoroughly enter into the spirit of the thing. His. acting was singularly unlike Wing, and the realistic. touches he threw in were peculiarly mirth-provok- ing. The part of Polly could not have had a better ,interpreter than Miss Hodson, whose acting was p,.-tr- haps the most admirable feature of the performance. ;Miss Edmiston was a capable exponent of the role of , Marquise de St. Maur, and Mr. J. T. Picton, as Sam erridge, undoubtedly contributed in no small de- gree to the success of a very successful entertain- ment. That the performers carried their audience with them was evidenced by the frequent applause, and on several occasions they were called before the curtain. The stage arrangements were admirably super intended by Mr. Jos. Davies. In the course of the evening several selections were excellently ren- dered by a large orchestra under the co-.aductorship of Mr. W. S. Woods. Last oirening Mr. H. J. Byron's popular comedy "Our Boys" was performed to a full house. The characters were taken as follows :--Sir Geoffrey Champneys, Mr, It. G. Fox; Talbot Champneys, Mr. A. Woods: Perkyn Middlewick )Ir. I. Davies ;

'She Pubtishars, in submitting the Pro- spectus of the Fifth Edition of the Direetory of this County, respectfully hope for a continuance of the patronage of their former subscribers. The work will contain a topographical account of each Parish, Village. Hamlet. and Township. with its distance from London and other chief towns. its position in the Division of the County under the " Redistribution of Seats Act, 1885." Hundred and Union. and County Ciurt'District,'and also the Diocese, Archdeaconry and Rural Deanery; the Population from the census of ; Description of the Churches, with the Value of the Living, and the names of the Patron and In- cumbent; the chief Landowners ; the Acreage. notice of Soil and Crops Local Charities, and description of the Principal Bests In the towns are also given a short historical account, particulars of the Local Clovernment ; an Archi- tectural Description of the Churches and other Public Buildings, Chapels of Different Denominations; Public Schools; a full account of the Principal Manufactures of which each town is the seat; the Markets, Fairs, and Races; Agricul- tural and Soientific Societies and Meetings, &C.; Objects of Natural Curiosity and Antiquities ; Hospitals, Almshouses and Charities. The Directory of each town comprises Lists of the Resident Clergy, and entry, and also a List of all engaged in Professional and Mercantile Pursuits. in Alphabetical Order. w HIS AFFECTIONATE MAMMA'S DESIRE.—A lad was found guilty of a serious infraction of discipline, and was directed by his teacher to tell his mother when he got home what misdemeanour he had committed. The neat morning the schoolmarm called Johnny to her desk, when the following dialogue ensued; "Well, Master Johnny, did you inform your mother what infraction of discipline you were guilty of yesterday, and the reprimand and punishment you re- ceived ?" "Yes'as," was the sententious reply. " Well, and what did your mother say ?" "She said she'd like to wring your neck for you." No more discipline reports were sent home to that mother. SHE WASN'T A PORTESS.—Judge Dusenberry took tea at the Sykes Mansion on Fifth-avenue ose night last week. Conversing with Miss Sykes, Judge Dusenberry remarked: "I am delighted, Miss Sykes, with the poetry of your friend, Miss Skimmerhorn, but, of course, you yourself don't write poetry." "How do you know that I don't write poetry ?" replied Miss Sykes, somewhat piqued, for she has written a number of poems for publication. "I know you are not a poetess, because as a rule, all ladies who write poetry are very homely." "You are quite right, Judge Dusenberry," replied Miss Sykes, with great dignity, "the cares of the household precludes me from cultivating the muses, even if I were ever so much disposed to do so." This DISCOVERY OF AMERICA.—This story comes from a school in the Midlands. The master told the boys of the third class to write a short essay upon Columbus. The fol- lowing was sent up by an ambitious essayist—" Clumbus was a man who could make an egg stand on end without breaking it. The King of Spain said to Clambus, Can you discover America ? "Yes,' said Clumbus, if you will give me a ship.' So he had a ship, and sailed over the sea in the direction where he thought America ought to be found. The sailors quarrelled, and said they believed there was no such place. But after many days the pilot came to him and said, 'Clumbus, I see laid:" Then that is America!' said Clumbus. When the ship got near, the land was full of black men. Ciambus said, 'ls this America?' • Yes, it is,' said they. 'Then,' he said, 'I suppose you are the niggers ? ' -Yes,' they said, 'we are.' The chief said, 'I suppose you are Clumbus?' 'You are right, said he. Then the chief turned to his men and said, There is no help for it; we are discovered at last!' "
